Build a simplified DDR3 or LPDDR4-style controller with a scheduler and refresh, verified with a cocotb testbench. Use Ramulator 2.0 or DRAMSim3 to compare scheduling policies. The FPGA board can then serve as the tester for the SRAM chip when it returns from the fab.

Phase Duration Work 0 Ramp-up 1–2 months Install tools, simulate 6T SNM, run OpenRAM 1 Circuit design 3–4 months Bitcell, periphery, timing; corners and Monte Carlo 2 Layout and verification 2–3 months DRC/LVS, extraction, post-layout corners, BIST RTL, test interface 3 Tapeout 1 month Integration, final checks, submission 4 While in fab 3–6 months KiCad test PCB, FPGA tester firmware, controller project 5 Silicon measurement 2–3 months Functional test, shmoo plots, Vmin, access time, leakage, correlation with simulation 6 Publish – GitHub release; conference papers (for example VLSI Design or VDAT in India)

From skills to jobs.

Skill shown by the project Matching job Bitcell and periphery design, Monte Carlo, Vmin Memory circuit design engineer (Intel, AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, Synopsys and Cadence memory-compiler teams) Layout, DRC/LVS, extraction Custom / memory layout engineer .lib characterisation Library / characterisation engineer BIST, test chip, measurement DFT / silicon validation engineer Controller RTL, cocotb or UVM-style verification RTL / design verification engineer (the largest hiring area) A real shuttle tapeout A rare differentiator for a fresh graduate

Many memory design teams are based in India, notably in Bengaluru and Hyderabad.

Honest limits

SRAM on 130 or 180 nm processes runs at roughly 100 to 300 MHz: industry values the methodology and the measurements, not the raw speed. Open DRC and LVS decks are accepted on open shuttles, but industry signoff uses Calibre. Fabrication access (shuttles, prices, providers) changes quickly.

docs.title: 17.3 Can a 4 GB RAM be designed with open-source tools?
docs.text:
A common question from students: could I design a complete 4 GB RAM myself with free tools? It depends on what "a 4 GB RAM" means.

Meaning Open tools? Manufacturable? A 4 GB RAM chip No No: no open DRAM process exists, and SRAM would be far too big A 4 GB module or board using commercial DRAM chips Yes: KiCad Yes: any PCB fab and assembly house A 4 GB memory system (your own controller and DRAM) Yes: LiteDRAM, Verilator, FPGA tools Runs on a real FPGA board

The short answer is: not as a single chip; yes as a module built from commercial DRAM chips; and yes as a memory system with your own controller.

Example 17.1: The area maths of a 4 GB chip

Without a DRAM process, the only memory one could build on an open PDK is SRAM. A quick calculation shows why that cannot reach 4 GB.

  1. 4 GB in bits: \(4 \times 2^{30} \times 8 = 34.4\) billion bits.
  2. SKY130 6T bitcell area: about 2 µm². With about 60 per cent array efficiency, the area per bit including periphery is about \(2/0.6 = 3.3\) µm².
  3. Total silicon area: \(34.4 \times 10^{9} \times 3.3\ \mu\text{m}^2 = 1.14 \times 10^{11}\ \mu\text{m}^2 \approx 114{,}000\ \text{mm}^2\), about 115,000 mm² or 1150 cm².
  4. The reticle limit (the largest single chip a scanner can expose) is about 858 mm² (26 × 33 mm), so \(114{,}000/858 \approx 133\): about 130 or more maximum-size chips.
  5. A 200 mm wafer has an area of \(\pi \times 100^2 = 31{,}400\) mm², so \(114{,}000/31{,}400 = 3.6\): about four full wafers of pure memory, and the yield of a maximum-size die at 130 nm is low without redundancy and repair.
  6. Compare a commercial 1β DRAM: its 1T1C cell is about 0.001 µm², roughly 2000 times smaller per bit than the SKY130 SRAM cell. A full 4 GB fits on a single DRAM die of very roughly 60 to 80 mm² (an estimate) that costs a few dollars to make. Array efficiency, the fraction of die area that is actual memory cells rather than decoders, sense amplifiers and wiring, matters as much as cell size.

How much SRAM does fit on open silicon?

Silicon available Area Approx. SRAM capacity One Tiny Tapeout tile ~0.016 mm² A few hundred bytes A typical shuttle slot ~10 mm² ~300 KB A full reticle-size chip ~858 mm² ~30 MB 4 GB – ~130 times the biggest possible chip

A realistic silicon target is therefore 1 KB to a few hundred KB, which is exactly what industry SRAM test chips look like anyway.

Option 1 (recommended): a 4 GB DDR4 SO-DIMM in KiCad. You can design a complete, working 4 GB module with open tools by using commercial DRAM chips: four 8 Gbit x16 DDR4 chips (from Micron, Samsung or SK hynix) give 4 GB in a single 64-bit rank (\(4 \times 16 = 64\) bits; \(4 \times 8\ \text{Gbit} = 32\ \text{Gbit} = 4\) GB). Add an SPD EEPROM, decoupling capacitors and termination resistors on a 6 to 8 layer impedance-controlled, length-matched PCB. The tools are KiCad for schematic and layout with length tuning and differential pairs; basic signal-integrity simulation with vendor IBIS models in KiCad's ngspice simulator; optionally openEMS for field-solver analysis; SPD contents written to the JEDEC SPD specification and verified with Linux decode-dimms; a functional test in a laptop or mini PC with Memtest86+; and fabrication files (Gerbers, drill, BOM, pick-and-place) for a PCB fab offering impedance control and BGA assembly. Antmicro has published open-source KiCad designs for DDR4 SO-DIMMs and DRAM test boards, which make excellent references. The difficulty is medium to hard, and a prototype costs a few hundred dollars.

Option 2: a memory system with your own controller. Use LiteDRAM as the reference design, simulate with Verilator and cocotb, explore policies with Ramulator 2.0, and run it on an ECP5 FPGA board with the Yosys and nextpnr flow. The controller design is the same for 128 MB or 4 GB: capacity comes from the DRAM chips, not the controller.

Option 3 (stretch): gain-cell eDRAM on an open PDK. A gain-cell eDRAM uses two or three ordinary transistors (2T or 3T) and stores charge on the gate of one of them instead of on a dedicated capacitor. Like DRAM, the charge leaks and must be refreshed, so you can measure retention time on real silicon, an active research topic. A classic 1T1C cell built with the MIM (metal-insulator-metal) capacitors available on these PDKs is impractical, because the capacitors are far too large.

Figure 17.1. Three combined open-source projects: an SRAM test chip (with a gain-cell eDRAM stretch) using Xschem, ngspice, Magic, KLayout, OpenRAM and LibreLane on a shuttle; a 4 GB DDR4 SO-DIMM in KiCad with openEMS and Memtest86+; and a memory controller on an FPGA using Verilator, cocotb, Yosys, nextpnr and Ramulator

Together the three projects cover the chip, the module and the controller.

docs.title: 17.4 Working with a systems partner
docs.text:
A memory design effort needs more than a fab. A systems partner, such as an Indian server maker that does not make chips, fills two other gaps: compute infrastructure for running EDA tools, and a system partner and customer, so that memory designs reach real servers. It cannot supply fabrication, PDKs or foundry bitcells, EDA licences, DRAM dies, or packaging and chip testing. The current products and capabilities of any named company should be confirmed with the company itself, as with every vendor and product named in this part of the book.

Figure 17.2. The memory product value chain: design (EDA on partner compute), fab (TSMC, GF or open PDK), package and test (OSATs), module or board (PCB fab and assembly) and system (servers and AI clusters), with the partner helping at design and system stages

India's ecosystem is growing around the middle stages too: Micron's assembly and test plant at Sanand, Gujarat, and Indian OSAT projects from Tata, Kaynes and CG Semi.

Sizing the compute.

Project CPU cores Big-memory servers Storage GPUs Open-PDK SRAM test chip 64–256 Not needed (256–512 GB fine) 10–50 TB Not needed TSMC N7 SRAM macro / compiler (10–30 engineers) 500–2000 2–4 with 1–2 TB 100–500 TB Optional TSMC N7 LPDDR5X / DDR5 controller and PHY (50–150 engineers) 2000–10,000 5–10 with 2–4 TB 0.5–2 PB Useful Full memory-centric SoC / AI accelerator 10,000+ 10+ with 4 TB Multi-PB Yes

An on-premise, isolated cluster run by a trusted partner can meet the strict security requirements of advanced-node PDKs more easily than a general-purpose cloud account.

Product opportunities.

Product What you design Feasibility CXL memory expander card CXL controller chip (N7 plus licensed PHY) and a card PCB with DDR5 High DDR5 RDIMM / MRDIMM made locally Module PCB, SPD, thermal design (DRAM dies bought in) Very high; the most achievable, no custom chip Memory-rich AI accelerator Large SRAM or compute-in-memory chip (N7) Medium; large effort, high impact SRAM compiler IP Compiler at N7 / GF 22FDX High; an IP business Memory test / validation platform Rowhammer, reliability, error-rate and CXL testing on real servers Very high; low cost, publishable Memory tiering software (DRAM, CXL and SSD) Linux kernel / runtime High; software only HBM / DRAM chips – Not possible; needs a DRAM maker

A phased roadmap: phase 1 (0 to 12 months) builds the team and methodology with an open-PDK SRAM test chip, an FPGA controller and a KiCad DDR4 or DDR5 module; phase 2 (6 to 18 months) delivers a first product with no custom chip, a DDR5 RDIMM qualified on partner servers, and a memory test platform; phase 3 (12 to 30 months) targets advanced-node silicon, a low-Vmin SRAM macro or compiler on a TSMC N7 shuttle; phase 4 (24 to 48 months) builds a system chip, a CXL memory expander controller or an SRAM or compute-in-memory AI accelerator. Still not possible: your own DRAM chip (DDR5, LPDDR6 or HBM DRAM dies) or NAND. The realistic route there is partnership with a DRAM maker, since HBM base dies are increasingly co-designed with customers. Programmes such as the India Semiconductor Mission and its Design Linked Incentive (DLI) scheme and the C2S programme support design and tapeout funding.

docs.title: 17.5 The toolbox and where to go next
docs.text:
The exercises of this book can all be done with free, open-source tools; the industry uses commercial equivalents, and knowing both helps when applying for jobs. The toolbox is:

A few first commands, to try each core tool in five minutes (the chip tools run best on Linux or WSL2):

R1 in out 1k
C1 out 0 1p

.control

ngspice rc.cir
kicad-cli pcb drc board.kicad_pcb
kicad-cli pcb export gerbers -o fab/ board.kicad_pcb

Three paths into the memory industry. Memory circuit design: SRAM cells, sense amplifiers and timing (Exercises 2.5, 2.6 and 15.6); employers are memory-compiler teams, CPU and GPU companies and DRAM makers' design centres. Board and signal integrity: module and motherboard design, high-speed signals and power (Exercises 12.4, 12.5, 13.5, 14.4 and 14.5); employers are module makers, server and PC companies. Controllers and verification: memory controllers in Verilog, testbenches and FPGA prototypes (Exercise 3.5); the largest hiring area in chip design.

docs.title: 17.6 Summary
docs.text:
• DRAM is a market of about USD 130 billion or more; DDR is about 40 per cent of revenue, LPDDR 25 to 30, HBM 20 to 30 and rising; SK hynix, Samsung and Micron lead, with CXMT rising.
  • The best open-source route to real RAM silicon is an SRAM macro test chip on an open PDK plus an FPGA controller; DRAM and the LPDDR6 PHY cannot be built with open processes.
  • A 4 GB SRAM chip would need about 115,000 mm², about 130 maximum-size chips; a 4 GB module (four 8 Gbit x16 DDR4 chips) can be designed in KiCad, and a memory system with your own controller can run on an FPGA.
  • A systems partner can supply compute and a path to market, not chips; the most achievable product is a locally made DDR5 module.
  • Three career paths: memory circuit design, board and signal integrity, controllers and verification.

docs.title: 17.7 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 17.1. How much SRAM fits into a 10 mm² shuttle slot at 3.3 µm² per bit, and how many bytes is that? Compare with the table in Section 17.3.

Answer

\(10\ \text{mm}^2 = 10^{7}\ \mu\text{m}^2\), and \(10^7/3.3 = 3.03 \times 10^{6}\) bits \(= 379\) KB. The table gives "about 300 KB", which allows for the pad ring and test circuits that take part of the area.

Exercise 17.2. Four 8 Gbit x16 DDR4 chips make a 4 GB module. How many chips would you need for an 8 GB single-rank module, and which chip organisation gives a 64-bit rank?

Answer

With 8 Gbit x16 chips, four chips give 64 bits and \(4 \times 1\ \text{GB} = 4\) GB. For 8 GB in one rank, use 16 Gbit x16 chips (four chips again), or eight 8 Gbit x8 chips for 8 GB (eight x8 chips give 64 bits, \(8 \times 1\ \text{GB} = 8\) GB).

Exercise 17.3. Run the RC netlist of Section 17.5 (R = 1 kΩ, C = 1 pF, a pulse from 0 V to 1 V lasting 5 ns). What is the time constant, and how close does the output come to 1 V within the 5 ns pulse?

Answer

\(\tau = RC = 1\ \text{k}\Omega \times 1\ \text{pF} = 1\) ns. After 5 ns the output has reached \(1 - e^{-5} = 0.993\) of the final value, about 0.993 V. After one time constant it reached 63 per cent.

Exercise 17.4. The module project of Chapters 11 to 14 uses KiCad, ngspice, Python, pytest and an automatic router. To which of the three career paths does each skill contribute: (a) writing the SPD checksum code; (b) simulating the termination study; (c) simulating a sense amplifier; (d) writing a cocotb timing checker?

Answer

(a) Board and signal integrity (module firmware and test data). (b) Board and signal integrity. (c) Memory circuit design. (d) Controllers and verification.

Exercise 17.5 (Assignment 14: capstone, pick one). Do real engineering on an open problem. Options: (a) solve the module's DRAM via fan-out (Section 14.2) as an integer program with scipy.optimize.milp; (b) plan a 1 KB SRAM test chip with a built-in self-test (March C−) and a measurement plan for Vmin and access time; (c) design a 4 GB DDR4 SO-DIMM in KiCad from an open reference design. Deliver code or design files plus a two-page report.

Answer

Success criteria: (a) every ball gets a via site and the tests pass; (b) the plan names every block and test; (c) design-rule check reports 0 violations, with a length-matching report. For (b), the March C− test is the sequence: up the addresses write 0; up: read 0, write 1; up: read 1, write 0; down: read 0, write 1; down: read 1, write 0; down: read 0. Scope it so you can finish it: a small finished project beats a big unfinished one.

docs.title: Chapter 4: The SRAM Family
docs.text: SRAM is the fastest memory that exists, and it needs no refresh. It is built from ordinary logic transistors, so it can sit on the same chip as the processor. Its weakness is size: each bit needs several transistors, so SRAM costs far more silicon area per bit than DRAM. This chapter surveys the variants of SRAM, from the six-transistor cell inside every cache to the content-addressable memories in network routers, and shows how each trades speed, density, power and interface simplicity. For each one it states how it works, its strengths and weaknesses, and where it is used.

docs.title: 4.1 6T SRAM
docs.text:
The six-transistor cell of Section 2.2 is the workhorse. Two cross-coupled inverters form a latch and two access transistors connect it to a bitline pair. To read, both bitlines are precharged high, the wordline is raised and a sense amplifier detects which bitline starts to fall. To write, strong drivers force the bitlines to opposite values and overpower the latch.

Strengths. Very fast, well under a nanosecond for small first-level cache arrays; no refresh; made in the same process as the logic.

Weaknesses. Six transistors per bit make it many times larger than a DRAM cell, and SRAM cell area has shrunk only slowly at the newest process nodes (Section 15.6). Idle cells still leak current. Reading must not flip the cell and writing must flip it, and these goals conflict as supply voltage drops.

Where it is used. Registers and register files, the L1, L2 and L3 caches of processors and graphics chips, GPU shared memory, on-chip buffers in AI accelerators and network chips, and stacked cache dies such as AMD's 3D V-Cache.

docs.title: 4.2 8T and 10T SRAM
docs.text:
An 8T cell adds a two-transistor read port to the 6T cell. A separate read wordline and read bitline sense the stored value through a buffer transistor, so a read never disturbs the latch. 10T designs add further transistors, for example for a differential read port or to allow reliable operation near the transistor threshold voltage.

Strengths. Read stability and write ability are designed separately, so the cell works at much lower supply voltages. The separate ports allow one read and one write in the same cycle, which suits register files.

Weaknesses. The cell is noticeably larger than 6T and needs extra wiring per cell, and the peripheral circuits are more complex.

Where it is used. Register files in processors and graphics chips, multi-ported buffers, and ultra-low-power chips for wearables and the Internet of Things that run at very low voltage to save energy.

docs.title: 4.3 Asynchronous SRAM
docs.text:
This is a standalone SRAM chip with no clock. The system places an address on the pins, asserts chip-enable together with output-enable (to read) or write-enable (to write), and the data is valid after a fixed access time: typically tens of nanoseconds for standard parts and around 10 ns for fast ones.

Strengths. Extremely simple to connect to a microcontroller, FPGA or older processor; predictable timing; low-power versions can retain data on a small battery for years.

Weaknesses. Slow and low in bandwidth by modern standards; small capacities (kilobits to tens of megabits); expensive per bit compared with DRAM.

Where it is used. Older embedded systems, industrial controllers, battery-backed configuration storage, retro computers and FPGA prototyping boards.

docs.title: 4.4 Synchronous SRAM
docs.text:
In a synchronous SRAM, inputs and outputs are registered on a clock edge. Pipelined versions add an output register for a higher clock speed; flow-through versions give data one cycle sooner. Burst modes read consecutive addresses automatically, and "zero bus turnaround" variants remove idle cycles when switching between reads and writes.

Strengths. Much higher throughput than asynchronous SRAM, and timing that is easy to fit into a clocked design.

Weaknesses. More pins and power; a shrinking niche because large on-chip SRAM has replaced most external caches.

Where it is used. Networking line cards, lookup tables in telecom and test equipment, and the external second-level caches ("pipeline burst cache") on PC motherboards of the 1990s.

docs.title: 4.5 QDR SRAM
docs.text:
Quad data rate SRAM has separate read and write data ports, and each port transfers data on both clock edges. Two words in plus two words out give four transfers per clock cycle. Because reads and writes never share a bus, there is no turnaround penalty, and fully random accesses run at full speed.

Strengths. A very high random-access rate with low, fixed latency, ideal when every access goes to a different address.

Weaknesses. Expensive, power-hungry, small in capacity and with many pins.

Where it is used. Packet lookup tables, flow statistics counters and queue pointers in routers and switches, and radar and other signal-processing equipment.

docs.title: 4.6 PSRAM (pseudo-static RAM)
docs.text:
Inside, PSRAM uses DRAM 1T1C cells, but a built-in controller refreshes them automatically, so the outside world sees a simple SRAM-like interface with no refresh commands. Modern parts often use a serial interface (quad SPI or 8-bit octal) with very few pins.

Strengths. Much denser and cheaper than SRAM, typically a few megabytes in a tiny package, with a very simple interface.

Weaknesses. Slower than true SRAM; an access that collides with an internal refresh can take longer; standby current is higher than that of SRAM.

Where it is used. Microcontroller boards such as ESP32 modules with a few MB of PSRAM, IoT devices that drive displays or buffer audio, and older mobile phones, where it was sold as "cellular RAM".

docs.title: 4.7 1T-SRAM
docs.text:
Developed by MoSys, 1T-SRAM uses a one-transistor DRAM cell but hides refresh and row management behind an SRAM-style interface, using many small banks so that refresh rarely gets in the way of an access.

Strengths. Several times denser than 6T SRAM while keeping SRAM-like, predictable latency.

Weaknesses. It needs licensed technology and process support and is largely a historical design today.

Where it is used. The Nintendo GameCube (main memory plus embedded memory in its graphics chip) and the Nintendo Wii.

docs.title: 4.8 TCAM (ternary content-addressable memory)
docs.text:
Normal RAM takes an address and returns data. A content-addressable memory works the other way round: you present a search key, every stored entry compares itself with the key in parallel, and the memory returns the address of the first match in a single operation. "Ternary" means each stored bit can be 0, 1 or X ("don't care"), so one entry can match a whole range, such as an IP prefix like 192.168.x.x. Each cell needs storage for the value and the mask, plus comparison logic.

Strengths. Constant-time lookup no matter how large the table is; ideal for longest-prefix matching and rule tables.

Weaknesses. Very high power (every entry is compared on every search), large area and high cost.

Where it is used. Routers and switches for IP route lookup, access-control lists and quality-of-service rules. Simpler binary CAMs also appear inside processors, for example in the translation lookaside buffers (TLBs) that translate virtual to physical addresses.

Example 4.1: A tiny TCAM lookup

A router table holds three entries, kept in order from the most specific to the least specific. A bit shown as X matches either value. For clarity the keys are written as dotted decimal, where x means all eight bits are X.

Entry Stored pattern Meaning Output port 1 10.1.2.x one subnet A 2 10.1.x.x a larger block B 3 x.x.x.x everything else C

Search for 10.1.2.7. All three entries compare at the same instant, and entries 1, 2 and 3 all match. The memory returns the first (highest-priority) match, entry 1, so the packet goes to port A. A search for 10.1.9.4 matches entries 2 and 3 only and returns B; 172.16.0.1 matches only entry 3 and returns C. Because the entries are ordered from longest prefix to shortest, "first match" is the same as "longest prefix match", which is what routers need.

docs.title: 4.9 SRAM family summary
docs.text: Type How it works Where it is used 6T SRAM 6 transistors per bit, no refresh needed CPU and GPU caches, registers, on-chip buffers 8T/10T SRAM Extra transistors for a separate read port and low-voltage stability Low-power chips, register files Asynchronous SRAM No clock, simple interface Older embedded systems Synchronous SRAM Clocked interface Networking, legacy caches QDR SRAM Separate read and write ports, 4 transfers per clock Network packet lookup PSRAM DRAM cell with built-in refresh and an SRAM-style interface Microcontrollers (ESP32), IoT, older phones 1T-SRAM DRAM cell behind an SRAM interface Nintendo GameCube and Wii TCAM Searches all entries at once by content Routers and switches (IP route lookup)

docs.title: 4.10 Summary
docs.text:
• SRAM is the fastest memory and needs no refresh, but costs the most area per bit.
  • Variants differ in cell (6T, 8T, 10T), interface (asynchronous, synchronous, QDR) and cell type behind the interface (PSRAM and 1T-SRAM hide DRAM cells).
  • 8T cells protect the latch from reads with a separate read port, and so work at lower voltage.
  • QDR separates read and write buses to give four transfers per clock without turnaround.
  • A TCAM compares all entries in parallel and supports "don't care" bits, giving constant-time longest-prefix lookup at a high power cost.

docs.title: 4.11 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 4.1. Why can PSRAM look like SRAM from outside although it is built from DRAM cells? What does it give up compared with true SRAM?

Answer

A built-in controller refreshes the 1T1C cells on its own, so the system never sends refresh commands and sees an SRAM-style interface. In return PSRAM is slower than true SRAM, an access that collides with an internal refresh can take longer, and standby current is higher. What it gains is density and cost: a few megabytes in a tiny, cheap package.

Exercise 4.2. Explain in two sentences why an 8T cell can work at a lower supply voltage than a 6T cell.

Answer

In a 6T cell the same access transistors are used for reading and writing, so read stability and write ability pull against each other as the voltage falls. An 8T cell reads through a separate two-transistor read port that never disturbs the latch, so the two goals can be designed separately.

Exercise 4.3. Choose the best SRAM type for each need: (a) a processor's first-level cache; (b) a router's per-packet lookup table where every access goes to a different address; (c) matching an IP address against a list of prefixes in one operation; (d) a microcontroller needing a few megabytes at low cost with few pins.

Answer

(a) 6T SRAM on the processor die. (b) QDR SRAM, with separate read and write ports and no turnaround penalty. (c) TCAM. (d) PSRAM with a quad or octal SPI interface.

Exercise 4.4. Using Example 4.1's table, which port does the address 10.2.0.1 go to, and why?

Answer

Entry 1 (10.1.2.x) needs the second number to be 1, so it does not match. Entry 2 (10.1.x.x) also needs the second number to be 1, so it does not match. Entry 3 matches everything, so the packet goes to port C.

Exercise 4.5. A QDR SRAM has two data ports, each 18 bits wide, on a clock of 400 MHz (a supposed figure for this exercise). Each port transfers on both clock edges. Find the data rate of one port and the total transfers per clock cycle.

Answer

One port makes 2 transfers per clock, so \(2 \times 400 = 800\) MT/s, and with 18 bits \(800 \times 18 / 8 = 1800\) MB/s \(= 1.8\) GB/s. Two ports (one read, one write) make \(2 + 2 = 4\) transfers per clock cycle, hence "quad" data rate; read and write together reach 3.6 GB/s, with no turnaround penalty because they never share a bus.

docs.title: Chapter 1: What RAM Is and Why There Are Several Kinds
docs.text: This chapter lays the groundwork for everything that follows. It explains what random-access memory does, how a bit and a byte relate to the capacity figures on a box, why computers stack several kinds of memory into a hierarchy, and how the family of RAM technologies is organised. It then defines the vocabulary of speed: clock frequency, megatransfers per second, bus width, bandwidth and latency, with the two formulas that every memory engineer uses daily. Later chapters use these terms without further comment, so it is worth working the examples here with a pencil.

docs.title: 1.1 What RAM is
docs.text:
Random-access memory is memory in which any location can be read or written in about the same time, no matter which location was used last. The processor gives the memory an address, a number that names a location, and the memory returns or stores the data held there. This is different from a tape or a spinning disk, where reaching data that is far from the current position takes much longer. In a computer, RAM holds the programs and the data the processor is working on right now, while slower storage (an SSD or a disk) holds everything else.

A kitchen is a useful picture. The processor is the chef, the SSD or hard disk is the pantry, huge but far away, and RAM is the counter next to the stove: smaller, but everything on it can be reached at once. Before cooking, ingredients are brought from the pantry to the counter. In the same way every program and file that is opened is copied from storage into RAM first. More RAM means more things can be open at once without the machine slowing down, in the way that a bigger counter lets the chef work on several dishes together.

Almost all RAM is built from millions or billions of tiny storage cells, each holding one bit. The cells are arranged in a grid of rows and columns. A horizontal wire called the wordline (WL) selects a row, and vertical wires called bitlines (BL) carry data in and out of the cells of that row. Small amplifiers at the edge of the array, the sense amplifiers, detect the very small signals on the bitlines and turn them into clean 0s and 1s. The next two chapters look inside these cells and this grid in detail.

Typical amounts are a few gigabytes to a few tens of gigabytes in a laptop or desktop and one to four terabytes in a large server.

docs.title: 1.2 Bits, bytes and capacity
docs.text:
A bit holds one of two states, 0 or 1, like a light switch that is off or on. Eight bits make a byte, which has \(2^8 = 256\) possible patterns, enough for one letter of text. Every photograph, song and program is a very long row of such switches.

The size of the numbers involved is easy to underestimate. A memory module that stores 32 GB of data holds \(32 \times 2^{30} \times 8 = 2^{38}\) bits, which is about 275 billion switches. Each one is a tiny electric charge that must be read and rewritten correctly, millions of times per second.

Example 1.1: How many cells in 32 GB?

  1. 1 GB of DRAM is \(2^{30}\) bytes, so 32 GB is \(32 \times 2^{30} = 2^{5} \times 2^{30} = 2^{35}\) bytes.
  2. Each byte is 8 bits \(= 2^3\), so the total is \(2^{35} \times 2^{3} = 2^{38}\) bits.
  3. \(2^{38} = 274{,}877{,}906{,}944\), about \(2.75 \times 10^{11}\), or roughly 275 billion bit cells.

Two unit conventions are used throughout the book. Capacity of memory is binary: a "gigabyte" of DRAM is \(2^{30}\) bytes, and chip sizes in gigabits (Gb) are binary multiples too. Bandwidth is decimal: 1 GB/s is 1000 MB/s. Mixing the two is a common source of small arithmetic errors, so units are always stated.

docs.title: 1.3 The memory hierarchy
docs.text:
No single memory is fast, large, cheap and low-power at once, so computers combine several. Small, very fast memories sit close to the processor and hold the data used most often; each level farther away is larger and cheaper per bit but slower. Hardware and software move data between the levels automatically, so most accesses are served by the fast levels. Figure 1.1 shows the levels as they stood in 2026; the numbers are typical orders of magnitude, not exact values for any particular machine.

Figure 1.1. The memory hierarchy as a pyramid: registers, SRAM caches, HBM or DRAM main memory, CXL far memory, SSD storage, with typical latency and capacity at each level

Registers and caches are SRAM, built inside the processor. Main memory is DRAM, the main subject of this book. A newer tier, CXL memory, sits between local DRAM and storage; it is DRAM reached over PCIe-style wires and is described in Chapter 8.

The gaps between levels are so wide that a logarithmic scale is needed to draw them. Figure 1.2 repeats the typical times and adds a second reading: if one processor step took one second, how long would each fetch take?

Figure 1.2. A log-scale bar chart of the time to fetch one piece of data: CPU register 0.3 ns, L1 1 ns, L3 10 ns, DRAM 80 ns, NVMe SSD 80 microseconds, hard disk 8 ms, each with its value scaled to a one-second processor step

The scaled figures make the point vividly. If a register access takes about one second, a DRAM access takes more than four minutes, an SSD more than three days and a hard disk about ten months. A processor that had to wait for storage on every access would spend nearly all its time idle. DRAM is roughly a thousand times faster than an SSD (80 ns against 80 µs), and that is why the working set of a program is kept in RAM.

docs.title: 1.4 Volatile and non-volatile memory
docs.text: Volatile memory loses its contents when power is removed. SRAM and DRAM, the two technologies behind almost all working memory, are volatile. Non-volatile memory keeps its data with the power off. Flash memory, used in SSDs and USB sticks, is non-volatile but is not true RAM: it is written in large pages, erased in even larger blocks and wears out after a limited number of writes. A family of emerging non-volatile RAMs (MRAM, FeRAM, ReRAM, phase-change memory) tries to combine RAM-like byte access with non-volatility; Chapter 9 describes them.

docs.title: 1.5 The RAM family tree
docs.text:
Figure 1.3 groups every memory covered in this book. The volatile branch splits into SRAM (on-chip memories and small standalone parts) and DRAM, which itself branches into families tuned for different goals: capacity and cost (DDR), power (LPDDR), per-pin speed (GDDR) and raw bandwidth (HBM). The non-volatile branch holds the emerging memories plus NVDIMMs, which combine DRAM with flash.

Figure 1.3. A tree with RAM at the top, splitting into volatile (SRAM and DRAM branches) and non-volatile (MRAM, FeRAM, ReRAM, PCM, NVDIMM)

A quick table fixes the personalities of the main families before the later chapters study each one in turn.

Type Personality Where you find it Speed today (approx.) DDR5 The all-rounder: big capacity, plug-in modules Desktops, servers 4800 to 8800 MT/s per pin LPDDR5X The energy saver: low voltage, soldered next to the processor Phones, thin laptops, Apple Silicon Macs 8533 to 10,700 MT/s per pin GDDR7 The sprinter: very fast pins, runs hot Graphics cards 28 to 32 Gbps per pin HBM3E The skyscraper: 8 to 12 dies stacked, 1024 wires wide AI accelerators about 1.2 TB/s per stack SRAM The pocket notebook: tiny, fastest, no refresh Caches inside every processor about 1 ns access

docs.title: 1.6 Speed terms: MHz, MT/s, Gbps and bandwidth
docs.text:
Memory speeds are quoted in several units that are easy to confuse.

  • Clock frequency (MHz) is how many clock cycles occur per second. Modern memory moves data on both the rising and the falling clock edge, so the clock number is half the data rate. Marketing labels such as "DDR5-6400" give the data rate, not the clock.
  • MT/s (megatransfers per second) counts how many times per second each data pin carries a new symbol. DDR5-6400 runs at 6400 MT/s on a 3200 MHz clock.
  • Gbps per pin is the same idea in larger units, used for very fast interfaces. 32 Gbps per pin for GDDR7 means 32,000 MT/s. With multi-level signalling a transfer can carry more than one bit (Section 3.4).
  • Bus width is how many data pins move in parallel: 64 bits for a standard DDR DIMM, 16 bits per LPDDR5 channel, 32 bits per GDDR chip, 1024 or 2048 bits per HBM stack.
  • Bandwidth is the total data moved per second: data rate multiplied by bus width.
\[\text{Bandwidth (GB/s)} = \frac{\text{data rate (MT/s)} \times \text{bus width (bits)}}{8 \times 1000}\]

Example 1.2: Peak bandwidth of one DDR5-6400 DIMM

  1. Data rate 6400 MT/s on a 64-bit bus: \(6400 \times 64 = 409{,}600\) megabits per second.
  2. Divide by 8 bits per byte: \(409{,}600 / 8 = 51{,}200\) MB/s.
  3. Divide by 1000 to get GB/s: 51.2 GB/s.
  4. A desktop with two such channels has a peak of \(2 \times 51.2 = 102.4\) GB/s.
  5. Real programs typically reach 70 to 90 per cent of the peak, because of refresh, bank conflicts and switching between reads and writes. For the dual-channel desktop that is about 72 to 92 GB/s.

For per-pin rates in Gbps the answer comes out directly in GB/s when multiplied by the width and divided by 8, which is how GDDR and HBM figures are usually worked.

docs.title: 1.7 Latency: CAS latency and nanoseconds
docs.text:
Latency is the delay between asking for data and receiving it. The most quoted number is CAS latency (CL): the number of clock cycles between a column read command and the first data appearing. Because the clock gets faster with each generation, CL has to be converted to nanoseconds before parts can be compared. The clock in MHz is half the data rate in MT/s, and one clock cycle lasts \(1000 / \text{MHz}\) nanoseconds, so a cycle lasts \(2000 / \text{data rate}\) nanoseconds. Hence

\[\text{CAS latency (ns)} = \frac{\text{CL} \times 2000}{\text{data rate (MT/s)}}\]

Example 1.3: The same ten nanoseconds twice

  • DDR4-3200 CL16: \(16 \times 2000 / 3200 = 10\) ns.
  • DDR5-6000 CL30: \(30 \times 2000 / 6000 = 10\) ns.
  • DDR5-4800 CL40: \(40 \times 2000 / 4800 \approx 16.7\) ns.

The first two answers are identical. The DRAM array has barely become faster in twenty years, so the extra speed of each generation goes into bandwidth and not into latency. The full time for a random access from a processor (cache miss, controller queueing, opening a row, CAS and the trip back) is typically 60 to 120 ns, much more than the CAS figure alone.

Do not compare CL numbers across generations

A DDR5 module with CL40 is not slower than a DDR4 module with CL16 in the sense the numbers suggest. Always convert to nanoseconds first.

docs.title: 1.8 Summary
docs.text:
• RAM gives any location about the same access time; it holds what the processor is working on, while storage holds the rest.
  • A bit is one of two states; a byte is eight bits; 32 GB of DRAM holds about 275 billion cells.
  • The memory hierarchy exists because speed, size and cost pull in opposite directions. DRAM is about a thousand times faster than an SSD; caches are built from SRAM.
  • RAM divides into volatile (SRAM, DRAM) and non-volatile families; flash is not true RAM.
  • Bandwidth is data rate times bus width divided by 8 (decimal units); peak figures are never fully reached.
  • CAS latency must be converted to nanoseconds: \(\text{CL} \times 2000 / \text{MT/s}\).

docs.title: 1.9 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1.1. A laptop has 16 GB of DRAM. How many bit cells is that, in powers of two and approximately in decimal?

Answer

\(16 \times 2^{30} \times 8 = 2^{4} \times 2^{30} \times 2^{3} = 2^{37}\) bits \(= 137{,}438{,}953{,}472\), about \(1.37 \times 10^{11}\) or 137 billion cells.

Exercise 1.2. Compute the peak bandwidth of a single 64-bit DDR5-4800 DIMM and of a dual-channel DDR5-6400 desktop. By what factor is the second larger?

Answer

DDR5-4800: \(4800 \times 64 / 8 / 1000 = 38.4\) GB/s. Dual-channel DDR5-6400: \(2 \times 51.2 = 102.4\) GB/s. The ratio is \(102.4 / 38.4 \approx 2.67\).

Exercise 1.3. Convert to nanoseconds and rank the three modules: DDR4-2400 CL17, DDR5-5600 CL36, DDR5-6400 CL32.

Answer

DDR4-2400 CL17: \(17 \times 2000 / 2400 = 14.17\) ns. DDR5-5600 CL36: \(36 \times 2000 / 5600 = 12.86\) ns. DDR5-6400 CL32: \(32 \times 2000 / 6400 = 10.0\) ns. From lowest latency to highest: DDR5-6400 CL32, DDR5-5600 CL36, DDR4-2400 CL17.

Exercise 1.4. DRAM takes about 80 ns to fetch a value and an NVMe SSD about 80 µs. If one processor step took one second, how long would each fetch take? Use 0.3 ns for the step.

Answer

The scale factor is \(1\,\text{s} / 0.3\,\text{ns} = 3.33 \times 10^{9}\). DRAM: \(80 \times 10^{-9} \times 3.33 \times 10^{9} = 267\) s, about 4.4 minutes. SSD: \(80 \times 10^{-6} \times 3.33 \times 10^{9} = 267{,}000\) s, about 3.1 days. The ratio is 1000.

Exercise 1.5 (Assignment 1: a bandwidth and capacity calculator). Write a small Python script with two functions, bandwidth(mts, width_bits) returning GB/s and capacity(chips, gbit_per_chip, ecc_chips) returning the data capacity and the raw capacity in GB. Use them to print a table for DDR5-4800 and DDR5-6400 on a 64-bit bus and for a module of 20 chips of 16 Gb of which 4 are ECC chips.

Answer 

def bandwidth(mts, width_bits):
    """Peak bandwidth in GB/s (decimal)."""
    return mts * width_bits / 8 / 1000

def capacity(chips, gbit_per_chip, ecc_chips):
    """Return (data GB, raw GB); 1 GB = 8 Gb."""
    raw = chips * gbit_per_chip / 8
    data = (chips - ecc_chips) * gbit_per_chip / 8
    return data, raw

for rate in (4800, 6400):
    print(f"DDR5-{rate}, 64-bit: {bandwidth(rate, 64):.1f} GB/s")
print("module:", capacity(20, 16, 4))
Expected output: DDR5-4800 gives 38.4 GB/s, DDR5-6400 gives 51.2 GB/s, and the module gives 32.0 GB of data from 40.0 GB raw. Hint: divide bits by 8 for bytes and by 1000 to go from MB/s to GB/s.

docs.title: About this book
docs.text: A course text on the RTL-to-GDSII flow: logic synthesis, floorplanning, placement, clock-tree synthesis, routing, static timing analysis, physical verification and tapeout, with worked examples, exercises and a hands-on OpenLANE and Sky130 laboratory.

docs.title: Chapter 5: Clock-Tree Synthesis
docs.text:
A data net connects a handful of pins. The clock net connects every flip-flop in the block, often tens of thousands of them, and every one must be told "now" at very nearly the same instant. No single gate can drive that much wire: the edge would crawl, and the flip-flops nearest the source would be clocked long before the farthest ones. Until now the clock has been treated as ideal, infinitely strong and arriving everywhere at once. Clock-tree synthesis (CTS) replaces that fiction with a real, buffered network.

Think of a starting pistol for ten thousand runners spread across a city. You cannot simply shout; you need relay stations so that everyone hears "go" at the same moment. This chapter defines the two numbers that describe how well the relays do their job, latency and skew; shows how skew moves the setup and hold slack; compares the three ways of building the tree; and explains what changes once the clock is real, above all that hold is repaired for the first time.

Learning outcomes

After this chapter you can:

  1. Explain why the clock net is special and what CTS builds.
  2. Define latency and skew and compute skew from two latencies.
  3. Show how positive and negative skew move setup and hold slack.
  4. Compare buffer trees, H-trees and meshes, and describe useful skew and clock gating.
  5. Describe the post-CTS flow: propagated clock, setup re-check and hold repair.

docs.title: 5.1 Why the clock is special
docs.text:
During synthesis and placement the clock is ideal: it is assumed to reach every flip-flop at once with zero delay. CTS makes it real by building a balanced tree of clock buffers or inverters from the clock source out to every flip-flop, so that arrival times stay tightly matched despite real wire delay. Afterwards the clock is propagated: timing analysis uses the actual delay to every flip-flop, and the timing is checked again against that reality.

The input to the stage is a floorplanned, placed and legalised design, optimised for setup against the ideal clock. Its output is the same design with a real clock tree and propagated (post-CTS) timing, ready for routing.

docs.title: 5.2 Two numbers: latency and skew
docs.text:
Latency, also called insertion delay, is the delay from the clock source (a port or a PLL output) to the clock pin of a given flip-flop. It has two parts: source latency (from the source to the block's clock root) and network latency (from the root to the flip-flop, built by CTS). Low latency is nice, but equal latency is what matters.

Skew is the difference in clock arrival time between two flip-flops:

\[\text{skew} = \text{latency}_{\text{capture}} - \text{latency}_{\text{launch}}\]

CTS aims for a global skew near zero so that the whole design sees the edge together. Skew is what actually eats into timing margins.

Example 5.1: Latency and skew

The delay from the clock source to the clock pin of FF_A is 412 ps and to FF_B is 468 ps. For a path from FF_A (launch) to FF_B (capture),

\[\text{skew} = 468 - 412 = +56 \text{ ps}.\]

Skew is positive: the capture clock arrives later than the launch clock (Figure 5.1).

Figure 5.1 Latency and skew. Two arrows from the clock source, 412 ps to FF_A and 468 ps to FF_B, with the 56 ps difference marked as skew.

docs.title: 5.3 How skew moves the slack
docs.text:
Skew changes the timing budget directly. With a launch-clock arrival \(t_{launch}\) and a capture-clock arrival \(t_{capture}\), the skew is \(t_{skew} = t_{capture} - t_{launch}\), and the slack formulas of Chapter 2 become

\[\text{setup slack} = (T + t_{skew} - t_{su}) - (t_{cq} + t_{logic,max})\] \[\text{hold slack} = (t_{cq} + t_{logic,min}) - (t_h + t_{skew})\]
  • Positive skew (the capture clock is later) gives the data extra time to arrive, so it helps setup; but the capture flip-flop keeps listening for longer after the edge, so it hurts hold.
  • Negative skew (the capture clock is earlier) does the reverse: it helps hold and hurts setup.

That is why CTS drives skew towards zero: neither check is starved, and both budgets stay balanced and predictable across thousands of endpoints. Deliberate skew is used only surgically (Section 5.5).

Example 5.2: One path, setup and hold, with skew

Take the path from FF_A to FF_B of Example 5.1, with \(T = 1000\) ps (1 GHz), \(t_{cq} = 90\) ps, slowest logic 700 ps, fastest logic 120 ps, \(t_{su} = 60\) ps and \(t_h = 40\) ps. The skew is \(+56\) ps.

Setup.

  1. Arrival \(= t_{cq} + t_{logic,max} = 90 + 700 = 790\) ps (measured from the launch edge).
  2. Required \(= T + t_{skew} - t_{su} = 1000 + 56 - 60 = 996\) ps.
  3. Slack \(= 996 - 790 = +206\) ps. Met; the positive skew added 56 ps of margin.

Hold.

  1. Arrival of the earliest new data \(= t_{cq} + t_{logic,min} = 90 + 120 = 210\) ps.
  2. Requirement \(= t_h + t_{skew} = 40 + 56 = 96\) ps.
  3. Slack \(= 210 - 96 = +114\) ps. Met.

If the skew grows to +180 ps: hold slack \(= 210 - (40 + 180) = -10\) ps, a hold violation. The skew that helped setup has eaten the hold margin. (Setup would still be \(1000 + 180 - 60 - 790 = +330\) ps.)

docs.title: 5.4 Three ways to build the tree
docs.text:
CTS balances arrival times by choosing a topology for the buffered network, and by sizing and placing its buffers so that every leaf path has matched delay. Figure 5.2 contrasts a single long wire with a balanced H-tree.

Figure 5.2 One wire versus a balanced tree. Left: one wire from the clock source to four flip-flops, with wires of different lengths. Right: an H-shaped tree with clock buffers at its joints so that every flip-flop is at the same wire distance from the root. Structure Idea Strengths Costs Buffer or inverter tree recursively cluster nearby flip-flops, drive each cluster with a buffer, drive those buffers from the next level up; the default in TritonCTS scales to millions of flip-flops; flexible; low area compared with a mesh; skew tuned per branch skew grows with depth; sensitive to on-chip variation along long branches H-tree a geometrically symmetric, fractal H shape so that every leaf is the same wire distance from the root excellent balance by construction; good for regular arrays and top-level distribution rigid; wastes wire when flip-flops are unevenly spread; hard on irregular floorplans Clock mesh or grid a dense metal grid driven from many points; flip-flops tap the nearest node very low skew and robust against variation; used in high-performance CPUs and GPUs large power and metal cost; complex to build and verify

Table 5.1 Three clock-distribution structures.

Two further techniques are applied on top of the balanced tree.

Useful skew. Instead of forcing zero skew everywhere, the tool can deliberately delay or advance a flip-flop's clock to lend time across a boundary: a tight path is given more setup room by delaying its capture clock, with the time borrowed from a neighbouring path that has margin to spare. It is applied path by path.

Clock gating. The clock network is often the single largest consumer of power, because it toggles every cycle across the whole chip. Clock-gating cells (integrated clock-gate, ICG, cells) switch the clock off to idle register banks. CTS must balance the tree through these gates so that the enable logic does not introduce skew.

docs.title: 5.5 After the tree: a real clock and hold repair
docs.text:
Once the tree exists, the clock becomes propagated, and two things happen.

Setup is re-verified. The clock buffers' own delays and the real skew shift every path's budget. Small setup regressions are cleaned up with further sizing and buffering, now against the true clock.

Hold is fixed for the first time. With an ideal clock hold looked fine everywhere. With the real clock, short paths between flip-flops whose clocks arrive at different times can now violate hold. The remedy is to slow the data path down: insert delay (hold) buffers on the short paths so that \(t_{cq} + t_{logic,min}\) grows past \(t_h + t_{skew}\).

# OpenROAD / TritonCTS: build the tree, then propagate and fix hold
clock_tree_synthesis -buf_list {sky130_fd_sc_hd__clkbuf_4 \
                                sky130_fd_sc_hd__clkbuf_8} \
                     -root_buf sky130_fd_sc_hd__clkbuf_16 \
                     -sink_clustering_enable

set_propagated_clock [all_clocks]           ;# from ideal to real clock
estimate_parasitics -placement
repair_timing -hold -hold_margin 0.05       ;# insert hold buffers on short paths
report_clock_skew                           ;# check the global skew achieved

In OpenLANE the stage is controlled by CTS_* variables in config.tcl:

set ::env(CTS_CLK_BUFFER_LIST)      "sky130_fd_sc_hd__clkbuf_4 sky130_fd_sc_hd__clkbuf_8"
set ::env(CTS_ROOT_BUFFER)          "sky130_fd_sc_hd__clkbuf_16"
set ::env(CTS_TARGET_SKEW)          "50"      ;# target skew, ps
set ::env(CTS_TOLERANCE)            "100"
set ::env(CTS_SINK_CLUSTERING_SIZE) "25"
set ::env(CLOCK_PORT)               "clk"
set ::env(CLOCK_PERIOD)             "10.0"    ;# ns

Reports for the stage land in runs/<tag>/reports/cts/.

Think about it

Why not fix hold earlier, during placement?

Answer

Hold depends on the real clock arrival times, which do not exist until the tree is built. A hold fix made against an ideal clock would be guesswork, and would waste buffers that must then be redone.

Before CTS (ideal clock) After CTS (propagated clock) Clock network does not exist buffers placed and connected (routed next) Skew assumed 0 real, small, non-zero (target near CTS_TARGET_SKEW) Latency 0 (or a modelled estimate) actual: hundreds of picoseconds Setup work done here: buffer, size, clone data paths re-checked and touched up against the real clock Hold work deferred: meaningless with an ideal clock done here: delay buffers on short paths Clock power not modelled significant, often the largest single item

Table 5.2 Before and after the clock tree.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Placement and early optimisation use an ideal clock. CTS replaces it with a buffered network (a buffer tree, an H-tree or a mesh) that delivers the edge to every flip-flop at nearly the same time.
  • Latency is the delay from the clock source to one flip-flop; skew is the difference between two flip-flops, capture minus launch.
  • Positive skew helps setup and hurts hold; negative skew does the reverse. CTS keeps skew near zero, with useful skew and clock gating applied deliberately.
  • After CTS the clock is propagated, setup is re-checked, and hold is repaired for the first time by inserting delay buffers on short paths.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 5.1: Skew of three paths

Clock latencies are FF1 310 ps, FF2 355 ps, FF3 290 ps, FF4 340 ps. The paths are FF1 to FF2, FF3 to FF4 and FF2 to FF3. Find the skew of each. Which path is most at risk for hold, and which for setup?

Answer

FF1 to FF2: \(355 - 310 = +45\) ps. FF3 to FF4: \(340 - 290 = +50\) ps. FF2 to FF3: \(290 - 355 = -65\) ps. Positive skew eats hold, so FF3 to FF4 (+50 ps) is most at risk for hold. Negative skew eats setup, so FF2 to FF3 (−65 ps) is most at risk for setup.

Exercise 5.2: Which check does it hurt?

Launch latency is 300 ps and capture latency is 250 ps. What is the skew, and which check does it hurt?

Answer

\(250 - 300 = -50\) ps, negative skew. The capture clock is early, so it hurts setup and helps hold.

Exercise 5.3: How much skew can hold take?

For the path of Example 5.2, find the largest skew for which hold slack is still non-negative, and the most negative skew for which setup slack is still non-negative.

Answer

Hold: \(210 - (40 + s) \ge 0\) gives \(s \le 170\) ps. Setup: \(1000 + s - 60 - 790 \ge 0\) gives \(s \ge -150\) ps. So this path tolerates skew from \(-150\) ps to \(+170\) ps. At \(+180\) ps (Example 5.2) it fails hold by 10 ps, as shown.

Exercise 5.4: Repairing the hold violation

In the +180 ps case of Example 5.2, how much delay must be inserted on the short path to repair hold, and does setup still pass?

Answer

Hold slack was \(-10\) ps, so at least 10 ps of extra minimum delay is needed (in practice a little more, as a hold margin). Even if the buffer's delay were added to the slowest route as well, setup slack would fall only from \(+330\) ps to about \(+320\) ps, so setup still passes comfortably.

Exercise 5.5: Why not a mesh everywhere?

A mesh gives the lowest skew. Why is a buffer tree the default?

Answer

A mesh costs a great deal of power and metal and is complex to build and verify. A buffer tree scales to millions of flip-flops at much lower area, and its skew can be tuned per branch; the small extra skew is acceptable for most designs. Meshes are kept for the highest-performance CPUs and GPUs.

docs.title: Chapter 3: Floorplanning and Power Planning
docs.text:
Synthesis hands the back end a gate-level netlist: a huge, position-less bag of standard cells and macros. Floorplanning is where that netlist first becomes a physical object. We decide how big the die is, what shape it has, where the memories and the input and output pins sit, and how power will reach every cell. These decisions are made before a single cell is placed, and every later stage, placement, clock-tree synthesis, routing and timing, can only optimise inside the box that the floorplan draws. A poor floorplan cannot be rescued by clever placement or routing; it has to be thrown away and redone. That is why this short chapter is worth more care per page than any other in the back end.

Learning outcomes

After this chapter you can:

  1. List what a floorplan fixes and explain why every later stage is bound by it.
  2. Tell the die from the core, and explain rows, sites and cell orientation.
  3. Choose a utilisation and compute core and die size from it.
  4. Describe the power grid (rings, straps, rails, vias) and why IR drop and electromigration make it matter.
  5. Place macros with halos, plan pins, and read the main OpenLANE floorplan variables.

docs.title: 3.1 What floorplanning decides
docs.text:
Floorplanning is the first physical step of the flow. Before anything is placed, it fixes:

  • Size: the total silicon area that you will pay the foundry for, and the usable region inside it.
  • Shape: the aspect ratio, height divided by width, of the core. It affects routing and how the block tiles into a larger chip.
  • Pins: where signals and power enter and leave the block.
  • Macros: where the large fixed blocks go: memories, clock generators, analogue parts. Placement must route around them.
  • Power: the distribution network, built before placement so that cells snap onto power.

Why it is the most consequential step

Placement, clock-tree synthesis, routing and timing all optimise within the box that floorplanning draws. A die that is too small, a macro that blocks a critical path or a weak power grid cannot be repaired later without ripping up the floorplan and starting again. Effort spent here pays back at every stage that follows. (Compare planning a building before the furniture arrives: move a stairwell later and everything else moves with it.)

docs.title: 3.2 Die and core, rows and sites
docs.text:
Two nested rectangles define the block's geometry (Figure 3.1).

Figure 3.1 Die, core, margin, macro, halo and pins. A die with a dashed core inside it, I/O pins on the die edge, a macro with a halo against the core edge, and standard-cell rows filling the rest of the core. Term Meaning Die area the whole piece of silicon, edge to edge, including any I/O ring or pad frame Core area the inner region where standard cells and macros are placed and routed Core margin the gap between the core boundary and the die edge, reserved for pins, the power ring and routing to pins; typically 10 to 30 µm per side Rows horizontal tracks, each one cell high, that tile the core; adjacent rows are flipped so that they share power and ground rails Sites the unit grid within a row; a cell's width is a whole number of sites, its height is one row; in the Sky130 unithd library a site is 0.46 µm × 2.72 µm Orientation each instance has an orientation (R0, MX, MY, R180 and so on); row flipping (MX) lets neighbouring rows abut VDD to VDD and VSS to VSS

Table 3.1 The vocabulary of floorplan geometry.

Every other row is flipped upside down, so that a rail is shared between two rows: VDD meets VDD and ground meets ground (Figure 3.2). Cells snap onto the site grid, and the placer is free to choose the orientation each row requires.

Figure 3.2 Rows, sites and row flipping. Two adjacent standard-cell rows sharing a VSS rail, with the site grid drawn, an upright cell in the first row and a flipped cell in the second.

Hard macros, such as compiled SRAM blocks, are placed first and usually pushed towards the edges or corners of the core so that they do not fragment the sea of standard-cell rows. Pins (in a block flow) or bonding pads (in a padded chip flow) are assigned to the die edges: data pins on the sides, and dedicated power and ground pins feeding the ring.

docs.title: 3.3 Utilisation: how full is the core?
docs.text:
Utilisation is the most important single number in a floorplan.

Definition: utilisation

Utilisation = total standard-cell area ÷ core area. At 0.70, cells cover 70 % of the core; the other 30 % is whitespace left for wiring, extra buffers, clock cells and legalisation.

Typical initial targets are 60 to 75 %. The trade-off is fundamental.

Utilisation Die size and cost Routability Verdict Low, about 50 % large, expensive, silicon wasted easy: plenty of room for wires wasteful 60 to 75 % reasonable congestion manageable the usual choice Above 85 % small, cheap congested, hard to route, timing suffers risky

Table 3.2 The utilisation trade-off.

A denser design looks cheaper, until a design that will not route, or that fails timing because there is no room to buffer a long net, costs weeks of extra iterations. Choose a target that leaves room for the clock buffers and repair buffers that later stages will add.

Example 3.1: Sizing a block

A block has 20 000 cells averaging 2 µm². Target utilisation 70 %, a square core, a margin of 20 µm.

  1. Total cell area \(= 20\,000 \times 2 = 40\,000\) µm².
  2. Core area \(= 40\,000 / 0.70 \approx 57\,143\) µm².
  3. A square core has side \(\sqrt{57\,143} \approx 239\) µm.
  4. The die adds the margin on both sides of each dimension: \(239 + 2 \times 20 \approx 279\) µm.
  5. Die area \(= 279 \times 279 \approx 77\,800\) µm².

At 80 % utilisation the core shrinks to \(40\,000 / 0.80 = 50\,000\) µm² (side about 224 µm) and the die to about \(264 \times 264 \approx 69\,500\) µm², some 11 % less silicon, but with much less room for wires.

The aspect ratio changes the shape but not the core area. With the aspect ratio \(r\) = height ÷ width and core area \(A\), the width is \(\sqrt{A/r}\) and the height \(\sqrt{A\,r}\).

docs.title: 3.4 Power planning: the distribution network
docs.text:
Every cell needs VDD and VSS. Power planning builds a robust metal network, before placement, so that current reaches every corner of the core with as little voltage lost on the way as possible. This is the power distribution network (PDN), and it has four layers of structure (Figure 3.3).

Figure 3.3 Rings, straps, rails and vias. A schematic of the PDN: concentric VDD and VSS rings around the core, a mesh of vertical and horizontal straps on upper metal, thin rails along every row, and a via stack joining the levels. Element Layer Role Power rings wide upper metal around the core edge two or more concentric rings carry VDD and VSS round the block; everything taps off them Straps (stripes) thick upper metals (for example met4 and met5) wide vertical and horizontal wires crossing the core, forming a mesh that spreads the current evenly Standard-cell rails met1 thin horizontal VDD and VSS rails along every row; cells connect their power pins here Vias and via stacks between all layers small metal plugs from one layer to the next that stitch the met1 rails up through the straps to the rings, so that current flows from the rings down into the cells

Table 3.3 The levels of the power network.

docs.title: Why the grid must be strong
docs.text:
Two physical effects set the requirements.

IR drop is the voltage lost across the resistance of the power metal, \(V = I \times R\). If the grid is too thin, a cell far from the ring sees a sagging supply. In the course's example a cell might see 0.75 V where the supply is 0.80 V, a sag of 0.05 V or 6.25 %. Such a cell switches more slowly, which can break timing, so IR drop must be kept within a budget of a few percent of VDD.

Electromigration (EM) is the gradual erosion of metal under sustained high current density: over years the atoms are pushed along the wire, which thins and finally breaks, and the chip dies in the field.

Both have the same cure: wider straps, more of them, more vias, and thick upper metal for the backbone. A strong grid is a reliability requirement and not a luxury.

docs.title: 3.5 Macros, halos, blockages and pins
docs.text:
Several devices keep cells out of places where they would do harm.

  • A halo is a guard band drawn around a hard macro in which no standard cells may be placed. It keeps the macro's pins reachable, leaves room to connect its power and reduces congestion at its edges.
  • A placement blockage is any region where cells are forbidden (hard blockage) or limited in density (soft or partial blockage). It is used to keep a routing channel open, to reserve space for buffers or to stay clear of sensitive circuits.
  • Pin planning places each input or output near the logic that uses it, shortening routes and easing timing. Power pins are spread around the edge so that current enters the ring from several sides.

When a block has several macros, how they are arranged shapes the whole floorplan.

Style Description When to use Channel macros separated by gaps through which wires and buffers pass flexible and easier to route, at a cost in area Abutted macros edge to edge with no gap saves area; needs careful pin alignment and power hook-up

Table 3.4 Two ways to arrange macros.

The general strategy is to place macros along the boundary, orient their pins towards the standard-cell area, group macros that talk to each other and always leave a halo. The aim is to keep the middle of the core one large, contiguous, routable sea of rows.

docs.title: 3.6 The real knobs: OpenLANE and OpenROAD
docs.text:
In the OpenLANE and Sky130 flow, floorplanning is driven by a handful of configuration variables, set in config.tcl (or config.json), and by OpenROAD commands. The most consequential are shown below.

# --- OpenLANE floorplan configuration (config.tcl) ---
set ::env(FP_CORE_UTIL)     45        ;# target core utilisation, % (start low)
set ::env(FP_ASPECT_RATIO)  1         ;# core height / width (1 = square)
set ::env(FP_SIZING)        relative  ;# 'relative': size the die from utilisation
set ::env(DIE_AREA)         "0 0 300 300" ;# used when FP_SIZING is 'absolute' (um)

# --- I/O pins ---
set ::env(FP_IO_MODE)       1         ;# equidistant pins around the die edge
set ::env(FP_IO_HMETAL)     met3      ;# layer for pins on horizontal edges
set ::env(FP_IO_VMETAL)     met2      ;# layer for pins on vertical edges

# --- macros and halo ---
set ::env(PL_MACRO_HALO)    "10 10"   ;# keep-out halo round macros, um

# --- power distribution network ---
set ::env(FP_PDN_VPITCH)    50        ;# vertical strap spacing, um
set ::env(FP_PDN_HPITCH)    50        ;# horizontal strap spacing, um
set ::env(FP_PDN_VWIDTH)    1.6       ;# strap width, um: wider means less IR drop
set ::env(FP_PDN_HWIDTH)    1.6
set ::env(FP_PDN_CORE_RING) 1         ;# build a VDD/VSS ring round the core

Under the hood OpenROAD runs the steps directly, which is useful to recognise when reading logs.

# --- what OpenLANE calls in OpenROAD ---
initialize_floorplan -utilization 45 -aspect_ratio 1 -site unithd   ;# rows, core and die
place_pins -hor_layers met3 -ver_layers met2                         ;# pins on the die edges
pdngen                                                               ;# rings + straps + rails

Lowering FP_CORE_UTIL spreads the cells out (easier routing, a bigger die); raising it packs them (a smaller die, more congestion). FP_ASPECT_RATIO reshapes the core. The FP_PDN_* widths and pitches trade the robustness of the PDN (the IR-drop and EM margin) against the routing area that the straps consume. The flow also places well-tap cells in the rows; they appear again in Chapter 8 when electrical rules are checked.

Variable names

The variable names above are those of the classic OpenLANE flow. Names and defaults change between versions of OpenLANE, so check them against the documentation of the version you install (Chapter 9) before relying on them.

docs.title: 3.7 A common misconception
docs.text:
Common misconception

"Higher utilisation is always better, because the die is smaller and cheaper." Not so. Above the sweet spot congestion explodes: nets cannot find a legal route, the tool inserts detours and buffers that eat the whitespace you saved, timing degrades, and you burn days on failed routing iterations. A slightly larger die that closes on the first pass is almost always cheaper, in engineering time, than a maximally packed one that will not converge.

Think about it

You set utilisation to 85 % and routing fails with congestion hot spots near the SRAMs. What do you try first, and why?

Answer

Try a bigger halo first. The congestion is local to the macros, not global, so the cheapest cure is local too. If that is not enough, lower utilisation by a few points, add placement blockages to steer cells away from the macro pins, or change the aspect ratio so that the congested dimension has more routing tracks.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Floorplanning fixes die and core size, shape, pins, macro positions and the power grid; everything later lives inside it.
  • Cells sit in rows divided into sites; alternate rows are flipped so that they share rails.
  • Utilisation is cell area divided by core area; 60 to 75 % balances cost against routability.
  • Rings, straps, rails and vias form the power network; IR drop and electromigration require that it be strong.
  • Macros go to the edges with halos, and pins go near the logic that uses them. In OpenLANE the main levers are FP_CORE_UTIL, FP_ASPECT_RATIO, PL_MACRO_HALO and the FP_PDN_* variables.

docs.title: Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 3.1: Size a block

A block has 50 000 cells of 2.5 µm² each, 62.5 % utilisation, a square core and a 10 µm margin. Find the core side and the die side.

Answer

Cell area \(= 50\,000 \times 2.5 = 125\,000\) µm². Core area \(= 125\,000 / 0.625 = 200\,000\) µm². Core side \(= \sqrt{200\,000} \approx 447\) µm. Die side \(= 447 + 2 \times 10 \approx 467\) µm.

Exercise 3.2: Square or tall?

A block has 35 000 cells averaging 3 µm², 65 % utilisation and a 15 µm margin. (a) Find the core side, die side and die area for a square core. (b) Repeat for an aspect ratio (height ÷ width) of 2. (c) Which shape uses less silicon, and why might you still choose the other?

Answer

(a) Cell area 105 000 µm²; core area \(105\,000 / 0.65 \approx 161\,538\) µm²; core side \(\approx 401.9\) µm; die side \(\approx 431.9\) µm; die area \(\approx 186\,550\) µm². (b) With the same core area, width \(= \sqrt{161\,538 / 2} \approx 284.2\) µm and height \(= 2 \times 284.2 = 568.4\) µm. The die is \(314.2 \times 598.4\) µm, about \(188\,000\) µm². (c) The square. For a fixed core area it has the shortest perimeter, so the margin costs least. A tall shape might still be chosen to fit a slot in a larger chip or to line up with pins.

Exercise 3.3: A slow cell in the middle

Cells in the middle of the chip are slower than identical cells near the edge. Which floorplan problem do you suspect, and what do you do?

Answer

IR drop: the supply sags far from the rings, so the cells there switch more slowly. Widen or add straps and add vias.

Exercise 3.4: Utilisation and die cost

For Example 3.1, compute the core area and the die side if utilisation is 60 % instead of 70 %. By how much does the die area grow compared with the 70 % case?

Answer

Core area \(= 40\,000 / 0.60 \approx 66\,667\) µm², side \(\approx 258.2\) µm. Die side \(= 258.2 + 40 = 298.2\) µm, die area \(\approx 88\,900\) µm². Compared with 77 800 µm² this is about 14 % more silicon, bought in exchange for more routing room.

Exercise 3.5: Why build the PDN first?

The power grid is built before placement, not afterwards. Give two reasons.

Answer

Standard cells can then snap straight onto the rails, and the placer and router know from the start which tracks and areas the straps occupy. Power also needs the best (thick, low-resistance) metal and the least flexibility; building it later would force it into whatever space the cells and signal wires had left over.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Antenna effect Damage to a thin gate oxide by charge that a long, still-unconnected metal wire collects from the plasma during fabrication. Cured by layer jumping or an antenna diode. See Chapter 6. ASIC Application-specific integrated circuit. In this book, a standard-cell ASIC built from a library of ready-made cells. ATPG Automatic test-pattern generation: computing the input vectors that expose manufacturing defects, usually under the stuck-at fault model. Blockage A region of the core where placement of cells is forbidden or density-limited. Buffer A cell that re-drives a signal without changing its logic value, used to break up long or heavily loaded nets or to add delay on a hold-critical path. Clock gating Switching the clock off to idle register banks to save power, using integrated clock-gate (ICG) cells. Clock-tree synthesis (CTS) Building a balanced, buffered network that delivers the clock to every flip-flop at nearly the same time. See Chapter 5. Clock uncertainty A margin subtracted from setup and hold slack for clock jitter and safety. Core The inner region of the die in which standard cells and macros are placed and routed. Corner A named combination of process, voltage and temperature at which cell delays are characterised: slow (SS), typical (TT) or fast (FF). CPPR (CRPR) Clock-path pessimism removal: crediting back pessimism counted twice on the part of the clock path that launch and capture share. Critical path The timing path with the smallest slack; it sets the maximum clock frequency. DEF Design Exchange Format: the file that records the placement and routing of a design. Density fill Non-functional dummy metal added after routing so that every window of every layer meets the foundry's minimum and maximum metal density. DFT Design for test: inserting structures, chiefly scan chains, that make a manufactured chip controllable and observable. Die The whole piece of silicon, edge to edge, including the margin around the core. DRC Design rule check: comparing every shape of the layout with the foundry's geometric rules. See Chapter 8. Drive strength The size of a cell's transistors, written _1, _2, _4 or ×1, ×2, ×4: bigger cells drive larger loads faster but cost area, power and input capacitance. Electromigration (EM) The slow erosion of metal under sustained high current density, which can finally open a wire. ERC Electrical rule check: finding floating gates, power-to-ground shorts, wrongly tied wells and missing taps. Floorplan The first physical stage: the die and core size, aspect ratio, pins, macro positions and the power grid. FPGA Field-programmable gate array: a reprogrammable fabric of look-up tables and other blocks. g-cell A coarse routing tile used by global routing and by congestion maps, many tracks wide. GDSII Graphic Design System II: the industry-standard binary stream format for a finished layout, pure geometry by layer. Halo A keep-out guard band around a hard macro in which no standard cells are placed. Hold time, hold slack The time for which data must stay steady after the clock edge, and the margin by which a path meets that requirement. Independent of the clock period. HPWL Half-perimeter wirelength: the width plus the height of the box enclosing all the pins of a net. IR drop The voltage lost across the resistance of the power grid, \(V = I \times R\). Latency (insertion delay) The delay from the clock source to a flip-flop's clock pin. LEC Logic equivalence checking: a formal proof that two designs, such as the RTL and the final netlist, compute the same function. LEF Library Exchange Format: the physical abstract of cells (outline, pins, blockages) and the technology (metal layers, vias, rules). Legalisation The placement phase that removes overlaps and snaps cells to rows and sites. Liberty (.lib) The characterised timing and power model of a cell library, one file per corner. LVS Layout versus schematic: extracting a netlist from the layout and proving that it matches the intended netlist. MCMM Multi-corner multi-mode analysis: timing every functional mode at every relevant corner. Net The logical connection of a set of pins in a netlist. The physical metal that realises it is its wire. OASIS Open Artwork System Interchange Standard: a compact successor to GDSII. OCV On-chip variation: the small differences between nominally identical cells on one die, modelled by derating. OpenLANE The open-source orchestrator that runs Yosys, OpenROAD, Magic, KLayout and netgen as one RTL-to-GDSII flow. PDK Process design kit: a foundry's design rules, device models, layer definitions and standard-cell library for one process. PDN Power distribution network: the rings, straps, rails and vias that carry VDD and VSS to every cell. Pitch The centre-to-centre distance between neighbouring routing tracks. PPA Power, performance, area: the three goals that pull against one another. PVT Process, voltage and temperature: the three variables that set a cell's delay. RTL Register-transfer level: a description of a circuit as registers and the logic between them. Scan chain Scan flip-flops linked into a shift register so that a tester can set and read every register. SDC Synopsys Design Constraints: the Tcl dialect that states clocks, input and output delays and timing exceptions. Setup time, setup slack The time for which data must be steady before the clock edge, and the margin by which a path meets its deadline. Depends on the clock period. Site The unit grid of a row; a cell's width is a whole number of sites. Skew The difference in clock arrival between two flip-flops: capture latency minus launch latency. Slack Required time minus arrival time. Negative slack is a violation. SPEF Standard Parasitic Exchange Format: the extracted resistance and capacitance of every net. Standard cell A pre-designed, pre-characterised logic gate of fixed height that the flow places in rows. STA Static timing analysis: exhaustive, vector-less checking of every timing path. Streaming out Writing the final layout as a GDSII or OASIS file. Tapeout The moment the final mask data is sent to the foundry. Timing arc A characterised delay from one input pin to one output pin of a cell, tabulated against input slew and output load. Timing closure Making every timing path meet its constraint at every corner and mode. TNS, WNS Total and worst negative slack: the sum of all negative slacks, and the single most negative one. Track A legal centre line for a wire on a routing layer. Utilisation Total standard-cell area divided by core area. Via A small metal plug joining a wire on one layer to a wire on the next. Wire-load model A statistical estimate of a net's capacitance from its fan-out, used before real wires exist.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
The tools and the process kit of this book are documented by their own projects, and the documentation is the place to settle any detail of a command or variable that changes between versions.

  • OpenLANE: the flow reference, every configuration variable and many example designs, at openlane.readthedocs.io, with the sources at github.com/The-OpenROAD-Project/OpenLane (the classic flow) and github.com/efabless/openlane2 (the Python rewrite).
  • OpenROAD: the place-and-route and timing engine, with an interactive Tcl command reference, at openroad.readthedocs.io and theopenroadproject.org.
  • The SkyWater Sky130 open process kit: layers, cells and rules, at skywater-pdk.readthedocs.io and github.com/google/skywater-pdk.
  • Matt Venn's "Zero to ASIC" course (zerotoasiccourse.com) and Tiny Tapeout (tinytapeout.com): the quickest route from a first design to a chip that is actually made.
  • Elsewhere in this library, the field guide ASIC Design: RTL to GDSII covers the same flow in plain language with a wider view of tools, standards and careers, and the companion books RTL Design and Hardware Description Languages and Microarchitecture and SoC Design describe the designs that enter this flow.

docs.title: Chapter 2: Logic Synthesis and Timing Basics
docs.text:
Synthesis is the first stage at which an abstract piece of Verilog stops being an idea and starts becoming hardware. The tool reads the RTL, works out the Boolean logic and the registers that it describes, and maps that logic onto real building blocks, the standard cells of one manufacturing process, while squeezing timing, area and power to meet the constraints it has been given. The output is a gate-level netlist: the same design, now written entirely in NANDs, AOIs, flip-flops and buffers that a foundry can actually make.

Synthesis is also where timing first matters. A gate-level netlist is useful only if its gates are fast enough, so this chapter introduces, alongside the tool flow, the arithmetic of setup and hold slack that the rest of the book builds on.

Learning outcomes

After this chapter you can:

  1. Describe the three phases of synthesis and read a small gate-level netlist.
  2. Explain timing arcs and drive strengths in a cell library.
  3. Compute setup and hold slack for a register-to-register path, and find the critical path and the maximum clock frequency.
  4. Write basic SDC constraints and read a Yosys synthesis script.
  5. Explain scan chains and say what synthesis does and does not prove.

docs.title: 2.1 What synthesis does
docs.text:
RTL describes behaviour: "on the rising clock edge, sum becomes a + b". Logic synthesis turns that behaviour into a structural netlist, an interconnection of standard cells, that is logically equivalent to the RTL but can be built in silicon. Three conceptual phases happen inside the tool.

Elaboration. The RTL is parsed, parameters are resolved, generate loops are unrolled and the hierarchy is built. Behavioural constructs (+, *, if, case, always blocks) become a generic, technology-independent netlist of abstract gates and inferred registers. This representation is often called GTECH or, in Yosys, RTLIL. No real cell has been chosen yet.

Technology mapping. Each generic gate and register is replaced by a real cell from the target .lib: a sky130_fd_sc_hd__nand2_1, a __dfrtp_2 flip-flop and so on. This is where an abstract AND becomes "this exact NAND followed by this inverter, with these delays".
