docs.title: 8.10.1 5G NR for UAV C2
docs.text: 3GPP Release 17 (2022) standardised NR-U2X (New Radio UAV-to-X) communications, including specific 5G NR features for low-latency (\(< 10\) ms), high-reliability (\(99.999\)%) command links for BVLOS drone operations. 5G NR at 3.5 GHz (mid-band) provides \(\sim\)100 Mbps aggregate per cell with network slicing to guarantee QoS for drone C2 independently of consumer traffic. By 2026, UTM (Unmanned Traffic Management) providers including NASA and EASA are piloting 5G drone corridors in major European cities.

docs.title: 8.10.2 Quantum Key Distribution (QKD)
docs.text: QKD (BB84 protocol, NIST SP 1800-38) distributes encryption keys using quantum photon states that cannot be eavesdropped without disturbance, providing information-theoretically secure key exchange. Satellite-based QKD (Chinese Micius satellite, 2016) demonstrated 1200 km quantum key distribution. Miniaturised QKD terminals for UAVs (\(< 5\) kg) are under development at Toshiba Research (UK) and QuiX Quantum (Netherlands), targeting practical deployment by the late 2020s for the most sensitive military UAV platforms.

docs.title: 8.10.3 Laser / Free-Space Optical Communications
docs.text:
High-data-rate laser communications (lasercom) at 1550 nm wavelength offer 1–10 Gbps throughput in narrow beams (\(< 0.01\)° divergence), with essentially zero probability of intercept. DARPA’s PACE (Persistent Aquatic Living Sensors) and LCRD (Laser Communications Relay Demonstration, NASA) have demonstrated Gbps optical links from GEO. For drone-to-ground lasercom, adaptive optics must compensate atmospheric turbulence — the phase distortion coherence diameter \(r_0\) (Fried parameter):

\[r_0 = 0.185\left(\frac{\lambda^2}{\bar{C}_n^2 L}\right)^{3/5}\tag{8.25}\]

where \(C_n^2\) is the refractive index structure parameter and \(L\) is path length. Typical \(r_0 = 5\)–20 cm at 1550 nm for 1 km slant path; deformable mirrors with 100–1000 actuators can correct down to \(r_0\) scale.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter has presented a comprehensive treatment of drone and missile communication systems, grounded in the fundamental physics of Maxwell’s equations and the Friis transmission equation. The link budget framework unifies the analysis of all communication links, from the simplest ExpressLRS RC control link to the Wideband Global SATCOM system. RC control links (ELRS, Crossfire) and telemetry systems (SiK, RFD900+) serve the short-to-medium range civilian and commercial drone market; military platforms require the anti-jam, authentication, and wideband capabilities of Link 16, CDL, and WGS. Video downlinks span analogue FPV (zero-latency, degraded quality) to COFDM encrypted HD systems. Satellite communications using Iridium, Inmarsat, Starlink, and WGS enable global BVLOS and persistent ISR operations. Cybersecurity — AES-256 encryption, ECDH key exchange, GNSS anti-spoofing, and zero-trust PKI architectures — is now inseparable from communications system design. Cognitive radio, 5G NR C2, quantum key distribution, and free-space optical links represent the next technology frontier for drone communications.

docs.title: 9.1 Introduction to UAV and Missile Payloads
docs.text:
The payload subsystem defines the operational utility of any unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) or guided weapon system. Whereas the airframe, propulsion, and avionics provide the means of flight, the payload delivers the mission effect — whether that effect is intelligence collection, precision strike, logistics delivery, or electronic warfare suppression. Modern unmanned platforms carry payloads that account for 20%–40% of gross take-off weight (GTOW), and the integration of these payloads into the airframe drives fundamental design constraints in aerodynamics, structural loading, electrical power budgets, thermal management, and electromagnetic compatibility.

This chapter provides comprehensive treatment of the principal payload classes employed on contemporary and next-generation UAVs and cruise missiles. The discussion spans the full spectrum from passive electro-optical (EO) and infrared (IR) sensors, through active synthetic aperture radar (SAR) and laser rangefinders, to offensive weapons, logistical delivery systems, and electronic warfare (EW) suites. Each section addresses physical operating principles, quantitative performance metrics, design equations, integration constraints, and representative fielded systems.

docs.title: 9.1.1 Payload Classification Taxonomy
docs.text:
Payloads are classified along two orthogonal axes: function (what the payload does) and interaction mode (whether it is passive, active, or kinetic). Table 9.1 summarises the principal categories.

Table 9.1. UAV and Missile Payload Classification Category Sub-type Interaction Primary Application Intelligence, Surveillance EO/IR Camera Passive ISR, targeting & Reconnaissance (ISR) Hyperspectral Passive MASINT, agriculture SAR/ISAR Active All-weather mapping LiDAR Active 3-D mapping, obstacle detect. SIGINT/ELINT Passive Signals collection Kinetic Effects Guided bombs Kinetic Precision strike Missiles Kinetic Stand-off strike Loitering munition Kinetic Time-critical targets Logistics Cargo pod Passive Resupply, medical Sling load Passive Outsized cargo Electronic Warfare Jammer Active Radar/comms denial DRFM repeater Active/Deceptive False target generation Decoy Active Missile saturation Communications Relay transponder Active BLOS communications Mesh node Active Swarm networking

docs.title: 9.1.2 Payload Performance Trade-space
docs.text:
The fundamental payload design trade is between aperture size (which drives sensing performance), mass (which reduces endurance or range), and power consumption (which heats the platform and demands larger batteries or generators). These interdependencies are captured in a generalised payload figure of merit:

\[\mathrm{FOM}_\mathrm{payload} = \frac{P_\mathrm{performance}}{m_\mathrm{payload} \cdot P_\mathrm{electric}}\tag{9.1}\]

where \(P_\mathrm{performance}\) is mission-relevant performance (e.g., spatial resolution in line-pairs/mm, detection range in km, or jam-to-signal ratio in dB), \(m_\mathrm{payload}\) is payload mass in kg, and \(P_\mathrm{electric}\) is average electrical power draw in watts.

docs.title: 9.2 Electro-Optical and Infrared Sensors
docs.text: Electro-optical sensors form the backbone of airborne reconnaissance, target acquisition, and precision guidance. They exploit reflected or emitted electromagnetic radiation in the visible (0.4–0.7 µ m), near-infrared (NIR, 0.7–1.0 µ m), shortwave infrared (SWIR, 1.0–2.5 µ m), mid-wave infrared (MWIR, 3–5 µ m), and longwave infrared (LWIR, 8–12 µ m) bands.

docs.title: 9.2.1 Visible-Band Cameras: CMOS vs CCD Sensors
docs.text:
Contemporary airborne cameras almost universally employ one of two focal plane array (FPA) technologies: charge-coupled device (CCD) or complementary metal-oxide semiconductor (CMOS) active pixel sensor (APS).

CCD Architecture. In a CCD, each pixel accumulates photo-generated charge in a potential well. At the end of the integration period, charge is transferred serially toward a single output amplifier by sequentially clocking gate voltages. This serial readout architecture produces outstanding uniformity (fixed-pattern noise \(<0.1\%\)) and very low read noise (2–5 \(e^-\) rms at slow pixel rates), making CCDs superior for faint-source astronomy or long-range surveillance where SNR is critical. However, the serial readout limits frame rate, and full-frame CCDs draw significant power during clocking.

CMOS Architecture. CMOS APS sensors place an amplifier, reset transistor, and select transistor within each pixel (three-transistor, 3T, or four-transistor, 4T architecture). Each pixel is addressed individually (random access), enabling rolling or global shutter readout at very high frame rates. Modern back-illuminated CMOS (BSI-CMOS) sensors achieve quantum efficiency \(>80\%\) across the visible band and read noise of 1–3 \(e^-\), closing much of the historical performance gap with CCD. CMOS sensors also integrate ADCs per column or pixel, dramatically reducing readout power. For UAV applications, CMOS dominates due to lower mass, lower power, and higher frame rates.

Key Sensor Metrics.

  • Resolution (megapixels): Total pixel count \(N = N_H \times N_V\). Common formats: 4K (\(3840 \times 2160 = 8.3\) MP), 61 MP (full-frame, \(9504 \times 6336\)), custom large-format mosaics up to 1.8 GP.

  • Pixel pitch \(p\): Physical size of one pixel, typically 1.4–8 µ m. Smaller pitch → denser array for fixed sensor format, but more diffraction-limited and lower dynamic range.

  • Dynamic Range: \(\mathrm{DR} = 20 \log_{10}(Q_\mathrm{sat}/\sigma_\mathrm{read})\) where \(Q_\mathrm{sat}\) is saturation charge capacity and \(\sigma_\mathrm{read}\) is read noise. Typical values 60–80 dB.

  • Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR): Under shot-noise-limited illumination:

\[\mathrm{SNR} = \frac{Q_e}{\sqrt{Q_e + Q_d t + \sigma_\mathrm{read}^2 + \sigma_\mathrm{ADC}^2}}\tag{9.2}\]

where \(Q_e = \eta \Phi t\) is the signal electrons (\(\eta\) = quantum efficiency, \(\Phi\) = photon flux, \(t\) = integration time), \(Q_d\) is dark current electrons per second, \(\sigma_\mathrm{read}\) is read noise, and \(\sigma_\mathrm{ADC}\) is ADC quantisation noise.

  • Modulation Transfer Function (MTF): The MTF describes spatial frequency response. The system MTF is the product of individual component MTFs:
\[\mathrm{MTF}_\mathrm{system}(f) = \mathrm{MTF}_\mathrm{lens}(f) \cdot \mathrm{MTF}_\mathrm{detector}(f) \cdot \mathrm{MTF}_\mathrm{motion}(f) \cdot \mathrm{MTF}_\mathrm{atm}(f)\tag{9.3}\]

The detector MTF for a square pixel of pitch \(p\) is:

\[\mathrm{MTF}_\mathrm{det}(f) = \left|\mathrm{sinc}(p \cdot f)\right| = \left|\frac{\sin(\pi p f)}{\pi p f}\right|\tag{9.4}\]

where \(f\) is spatial frequency in cycles per mm. The Nyquist frequency is \(f_N = 1/(2p)\).

docs.title: 9.2.2 Lens Optics and Field of View
docs.text:
The fundamental thin-lens equation relates object distance \(d_o\), image distance \(d_i\), and focal length \(f\):

\[\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{d_o} + \frac{1}{d_i}\tag{9.5}\]

For airborne systems, \(d_o \gg f\) (object at near-infinity), so \(d_i \approx f\). The f-number (f/#) is defined as:

\[f/\# = \frac{f}{D_\mathrm{aperture}}\tag{9.6}\]

A lens with a lower f/# collects more light (irradiance \(\propto 1/(f/\#)^2\)) but is harder to correct for aberrations and is physically larger. Airborne EO lenses typically range from f/2.8 to f/5.6.

The full-angle field of view (FOV) in the horizontal direction is:

\[\mathrm{FOV}_H = 2 \arctan\!\left(\frac{W_\mathrm{sensor}}{2f}\right)\tag{9.7}\]

where \(W_\mathrm{sensor}\) is the sensor width. For example, a 36 mm sensor with a 50 mm lens: \(\mathrm{FOV}_H = 2\arctan(18/50) = 39.6°\).

docs.title: 9.2.3 Ground Sample Distance
docs.text:
The ground sample distance (GSD) is the ground-projected size of one pixel — the most operationally significant metric linking camera optics to image intelligence. It is given by:

\[\mathrm{GSD} = \frac{H \cdot p}{f \cdot 1000}\tag{9.8}\]

where \(H\) is altitude above ground level (AGL) in metres, \(p\) is pixel pitch in µ m, \(f\) is focal length in mm, and GSD is in metres per pixel. Rearranging to find the required focal length for a target GSD:

\[f_\mathrm{required} = \frac{H \cdot p}{\mathrm{GSD} \cdot 1000}\tag{9.9}\]

Example: A UAV at \(H = 300\) m, sensor pixel pitch \(p = 3.76\) µ m (Sony IMX477), requires \(\mathrm{GSD} = 5\) cm. The required focal length is:

\[f = \frac{300 \times 3.76}{5 \times 1000 \times 10^{-2} \times 1000} = \frac{1128}{50} = 22.56\,\mathrm{mm}\]

The total swath width on the ground at this altitude with a 12.33 mm wide sensor (Sony IMX477, \(4056\times3040\), \(3.76\) µ m pitch):

\[W_\mathrm{swath} = \frac{W_\mathrm{sensor} \cdot H}{f} = \frac{12.33 \times 300}{22.56} \approx 164\,\mathrm{m}\tag{9.10}\]

Table 9.2 shows GSD for representative sensor/altitude combinations.

Table 9.2. GSD as a Function of Altitude and Focal Length (pixel pitch = 4 µ m) Alt (m) f = 8 mm f = 16 mm f = 25 mm f = 50 mm f = 100 mm 100 5.0 cm 2.5 cm 1.6 cm 0.8 cm 0.4 cm 300 15.0 cm 7.5 cm 4.8 cm 2.4 cm 1.2 cm 1000 50.0 cm 25.0 cm 16.0 cm 8.0 cm 4.0 cm 3000 150 cm 75 cm 48 cm 24 cm 12 cm 10000 500 cm 250 cm 160 cm 80 cm 40 cm

docs.title: 9.2.4 Infrared Cameras
docs.text:
Infrared cameras detect thermal emission from objects according to Planck’s radiation law. The spectral radiance of a blackbody at temperature \(T\) is:

\[L_\lambda(T) = \frac{2hc^2}{\lambda^5} \cdot \frac{1}{e^{hc/\lambda k_B T} - 1}\tag{9.11}\]

where \(h = 6.626\times10^{-34}\) J s is Planck’s constant, \(c = 3\times10^8\) m/s, \(k_B = 1.381\times10^{-23}\) J/K. Peak emission shifts with temperature according to Wien’s displacement law: \(\lambda_\mathrm{peak} = 2898/T\) µ m (with \(T\) in kelvin). For room-temperature objects (\(T \approx 300\) K), \(\lambda_\mathrm{peak} \approx 9.7\) µ m, well within the LWIR band.

MWIR (3–5 µ m) detectors are predominantly InSb (indium antimonide) or MCT (mercury cadmium telluride, HgCdTe). InSb requires cryogenic cooling to 77 K using a Stirling-cycle cooler to suppress thermally generated dark current. MCT detectors can be bandgap-engineered by varying the Cd/Hg ratio to cover any wavelength from 1–25 µ m and can achieve higher operating temperatures (HOT detectors, up to 150 K) by engineering wider bandgaps. MWIR is preferred when imaging hot targets (jet exhausts, missile plumes), where the contrast against background is maximum.

LWIR (8–12 µ m) detectors include cooled MCT, quantum well infrared photodetectors (QWIPs), and uncooled microbolometers. Uncooled microbolometers use resistive temperature sensors (vanadium oxide, VOx, or amorphous silicon, a-Si) that heat up when IR radiation is absorbed, changing their resistance. Arrays of 640\(\times\)480 or 1024\(\times\)768 are standard; 17 µ m or 12 µ m pitch bolometer arrays are now common. Uncooled detectors eliminate the mass, power, and reliability burden of cryocoolers, making them attractive for small UAVs.

Noise Equivalent Temperature Difference (NETD) is the most important figure of merit for thermal cameras:

\[\mathrm{NETD} = \frac{\Delta T_\mathrm{noise}}{\Delta T_\mathrm{scene}} = \frac{V_\mathrm{noise}}{\partial V / \partial T}\tag{9.12}\]

where \(\Delta T_\mathrm{noise}\) is the apparent temperature fluctuation due to detector noise, and \(\partial V / \partial T\) is the responsivity. High-performance cooled cameras achieve NETD \(<20\) mK; quality uncooled bolometers achieve 40–60 mK; budget sensors may be 80–120 mK. NETD \(<50\) mK is generally considered the threshold for reliable target recognition at operationally relevant distances.

The Johnson criteria relate target detection, recognition, and identification (DRI) to the number of resolved cycles across the critical dimension of the target:

\[N_\mathrm{cycles} = \frac{d_\mathrm{target}}{2 \cdot \mathrm{GSD}}\tag{9.13}\]

Detection requires \(N \geq 1\), recognition \(N \geq 4\), identification \(N \geq 8\).

docs.title: 9.2.5 Thermal Imaging System Design
docs.text:
The signal chain for a thermal imaging system involves the detector, readout integrated circuit (ROIC), and digital processing. The charge generated per pixel per frame:

\[Q = \eta \cdot I_\lambda \cdot A_\mathrm{pixel} \cdot t_\mathrm{int} / (h\nu)\tag{9.14}\]

where \(\eta\) is quantum efficiency (50–80% for cooled MCT), \(I_\lambda\) is photon irradiance, \(A_\mathrm{pixel}\) is pixel area, and \(t_\mathrm{int}\) is integration time. The ROIC capacitance sets maximum charge storage:

\[Q_\mathrm{max} = C_\mathrm{ROIC} \cdot V_\mathrm{swing}\tag{9.15}\]

Typical ROIC capacitances are 10–200 fF with voltage swings of 1–3 V, giving well capacities of \(10^7\)–\(10^9\) electrons.

Table 9.3 compares key IR detector technologies.

Table 9.3. Comparison of Infrared Detector Technologies Technology Band Cooling NETD D* Mass Power (µ m) (K) (mK) (cm\(\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}\)/W) (kg) (W) InSb FPA 3–5 77 10–20 \(3\times10^{11}\) 0.5–1.5 5–15 MCT MWIR FPA 3–5 77–150 10–30 \(2\times10^{11}\) 0.5–2.0 3–10 MCT LWIR FPA 8–12 77 15–25 \(2\times10^{10}\) 0.5–2.0 5–15 QWIP FPA 8–10 77 20–40 \(5\times10^{9}\) 0.5–1.5 5–12 VOx Bolometer 8–14 Uncooled 40–80 \(2\times10^{8}\) 0.1–0.5 1–3 a-Si Bolometer 8–14 Uncooled 50–100 \(1\times10^{8}\) 0.05–0.3 0.5–2

docs.title: 9.2.6 Gimbal Stabilisation Systems
docs.text:
A gyroscopically stabilised gimbal decouples the sensor from airframe motion, maintaining pointing toward a target while the UAV pitches, rolls, and yaws. The performance requirements are stringent: airframe angular rates during turbulence can reach 20–50 deg/s, while image stabilisation requires residual motion \(<0.1\) mrad (equivalent to sub-pixel movement).

2-Axis Gimbals (pan, tilt) are adequate for forward-looking and downward-looking sensors where roll-stabilisation is provided by the airframe’s own roll attitude. They are lighter and simpler.

3-Axis Gimbals (roll, pitch, yaw) provide full decoupling and are required for precision targeting or when the UAV operates with significant roll. The Wescam MX-15D, Raytheon Multi-Spectral Targeting System (MTS-B), and DJI Zenmuse X7 are examples spanning military and commercial markets.

The gimbal control architecture employs cascaded loops:

\[\theta_\mathrm{gimbal}(s) = \frac{G_\mathrm{pos}(s)}{1 + G_\mathrm{pos}(s) G_\mathrm{rate}(s) P(s)} \cdot \theta_\mathrm{cmd}(s)\tag{9.16}\]

where \(G_\mathrm{rate}(s)\) is the inner angular rate controller (typically a lead-lag compensator), \(G_\mathrm{pos}(s)\) is the outer position loop, and \(P(s)\) is the plant transfer function. The inner rate loop bandwidth must exceed 10 Hz to reject airframe vibration; outer position loop bandwidth is typically 1–3 Hz. Gyroscopes mounted directly on the camera head (not on the airframe) are essential for inertial rate feedback — this prevents the base motion from appearing as a torque disturbance before the inner loop can reject it.

The required torque motor stiffness against disturbance:

\[T_\mathrm{disturbance} = J \ddot{\theta}_\mathrm{airframe} + B \dot{\theta}_\mathrm{airframe}\tag{9.17}\]

where \(J\) is the gimbal axis inertia and \(B\) is bearing friction. For a 1-kg gimbal with axis radius of gyration 0.05 m, \(J \approx 2.5\times10^{-3}\) kg m\(^2\). At 50 deg/s\(^2\) angular acceleration, \(T \approx 0.22\) N m, setting the motor torque requirement.

docs.title: 9.2.7 Multi-Spectral and Hyperspectral Imaging
docs.text:
Multi-spectral imagers capture images in a discrete set of spectral bands, typically: Blue (450 nm), Green (560 nm), Red (650 nm), Red-Edge (730 nm), NIR (840 nm), and optionally SWIR (1550 nm). Separate bandpass filters are applied to each detector or, in a single-sensor design, to a tiled Bayer-like mosaic.

The Normalised Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), used extensively in agricultural UAV applications, is:

\[\mathrm{NDVI} = \frac{\rho_\mathrm{NIR} - \rho_\mathrm{Red}}{\rho_\mathrm{NIR} + \rho_\mathrm{Red}}\tag{9.18}\]

where \(\rho\) denotes band reflectance. NDVI ranges from \(-1\) (water) through 0 (bare soil) to \(+1\) (dense vegetation). Extended indices include the Red-Edge Chlorophyll Index (CIre) and the Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI):

\[\mathrm{EVI} = 2.5 \cdot \frac{\rho_\mathrm{NIR} - \rho_\mathrm{Red}}{\rho_\mathrm{NIR} + 6\rho_\mathrm{Red} - 7.5\rho_\mathrm{Blue} + 1}\tag{9.19}\]

Hyperspectral imaging captures a continuous spectrum at each pixel — typically 100–400 narrow spectral bands across 400–2500 nm with 5–10 nm spectral resolution. Pushbroom scanners use a line array of pixels with a dispersing element (prism or grating) spreading wavelengths along one dimension of a 2-D detector. As the platform moves, successive lines are scanned, building a 3-D data cube [\(x\), \(y\), \(\lambda\)]. Spectral unmixing algorithms (matched filter, fully constrained least squares) identify material abundances at sub-pixel scale. Representative airborne hyperspectral payloads: Headwall Photonics Nano-Hyperspec (397–1003 nm, 270 bands, 0.36 kg), SPECIM AFX10 (400–1000 nm, 3.0 kg).

docs.title: 9.3 Synthetic Aperture Radar
docs.text: Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) overcomes the fundamental limitation of optical sensors — dependence on daylight and cloud-free conditions — by actively illuminating the scene with microwave or millimetre-wave energy and forming images from the coherent backscatter. SAR is employed on strategic ISR platforms (Global Hawk Block 30 with MP-RTIP), tactical UCAVs, and small commercial SAR satellites (Capella Space, ICEYE), and increasingly on tactical UAVs (\(<100\) kg) carrying miniaturised SAR payloads.

docs.title: 9.3.1 Aperture Synthesis Principle
docs.text:
A real-aperture side-looking radar (SLAR) achieves azimuth (along-track) resolution:

\[\delta_\mathrm{az}^\mathrm{SLAR} = \frac{\lambda R}{D}\tag{9.20}\]

where \(\lambda\) is wavelength, \(R\) is slant range, and \(D\) is physical antenna length. At \(R = 10\) km, \(\lambda = 0.03\) m (X-band), \(D = 0.5\) m: \(\delta_\mathrm{az}^\mathrm{SLAR} = 600\) m — tactically useless.

SAR synthesises a large aperture \(L_\mathrm{SA}\) equal to the distance flown while the target remains within the antenna beam. For a focused SAR, the coherent processing gain gives:

\[\delta_\mathrm{az}^\mathrm{SAR} = \frac{D}{2}\tag{9.21}\]

This remarkable result shows that SAR azimuth resolution is independent of range and inversely proportional to physical aperture size — a smaller antenna gives finer azimuth resolution because it has a wider beam, dwelling on each point for longer. For \(D = 0.5\) m, \(\delta_\mathrm{az}^\mathrm{SAR} = 0.25\) m regardless of range.

docs.title: 9.3.2 Range Resolution and Chirp Bandwidth
docs.text:
Range (cross-track) resolution is determined by the transmit signal bandwidth. For a linear frequency modulated (LFM, or chirp) pulse with bandwidth \(B\):

\[\delta_r = \frac{c}{2B}\tag{9.22}\]

where \(c = 3\times10^8\) m/s. To achieve \(\delta_r = 0.3\) m, the required bandwidth is \(B = c/(2\delta_r) = 500\) MHz. The time-bandwidth product of the chirp is:

\[\mathrm{TBP} = B \cdot \tau = \frac{c}{2\delta_r} \cdot \tau\tag{9.23}\]

A long pulse (\(\tau = 10\) µ s) with \(B = 500\) MHz gives TBP \(= 5000\), yielding 5000:1 pulse compression gain in signal-to-noise ratio versus a single-frequency pulse of the same energy.

The slant-range resolution maps to ground-range resolution as:

\[\delta_\mathrm{gr} = \frac{\delta_r}{\sin\theta_\mathrm{inc}}\tag{9.24}\]

where \(\theta_\mathrm{inc}\) is the incidence angle. At \(\theta_\mathrm{inc} = 45°\), \(\delta_\mathrm{gr} = \sqrt{2}\,\delta_r\).

docs.title: 9.3.3 SAR Modes of Operation
docs.text:
Stripmap SAR: The antenna beam is fixed relative to the platform. The synthetic aperture length is \(L_\mathrm{SA} = \lambda R / D\), and azimuth resolution equals \(D/2\) as derived above. Continuous strip mapping trades unlimited along-track coverage for fixed azimuth resolution.

Spotlight SAR: The antenna steers electronically or mechanically to dwell on a specific patch, extending the synthetic aperture to \(L_\mathrm{SA} \gg \lambda R/D\). Azimuth resolution is now:

\[\delta_\mathrm{az}^\mathrm{spot} = \frac{\lambda R}{2 L_\mathrm{SA}}\tag{9.25}\]

Spotlight mode achieves sub-0.1 m azimuth resolution at the cost of limited area coverage and more complex Doppler processing (non-linear phase history).

ScanSAR: The beam steps in elevation to cover multiple sub-swaths, widening total swath at the cost of reduced azimuth resolution (reduced dwell per sub-swath). Total swath width can be increased 3–5× compared to stripmap.

Burst-mode (TOPS): Terrain Observation with Progressive Scans (TOPS) sweeps the beam in azimuth, forcing uniform azimuth resolution across a wide swath; used in Sentinel-1.

docs.title: 9.3.4 Pulse Repetition Frequency Constraints
docs.text:
The PRF must satisfy two competing constraints simultaneously:

\[\begin{align*} \mathrm{PRF} &> \frac{2V}{D} \quad \text{(Nyquist sampling of Doppler history)} \\ \mathrm{PRF} &< \frac{c}{2 \Delta r_\mathrm{swath}} \quad \text{(avoid range ambiguities)} \end{align*}\]

where \(V\) is platform velocity and \(\Delta r_\mathrm{swath}\) is swath extent in slant range. For a \(V = 100\) m/s UAV, \(D = 0.3\) m antenna: PRF \(> 667\) Hz. For a 10 km swath at 45° incidence, \(\Delta r_\mathrm{swath} = 14.1\) km, requiring PRF \(< 10.6\) kHz. The window 667–10,600 Hz is a valid PRF range.

docs.title: 9.3.5 Interferometric SAR and DEM Generation
docs.text:
InSAR uses two SAR images acquired from slightly different positions (baseline \(B_\perp\) perpendicular to the line-of-sight). The interferometric phase difference \(\Delta\phi\) between corresponding pixels is:

\[\Delta\phi = \frac{4\pi}{\lambda} \cdot \frac{B_\perp \sin\theta_\mathrm{inc}}{R} \cdot \Delta h\tag{9.28}\]

where \(\Delta h\) is the terrain height difference. The height ambiguity (height difference producing \(2\pi\) phase change) is:

\[h_\mathrm{amb} = \frac{\lambda R}{2 B_\perp \sin\theta_\mathrm{inc}}\tag{9.29}\]

Phase unwrapping (Goldstein branch-cut algorithm, minimum cost flow) converts wrapped phase to absolute height. At X-band (\(\lambda = 31\) mm), \(R = 5\) km, \(B_\perp = 20\) m, \(\theta = 45°\): \(h_\mathrm{amb} \approx 5.5\) m, providing sub-metre height accuracy after unwrapping. TanDEM-X achieves a global DEM with 12 m posting and 2 m absolute vertical accuracy.

docs.title: 9.3.6 Polarimetric SAR
docs.text:
Full-polarimetric (quad-pol) SAR transmits and receives horizontal (H) and vertical (V) polarisations, yielding the \(2\times2\) scattering matrix \(\mathbf{S}\):

\[\mathbf{S} = \begin{pmatrix} S_{HH} & S_{HV} \\ S_{VH} & S_{VV} \end{pmatrix}\tag{9.30}\]

The Pauli decomposition decomposes \(\mathbf{S}\) into a basis of canonical scatterers:

\[\mathbf{S} = \frac{S_{HH}+S_{VV}}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix} + \frac{S_{HH}-S_{VV}}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix} + S_{HV}\sqrt{2} \begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\tag{9.31}\]

The three Pauli components correspond to: odd-bounce (surface) scattering, double-bounce (corner reflectors, buildings, trees), and volume (diffuse, vegetation). False-colour Pauli composites allow rapid scene interpretation: urban areas appear bright in the double-bounce channel; forests appear bright in the volume channel.

docs.title: 9.3.7 Miniaturised UAV SAR Systems
docs.text: The IMSAR NSP-5 is representative of a modern miniaturised UAV SAR: 1.5 kg, 30 W, Ku-band, 0.3 m resolution in stripmap, deployable on Group 2 UAVs (MTOW 10–25 kg). The Capella Space X-band satellite SAR constellation achieves 0.5 m spotlight resolution from orbit. Key miniaturisation challenges are: (1) achieving sufficient pulse energy within regulatory emission limits; (2) vibration isolation of the antenna to maintain phase coherence; (3) real-time on-board processing (GPU-accelerated backprojection algorithm) to avoid high-bandwidth downlinks.

docs.title: 9.4 LiDAR and 3D Mapping
docs.text: Light detection and ranging (LiDAR) uses pulsed or modulated laser light to measure distance with centimetre-level accuracy. Airborne LiDAR is the enabling technology for high-resolution terrain models, infrastructure inspection, forest characterisation, and autonomous navigation.

docs.title: 9.4.1 LiDAR Operating Principles
docs.text:
Pulsed time-of-flight (ToF) LiDAR measures the round-trip travel time of a laser pulse:

\[R = \frac{c \cdot \Delta t}{2 n}\tag{9.32}\]

where \(\Delta t\) is time delay between transmit and receive, and \(n\) is refractive index of air (\(\approx 1.0003\)). Timing resolution of 50 ps corresponds to a range precision of \(\approx 7.5\) mm. Laser wavelengths used: 905 nm (lower cost, Class 1 eye-safety with difficulty), 1064 nm (Nd:YAG, high peak power), 1550 nm (erbium-doped fibre, eye-safe at higher power, preferred for aviation).

Geiger-mode APD arrays operate individual avalanche photodiodes in single-photon Geiger mode. A single reflected photon triggers an avalanche and is registered as a detection event. Lidar Associates’ Jigsaw system demonstrated 1.6 billion pulses/second with mm-level resolution. Very low pulse energy is required, permitting high PRF and dense point clouds.

FMCW LiDAR (frequency-modulated continuous wave) transmits a chirped laser and measures range by the beat frequency between transmitted and received signals:

\[f_\mathrm{beat} = \frac{2 R \cdot \Delta f}{c \cdot T_\mathrm{sweep}}\tag{9.33}\]

where \(\Delta f\) is chirp bandwidth and \(T_\mathrm{sweep}\) is sweep period. FMCW also inherently measures radial velocity from the Doppler shift:

\[v_r = \frac{f_\mathrm{Doppler} \cdot \lambda}{2}\tag{9.34}\]

This simultaneous range and velocity measurement makes FMCW LiDAR attractive for autonomous vehicle obstacle avoidance. Companies including Aeva, Aurora, and Luminar have commercialised FMCW LiDAR.

docs.title: 9.4.2 Point Cloud Metrics and Full-Waveform Analysis
docs.text:
Airborne LiDAR point density (points per square metre) is:

\[\rho_\mathrm{pts} = \frac{\mathrm{PRF} \cdot n_\mathrm{lines}}{V_\mathrm{GS} \cdot W_\mathrm{scan}}\tag{9.35}\]

where \(n_\mathrm{lines}\) is scan lines per second, \(V_\mathrm{GS}\) is ground speed, \(W_\mathrm{scan}\) is scan strip width. Typical topographic mapping requires \(\geq 4\) pts/m\(^2\); structural inspection requires \(\geq 50\) pts/m\(^2\).

Full-waveform LiDAR digitises the entire returned pulse at 1–2 GHz sampling rate, yielding a waveform \(I(t)\) that encodes the vertical distribution of reflecting surfaces. Decomposition by Gaussian fitting:

\[I(t) = \sum_{k=1}^{N} A_k \exp\!\left(-\frac{(t - t_k)^2}{2\sigma_k^2}\right)\tag{9.36}\]

extracts \(N\) discrete returns with amplitude \(A_k\), range \(R_k = c t_k/2\), and pulse width \(\sigma_k\). This enables canopy penetration for forest biomass estimation, detection of low-lying terrain under vegetation, and characterisation of surface roughness.

docs.title: 9.4.3 3D Mapping Pipeline
docs.text:
The airborne LiDAR mapping pipeline integrates multiple sensor streams:

\[\mathbf{p}_\mathrm{world} = \mathbf{T}_\mathrm{world}^\mathrm{IMU}(t) \cdot \mathbf{T}_\mathrm{IMU}^\mathrm{laser} \cdot \mathbf{p}_\mathrm{laser}\tag{9.37}\]

where \(\mathbf{p}_\mathrm{laser} = [R\cos\theta, R\sin\theta, 0]^T\) is the point in laser-scanner frame, \(\mathbf{T}_\mathrm{IMU}^\mathrm{laser}\) is the boresight calibration transform (determined in a calibration flight), and \(\mathbf{T}_\mathrm{world}^\mathrm{IMU}(t)\) is the IMU/GNSS trajectory. GNSS-aided inertial navigation provides position accuracy \(\leq 5\) cm (RTK GNSS) and angular accuracy \(\leq 0.02°\) (tactical-grade IMU), driving absolute point accuracy of 2–5 cm vertically.

LiDAR SLAM algorithms (LOAM, LIO-SAM) fuse point clouds with IMU data to estimate ego-motion without GPS, critical for indoor or GPS-denied environments. The LIO-SAM factor graph optimises IMU preintegration factors, LiDAR odometry factors, and GPS factors simultaneously using GTSAM.

docs.title: 9.5 SIGINT and ELINT Payloads
docs.text: Signals Intelligence (SIGINT) payloads are passive electronic sensors that intercept, record, and analyse electromagnetic emissions. SIGINT divides into Communications Intelligence (COMINT, intercepting communications signals) and Electronic Intelligence (ELINT, characterising radar and electronic systems).

docs.title: 9.5.1 Electronic Support Measures (ESM)
docs.text:
An ESM system is fundamentally a broad-band receiver covering 0.1–18 GHz (sometimes 40 GHz) that detects, measures, and classifies emitters of interest. Key functions:

  1. Frequency measurement: Instantaneous frequency measurement (IFM) receiver resolves frequency to 1 MHz accuracy within nanoseconds.

  2. Direction finding (DF): Determines the azimuth to the emitter.

  3. Pulse parameter extraction: RF frequency, pulse width, pulse repetition interval (PRI), scan period, antenna polarisation.

  4. Emitter identification: Match measured parameters against an emitter library (Electronic Order of Battle, EOB).

docs.title: 9.5.2 Direction Finding Techniques
docs.text:
Angle-of-Arrival (AOA) interferometry exploits the phase difference between signals received at two antennas separated by baseline \(d\):

\[\Delta\phi = \frac{2\pi d \sin\theta}{\lambda}\tag{9.38}\]

where \(\theta\) is the bearing to the emitter. Solving for \(\theta\):

\[\theta = \arcsin\!\left(\frac{\lambda \Delta\phi}{2\pi d}\right)\tag{9.39}\]

Ambiguities arise when \(d > \lambda/2\) (the phase difference exceeds \(2\pi\)). Multi-baseline interferometers (short, medium, and long baselines) resolve ambiguities: the short baseline (typically \(d = \lambda/2\)) provides unambiguous but coarse angle; the long baseline (up to \(10\lambda\)) provides fine resolution. DF accuracy \(\sigma_\theta\):

\[\sigma_\theta = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi d \cos\theta \cdot \mathrm{SNR}^{1/2}}\tag{9.40}\]

TDOA (Time Difference of Arrival): Multiple UAVs or sensors measure the arrival time difference of the same emitter signal. Two TDOA measurements from three platforms yield two hyperbolic LOBs whose intersection fixes the emitter position. TDOA accuracy depends on timing synchronisation (GPS PPS to 100 ns) and signal bandwidth.

docs.title: 9.5.3 Software-Defined Radio SIGINT Platforms
docs.text:
Modern SIGINT payloads are almost universally SDR-based, providing reconfigurability across frequency bands and waveforms:

  • HackRF One: 1 MHz–6 GHz; 20 MHz BW; 8-bit ADC; $320. Useful for hobby/research.

  • Ettus USRP B210: 70 MHz–6 GHz; 56 MHz BW; 12-bit ADC; \(\approx\)$1,100. Research/academic.

  • Pentek Jade XMC: DC–3 GHz; 3.2 GS/s; 16-bit; rugged; MIL-grade.

  • Mercury Systems ECDR-214: 2-channel wideband; VITA 57.1 FMC; FPGA processing.

The instantaneous dynamic range requirement for a military SIGINT payload is typically \(>70\) dB (to simultaneously detect weak signals in the presence of strong interferers), driving ADC bit depth to 14–16 bits and requiring low-noise front-end LNAs with \(<2\) dB noise figure.

docs.title: 9.6 Weapons Payloads for UCAVs
docs.text: Unmanned combat aerial vehicles (UCAVs) carry a range of precision guided munitions (PGMs), air-to-surface missiles, and loitering munitions. The integration of weapons onto UAV platforms introduces unique challenges related to structural certification, arming safety, and release dynamics.

docs.title: 9.6.1 Electrical and Mechanical Integration
docs.text:
The NATO standard electrical interface for smart weapons is MIL-STD-1760, defining a 38-pin electrical connector that carries:

  • MIL-STD-1553B data bus (1 Mbit/s) for weapon initiation/status commands

  • 28 V DC power for weapon electronics

  • Umbilical safety wire (fires weapon enable when released)

  • Fuze arming and firing discrete signals

  • High-speed Ethernet (1000BASE-T) in the latest Block D revision

The suspension and release unit (SRU) must provide the correct ejection force to clear the weapon from the aerodynamic wake before fins deploy. Ejection force \(F_e\) must satisfy:

\[F_e \geq m_w \left( a_\mathrm{escape} + g \sin\gamma + \frac{q S_\mathrm{ref} C_{D,w}}{m_w} \right)\tag{9.41}\]

where \(m_w\) is weapon mass, \(a_\mathrm{escape}\) is required separation acceleration (\(\geq 9.81\) m/s\(^2\)), \(\gamma\) is flight path angle, \(q\) is dynamic pressure, and \(C_{D,w}\) is weapon drag coefficient.

docs.title: 9.6.2 Representative Guided Weapons
docs.text:
GBU-39 Small Diameter Bomb (SDB): Mass 110 kg; GPS/INS guidance; 13 cm diameter; 1.8 m length; glide range \(>110\) km from 40,000 ft release; CEP \(<5\) m. The SDB’s small cross-section (0.013 m\(^2\)) allows four weapons per standard 1000 lb hardpoint station. SDB II (GBU-53/B) adds tri-mode seeker (MMW, IR, semi-active laser) for moving target engagement.

AGM-114 Hellfire: Mass 49 kg; length 1.63 m; diameter 178 mm; warhead 9 kg shaped charge HEAT; range 8 km; guidance: semi-active laser (SAL) homing or millimetre-wave (MMW) radar seeker (AGM-114L Longbow). Variants include thermobaric (AGM-114N) and kinetic energy rod (AGM-114R9X) warheads. Reaper (MQ-9) carries four Hellfire on two wing pylons.

Brimstone: BAE Systems dual-mode SAL/MMW missile; mass 48.5 kg; range 12+ km (powered, sea-skimming capable); active MMW seeker (Ku-band FMCW) enables autonomous target selection within a pre-defined engagement zone, permitting salvo firing without per-missile laser designation. Brimstone is qualified on the Protector (MQ-9B).

The guidance accuracy for a laser-homing seeker follows a proportional navigation law; the miss distance (CEP) is a function of seeker noise and navigation ratio \(N'\):

\[\mathrm{CEP} = K_\sigma \cdot \sigma_\varepsilon \cdot t_\mathrm{go}^2\tag{9.42}\]

where \(\sigma_\varepsilon\) is seeker angular noise (mrad), \(t_\mathrm{go}\) is time-to-go (s), and \(K_\sigma\) depends on navigation ratio (typically \(K_\sigma \approx 0.3\) for \(N' = 4\)).

docs.title: 9.7 Cargo and Logistics Payloads
docs.text: The application of UAVs to logistics — medical resupply, e-commerce last-mile delivery, and military forward resupply — has driven a distinct class of payload integration requirements focused on load carriage, quick release, and delivery accuracy.

docs.title: 9.7.1 Load Carrying and Centre of Gravity Management
docs.text:
For a UAV with gross take-off weight \(W_\mathrm{GTOW}\), the payload CG offset \(\Delta x\) shifts the total CG by:

\[\Delta x_\mathrm{total} = \frac{m_\mathrm{payload} \cdot \Delta x_\mathrm{payload}}{m_\mathrm{payload} + m_\mathrm{airframe}}\tag{9.43}\]

CG shift must remain within the flight envelope CG envelope (typically \(\pm 5\)% MAC for fixed-wing, \(\pm 30\) mm from gimbal centre for multirotor). Adjustable payload rails or ballast systems compensate for variable payload masses.

Vibration isolation of fragile cargo (medical diagnostics, blood products) uses passive elastomeric isolators designed so:

\[f_\mathrm{nat} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} < \frac{f_\mathrm{vibration}}{2}\tag{9.44}\]

to place the natural frequency below the dominant airframe vibration frequency (propeller fundamental and harmonics, typically 80–200 Hz for small multirotor). Isolation effectiveness at frequency ratio \(r = f/f_\mathrm{nat}\):

\[T_\mathrm{isolation} = \sqrt{\frac{1 + (2\zeta r)^2}{(1 - r^2)^2 + (2\zeta r)^2}}\tag{9.45}\]

For \(r = 10\) and \(\zeta = 0.05\): \(T_\mathrm{isolation} \approx 0.011\) (-39 dB), meaning only 1.1% of vibration amplitude is transmitted to the payload.

docs.title: 9.7.2 Precision Delivery Systems
docs.text:
Zipline uses a fixed-wing UAV that flies overhead and drops a package on a winch-lowered cord, achieving \(\pm 3\) m delivery accuracy in rural Rwanda and Ghana. A simple drop delivery without winch relies on GPS waypoint positioning plus wind compensation:

\[x_\mathrm{release} = x_\mathrm{target} - \left( V_\mathrm{UAV} + V_\mathrm{wind} \right) \cdot \sqrt{\frac{2H}{g}}\tag{9.46}\]

where \(H\) is release altitude and \(\sqrt{2H/g}\) is approximate free-fall time. Wing (Alphabet) hovers the delivery drone above the target and lowers the package on a tether, achieving \(\pm 5\) m accuracy without landing. Amazon Prime Air uses sensor fusion (computer vision + GPS) for \(\pm 30\) cm positioning.

docs.title: 9.8 Electronic Warfare Payloads
docs.text: Electronic warfare payloads carried by UAVs range from small battery-powered spot jammers on loitering munitions to sophisticated multi-function EW suites on MALE/HALE platforms. EW payloads are categorised as: Electronic Attack (EA), Electronic Protection (EP), and Electronic Support (ES).

docs.title: 9.8.1 Radar Jamming Principles
docs.text:
For a jammer to effectively deny a radar’s ability to detect a target, the jammer-to-signal (J/S) ratio at the radar receiver must exceed a threshold \(\Gamma_J\). The J/S ratio for a stand-off jammer is:

\[\frac{J}{S} = \frac{P_J G_J \sigma_T R_T^4}{P_T G_T^2 \lambda^2 R_J^2 (4\pi)^2}\tag{9.47}\]

where \(P_J\) is jammer power, \(G_J\) is jammer antenna gain toward the radar, \(\sigma_T\) is target RCS, \(R_T\) is target-to-radar range, \(P_T\) is radar transmit power, \(G_T\) is radar antenna gain, and \(R_J\) is jammer-to-radar range. This shows J/S improves as \(R_J^{-2}\) while signal falls as \(R_T^{-4}\) — jamming becomes relatively easier as the jammer approaches the radar.

Digital RF Memory (DRFM) Jammer: A DRFM samples the incoming radar pulse, stores it in digital memory, and retransmits it with programmable delay and Doppler modifications. This creates false target echoes that the radar cannot distinguish from real targets. The false target range offset:

\[\Delta R_\mathrm{false} = \frac{c \cdot \Delta\tau_\mathrm{delay}}{2}\tag{9.48}\]

A 100 ns additional delay creates a false target 15 m further away. DRFM jammers are the primary counter-measure against modern pulse Doppler and FMCW seekers.

docs.title: 9.8.2 GPS Denial
docs.text:
The minimum received GPS signal power at the antenna is \(-130\) dBm (L1 C/A). A GPS jammer with EIRP of \(P_J G_J\) watts denies GPS reception within a radius \(R_J\) where:

\[R_J = \sqrt{\frac{P_J G_J}{4\pi \cdot P_\mathrm{threshold} \cdot (C/N_0)_\mathrm{required}}}\tag{9.49}\]

More practically, GPS receivers track signals when the jamming-to-noise ratio \(J/N_0 > C/N_0 - 3\) dB. At this margin, tracking becomes unreliable. A 1 W omnidirectional GPS jammer (\(0\) dBi) denies standard GPS receivers at roughly 25 km radius (free space); in practice terrain and blockage reduce this to 5–15 km for airborne jammers.

docs.title: 9.9 Payload Integration Engineering
docs.text: Payload integration is a systems engineering discipline that bridges payload performance requirements with airframe structural, electrical, and thermal constraints. Failures in integration — unexpected vibration, EMI corruption of sensor data, CG shifts beyond limits — are a leading source of mission failure in operational UAV programmes.

docs.title: 9.9.1 Weight, Balance, and Mass Properties
docs.text:
The payload mass fraction, defined as \(f_\mathrm{pl} = m_\mathrm{payload}/m_\mathrm{GTOW}\), directly determines endurance through the Breguet range equation. For a multirotor UAV:

\[E_\mathrm{hover} = \frac{m_\mathrm{battery} \cdot E_\mathrm{sp}}{P_\mathrm{hover}}\tag{9.50}\] \[P_\mathrm{hover} = \sqrt{\frac{(m_\mathrm{GTOW} g)^3}{2 \rho A_\mathrm{disk}}}\tag{9.51}\]

where \(A_\mathrm{disk}\) is the total rotor disk area and \(\rho\) is air density. Adding payload mass \(\Delta m\) reduces endurance by:

\[\frac{\Delta E}{E} \approx -\frac{3}{2} \cdot \frac{\Delta m}{m_\mathrm{GTOW}}\tag{9.52}\]

A 10% payload mass increase reduces hover endurance by approximately 15%.

docs.title: 9.9.2 Electrical Interface Standards
docs.text:
Table 9.4 summarises the principal electrical and data bus standards used for UAV payload integration.

Table 9.4. Payload Electrical Interface Standards Standard Type Data Rate Max Nodes Application MIL-STD-1553B Serial, half-duplex 1 Mbit/s 31 RTs Weapons, avionics RS-422 Serial, full-duplex 10 Mbit/s 10 receivers Sensors, comms RS-485 Serial, half-duplex 10 Mbit/s 32 nodes Multi-drop bus CAN bus Serial, half-duplex 1 Mbit/s 127 nodes Actuation, ESC 100BASE-TX Eth Full-duplex 100 Mbit/s Unlimited Video, high-BW 1000BASE-T Eth Full-duplex 1 Gbit/s Unlimited SAR, hyperspectral ARINC 429 Serial, unidirectional 100 kbit/s 1 Tx/20 Rx Legacy avionics SpaceWire Serial, full-duplex 200 Mbit/s 32 nodes Space/mil sensors

Hot-plug protection must prevent inrush currents from damaging power rails when payloads are connected with power applied. A simple solution uses a P-channel MOSFET with gate-drive slew rate limiting (inrush \(= C_\mathrm{bypass} \cdot dV/dt\)). For a payload with 1 mF bypass capacitance and a target inrush \(<1\) A: \(dV/dt < 1000\) V/s, achieved with a 10 ms power-up ramp.

docs.title: 9.9.3 Vibration Isolation Design
docs.text:
Airframe vibrations originate primarily from rotor/propeller blade passing frequencies. For an electric multirotor with \(N_p\) propeller blades at RPM \(n\):

\[f_\mathrm{BPF} = \frac{N_p \cdot n}{60}\tag{9.53}\]

A hex-rotor at 8000 RPM with 3-blade propellers: \(f_\mathrm{BPF} = 400\) Hz. A 3-axis passive isolator using D30 polymer mounts achieves 20 dB insertion loss at 400 Hz when natural frequency is designed at \(f_\mathrm{nat} \approx 25\) Hz (\(r = 16\)).

docs.title: 9.9.4 Thermal Management
docs.text:
Payload waste heat must be conducted and/or convected to the airstream. The thermal resistance from payload junction to ambient:

\[\theta_{j-a} = \theta_{j-c} + \theta_{c-h} + \theta_{h-a}\tag{9.54}\]

where \(\theta_{j-c}\) is junction-to-case (device), \(\theta_{c-h}\) is case-to-heatsink (TIM), and \(\theta_{h-a}\) is heatsink-to-ambient. For a 10 W payload in a 60°C ambient with maximum junction temperature 125°C:

\[\theta_{j-a} \leq \frac{125 - 60}{10} = 6.5\,\mathrm{K/W}\tag{9.55}\]

Forced convection cooling achieves \(h \approx 50\) W/m\(^2\) K on a finned surface. Required fin area: \(A_\mathrm{fin} = P / (h \cdot \Delta T) = 10 / (50 \times 30) = 0.0067\) m\(^2 = 67\) cm\(^2\).

docs.title: 9.9.5 EMI/EMC Compliance
docs.text:
MIL-STD-461G specifies emission and susceptibility limits for equipment installed on military vehicles and aircraft. Key requirements:

  • CE101/CE102: conducted emissions on power leads (30 Hz–10 MHz)

  • RE102: radiated emissions from equipment (2 MHz–18 GHz)

  • CS101/CS114: conducted susceptibility

  • RS103: radiated susceptibility (field strength 10–200 V/m)

Digital payload processors switching at clock frequencies 100 MHz–2 GHz radiate clock harmonics across the RF spectrum. Shielding attenuation for a metal enclosure with aperture:

\[\mathrm{SE}_\mathrm{aperture} = 20 \log_{10}\!\left(\frac{\lambda}{2L_\mathrm{aperture}}\right) \quad \text{for } L_\mathrm{aperture} < \lambda/2\tag{9.56}\]

An aperture of 10 mm at 10 GHz (\(\lambda = 30\) mm): SE \(= 20\log_{10}(30/20) = 3.5\) dB — marginal. Waveguide-below-cutoff honeycomb panels achieve \(>100\) dB shielding for the same physical opening by cutting off propagation of wavelengths \(\lambda > 2d_\mathrm{cell}\).

Figure 9.1. Three-axis gimbal stabilisation control architecture showing inner rate loop and outer position loop. The IMU is mounted on the gimbal head itself to provide inertial stabilisation independent of airframe motion. Figure 9.2. Miniaturised UAV SAR payload block diagram showing transmit (TX) waveform generation, power amplification, T/R switching, receive LNA, downconversion, and digital signal processing chain. Motion compensation uses INS/GNSS navigation data to correct phase history.

docs.title: 9.9.6 Payload Management System Architecture
docs.text:
The payload management system (PMS) is the onboard computing and software layer that orchestrates multiple payload subsystems, manages recording, and provides the interface to the ground control station. Modern PMS architectures use a publish-subscribe middleware (DDS or ROS2) to decouple payload drivers from mission logic. Key PMS functions:

  1. Payload health monitoring: Periodic health-check messages; watchdog timers; power cycling on fault.

  2. Recording management: Circular buffer with time-tagged sensor data; metadata injection (GPS, IMU, time); STANAG 4609 KLV metadata for EO/IR video.

  3. Tasking and scheduling: Priority-based payload tasking queue; sensor slewing commands; coordinate transforms.

  4. Data compression: H.264/H.265 video encoding; LAS compression for point clouds; CCSDS lossless compression for science data.

  5. Downlink management: STANAG 4607 GMTI reports; STANAG 4609 video; prioritised delivery over constrained satellite or radio links.

docs.title: 9.10 Conclusion
docs.text:
Payloads define the operational value of any unmanned system. The design and integration of EO/IR sensors, SAR, LiDAR, SIGINT, weapons, cargo, and EW equipment demands mastery of optics, microwave engineering, structural mechanics, power electronics, and software engineering. The trend toward sensor fusion — combining passive EO/IR with active SAR and LiDAR, coupled with onboard AI for real-time exploitation — is transforming UAV payloads from simple data-collecting devices into autonomous battlespace decision-support systems. The following chapters on Software and AI (Chapter 10) and Communications (Chapter 12) examine the enabling digital infrastructure that extracts operational value from the raw data these sensors produce.

Key quantitative takeaways:

  • GSD \(= H \cdot p / (f \times 10^3)\); for sub-10 cm GSD at 300 m altitude, focal lengths of 15–25 mm with 4 µ m pitch sensors are required.

  • SAR azimuth resolution \(= D/2\) (independent of range); range resolution \(= c/(2B)\) requiring \(>500\) MHz bandwidth for sub-30 cm resolution.

  • Thermal cameras: NETD \(< 50\) mK required for reliable target recognition; cooled MCT achieves \(< 20\) mK; uncooled VOx achieves 40–80 mK.

  • Vibration isolation: target natural frequency \(<\)20 Hz for 40 dB+ rejection of propeller harmonics at 200–400 Hz.

  • DRFM jammers create false targets with delay-controlled range offset \(\Delta R = c \Delta\tau / 2\).

docs.title: Chapter 10: Software, Autonomy and Artificial Intelligence
10.1 Introduction to UAV Software Architecture
docs.text:
The software stack of a modern unmanned aerial vehicle is among the most complex embedded systems in production engineering. It must concurrently execute hard real-time control loops at 400 Hz, run sensor fusion algorithms at 50–200 Hz, interface with heterogeneous hardware peripherals over a dozen bus protocols, support mission management logic, stream gigabytes of sensor data to onboard storage and downlinks, and increasingly, run deep neural network inference for real-time perception — all within severe constraints on mass (\(<200\) g compute node), power (\(<15\) W), and vibration, temperature, and EMI tolerance.

This chapter develops the full software stack from the hardware abstraction layer through flight control algorithms, mission planning, computer vision, SLAM, AI/ML inference, swarm coordination, simulation, cybersecurity, and airworthiness certification. Every subsystem is treated quantitatively, with reference to open-source implementations (ArduPilot, PX4, ROS2, ORB-SLAM3), academic literature, and military standards.

docs.title: 10.2.1 ArduPilot Architecture
docs.text:
ArduPilot is the world’s most widely deployed open-source autopilot framework, with over one million vehicles flying on ArduPilot firmware as of 2024. Its architecture is structured into three tiers:

Tier 1 — Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL). The AP_HAL namespace defines a pure-virtual C++ interface for every hardware resource: UART, I2C, SPI, PWM, ADC, storage, and scheduler. Platform-specific implementations (AP_HAL_ChibiOS for Pixhawk hardware running ChibiOS RTOS, AP_HAL_Linux for Raspberry Pi/Navio2, AP_HAL_SITL for software-in-the-loop simulation) inherit from AP_HAL::HAL and implement the virtual methods. This strict separation means that vehicle code (Copter, Plane, Rover, Sub) is portable across hardware without modification.

Tier 2 — Libraries. The libraries/ directory contains sensor drivers (AP_InertialSensor, AP_GPS, AP_Baro, AP_Compass), state estimators (AP_NavEKF3 — a 24-state extended Kalman filter), controllers (AC_PID, AC_AttitudeControl, AC_PosControl), and utilities (AP_Math, AP_AHRS, AP_Mission). The EKF3 state vector includes: position (3), velocity (3), attitude quaternion (4), IMU bias (6), earth magnetic field (3), and body magnetic field (3), plus optional wind velocity (3) and terrain height (1).

Tier 3 — Vehicle code. ArduCopter/, ArduPlane/, etc. define the top-level vehicle loop (loop()/fast_loop() structure), flight mode FSM, and vehicle-specific control mixing.

The ArduPilot scheduler runs tasks at fixed rates using a cooperative scheduler built on the HAL timer. Each task has a declared period and maximum execution time (budget):

\[U_\mathrm{CPU} = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{C_i}{T_i} \leq 1\tag{10.1}\]

where \(C_i\) is worst-case execution time and \(T_i\) is period of task \(i\). ArduPilot’s fast loop (400 Hz, \(T = 2.5\) ms) executes attitude control and motor output with a budget of \(<400\) µ s, leaving headroom for medium (50 Hz) and slow (10 Hz) tasks.

docs.title: 10.2.2 PX4 Architecture and uORB Middleware
docs.text:
PX4 Autopilot uses a fundamentally different architecture centred on the uORB (Micro Object Request Broker) publish-subscribe middleware. Modules communicate exclusively by publishing to and subscribing from named message topics (defined as .msg files), with no direct function calls between modules. This enforces modularity and testability.

Each module runs as an independent NuttX (RTOS) task or workqueue callback, publishing its outputs at a defined rate. Key modules:

  • sensors: reads and calibrates all IMU, barometer, magnetometer; publishes sensor_combined

  • ekf2: 23-state iterated EKF; subscribes sensor_combined, publishes vehicle_odometry, estimator_status

  • mc_att_control: multi-copter attitude controller; subscribes vehicle_attitude_setpoint, publishes actuator_controls

  • mc_pos_control: position/velocity controller; publishes attitude setpoints

  • commander: flight mode FSM, arming logic, health monitoring

  • navigator: waypoint sequencing, geofence enforcement

  • mavlink: MAVLink protocol bridge to GCS

The uORB layer implements lock-free single-producer multi-consumer queues with priority-based semaphore signalling. Publication latency is \(<10\) µ s on NuttX; copy overhead for a 256-byte message is \(<5\) µ s.

docs.title: 10.2.3 RTOS Fundamentals for Flight Control
docs.text:
Real-Time Operating Systems used in flight control (NuttX, ChibiOS, FreeRTOS, VxWorks) implement preemptive priority-based scheduling. The rate-monotonic scheduling (RMS) algorithm assigns priorities inversely proportional to period; for \(N\) periodic tasks, the CPU utilisation bound for guaranteed schedulability is:

\[U \leq N\left(2^{1/N} - 1\right) \xrightarrow{N\to\infty} \ln 2 \approx 0.693\tag{10.2}\]

The deadline monotonic scheduling (DMS) algorithm extends RMS to tasks with deadlines \(D_i < T_i\). Worst-case response time analysis (WCRT) for task \(i\):

\[R_i^{(n+1)} = C_i + \sum_{j \in \mathcal{H}(i)} \left\lceil \frac{R_i^{(n)}}{T_j} \right\rceil C_j\tag{10.3}\]

where \(\mathcal{H}(i)\) is the set of tasks with higher priority than \(i\). Convergence is achieved when \(R_i^{(n+1)} = R_i^{(n)}\). For flight control, the attitude control task at 400 Hz (\(T = 2.5\) ms) requires \(R_\mathrm{attitude} < 2.5\) ms; WCRT analysis with ChibiOS interrupt latency and context switch time (\(<10\) µ s) confirms feasibility.

Interrupt latency is the delay from hardware interrupt assertion to first instruction of the ISR. With a Cortex-M7 at 480 MHz, interrupt latency is 12 cycles \(= 25\) ns, satisfying even microsecond-level timing requirements.

docs.title: 10.2.4 Middleware: ROS and microROS
docs.text:
The Robot Operating System (ROS2) provides a full-featured middleware layer above the RTOS, using the DDS (Data Distribution Service) standard for IPC. ROS2 nodes communicate via topics (publish/subscribe), services (request/reply), and actions (goal/result/feedback). The quality-of-service (QoS) settings (reliability, durability, deadline) allow tuning for real-time applications.

microROS ports the ROS2 client library to microcontrollers (\(<1\) MB RAM) running bare-metal or RTOS, using the micro-XRCE-DDS transport to bridge UART/USB to a ROS2-enabled host computer. This allows a Cortex-M4 flight controller to appear as a ROS2 node, publishing sensor_msgs/Imu and subscribing to geometry_msgs/TwistStamped setpoints — a common pattern for integrating PX4 with a companion computer running ROS2 mission logic.

docs.title: 10.2.5 Software-in-the-Loop and Hardware-in-the-Loop Simulation
docs.text:
SITL runs the full autopilot firmware binary (ArduPilot or PX4) on a Linux host with a simulated flight dynamics model (JSBSim for fixed-wing, MultiRotor dynamics for copters). The firmware receives simulated sensor data and outputs actuator commands to the dynamics model, forming a closed simulation loop:

\[\mathbf{x}_{k+1} = f(\mathbf{x}_k, \mathbf{u}_k, \mathbf{w}_k)\tag{10.4}\]

where \(\mathbf{x}\) is the flight dynamics state (position, velocity, attitude, angular rates), \(\mathbf{u}\) is the actuator command vector, and \(\mathbf{w}\) is environmental disturbance (wind, turbulence). SITL enables regression testing of mission planning logic, geofence enforcement, failsafe behaviours, and navigation algorithms without hardware risk.

HITL uses real autopilot hardware but injects simulated sensor data via the hardware’s serial ports, exercising the firmware on real silicon to test timing behaviour and hardware-dependent code paths. HITL is mandatory before first flights of new firmware on new hardware.

docs.title: 10.3.1 MAVLink Mission Protocol
docs.text:
MAVLink is the de-facto standard lightweight messaging protocol for UAV ground control. Version 2 (MAVLink 2.0) provides a 14-byte header with 24-bit message ID space and optional signing. Mission commands follow the MAV_CMD namespace (Table 10.1).

Table 10.1. Key MAVLink Mission Commands (MAV_CMD) Command ID Name Parameters 16 NAV_WAYPOINT Hold time (s), acceptance radius (m), pass-through, yaw (°), lat, lon, alt 17 NAV_LOITER_UNLIM Radius (m), yaw, lat, lon, alt 18 NAV_LOITER_TURNS Turns, radius, lat, lon, alt 19 NAV_LOITER_TIME Time (s), radius, lat, lon, alt 20 NAV_RETURN_TO_LAUNCH — 21 NAV_LAND Abort alt (m), land mode, lat, lon, yaw 22 NAV_TAKEOFF Min pitch, yaw, lat, lon, alt 93 NAV_DELAY Delay (s), hour, minute, second 177 DO_SET_SERVO Servo number, PWM value 178 DO_REPEAT_SERVO Servo, PWM, repeat count, delay (s) 181 DO_DIGICAM_CONTROL On/off, zoom step, zoom pos, focus lock, shot, command ID 201 DO_SET_ROI ROI mode, WP index, ROI index, lat, lon, alt

The MAVLink mission upload sequence: GCS sends MISSION_COUNT (total items); UAV acknowledges; GCS sends each MISSION_ITEM_INT (integer lat/lon in \(10^{-7}\) degrees for precision); UAV ACKs each item; GCS sends MISSION_ACK. The current waypoint index is broadcast in heartbeat telemetry.

docs.title: 10.3.2 Path Planning Algorithms
docs.text:
A* Algorithm: Finds the minimum-cost path from start node \(s\) to goal \(g\) in a graph. The heuristic evaluation function:

\[f(n) = g(n) + h(n)\tag{10.5}\]

where \(g(n)\) is the known cost from \(s\) to node \(n\), and \(h(n)\) is an admissible heuristic estimate of cost from \(n\) to \(g\). For grid-based obstacle maps, the Euclidean distance heuristic \(h(n) = \|n - g\|_2\) is admissible (never overestimates). A* is optimal and complete when \(h\) is admissible and consistent.

Rapidly-exploring Random Tree (RRT): A sampling-based planner that builds a tree by random sampling of the configuration space. At each iteration, a random point \(q_\mathrm{rand}\) is sampled; the nearest tree node \(q_\mathrm{near}\) is extended by step \(\delta\) toward \(q_\mathrm{rand}\):

\[q_\mathrm{new} = q_\mathrm{near} + \delta \cdot \frac{q_\mathrm{rand} - q_\mathrm{near}}{\|q_\mathrm{rand} - q_\mathrm{near}\|}\tag{10.6}\]

If \(q_\mathrm{new}\) is collision-free, it is added to the tree. RRT* adds a rewiring step that asymptotically converges to the optimal path:

\[\text{Rewire: if } c(q_\mathrm{near}) + d(q_\mathrm{near}, q') < c(q'), \text{ set } \mathrm{parent}(q') = q_\mathrm{near}\tag{10.7}\]

Minimum-Snap Trajectory for quadrotors: The minimum-snap formulation minimises the integral of snap (4th derivative of position) to produce smooth, dynamically feasible trajectories. For a segment from \(t_0\) to \(t_f\), position is represented as a degree-7 polynomial:

\[p(t) = \sum_{k=0}^{7} c_k t^k\tag{10.8}\]

The cost functional:

\[J = \int_0^T \left\| \frac{d^4 \mathbf{p}}{dt^4} \right\|^2 dt\tag{10.9}\]

is minimised subject to boundary conditions (position, velocity, acceleration, jerk at waypoints). This yields a quadratic programme (QP) that can be solved efficiently with standard QP solvers (OSQP, qpOASES).

docs.title: 10.4.1 Image Processing Pipeline
docs.text:
The standard computer vision pipeline for a UAV perception system consists of:

  1. Capture and synchronisation: Hardware trigger synchronises camera frame with IMU timestamp (\(<1\) µ s accuracy); rolling shutter correction requires IMU interpolation.

  2. Preprocessing: Debayering (Malvar-He-Cutler algorithm for \(3\times\) faster vs bilinear with less aliasing); lens distortion correction using calibrated \(\mathbf{K}\) intrinsic matrix and \((k_1, k_2, p_1, p_2, k_3)\) distortion coefficients.

  3. Feature extraction or detection inference.

  4. Downstream task: Detection, tracking, segmentation, depth estimation, or flow.

Camera calibration: the projection of a 3D point \(\mathbf{P}_w = [X, Y, Z]^T\) in world frame to pixel \(\mathbf{p} = [u, v]^T\):

\[\begin{pmatrix} u \\ v \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \mathbf{K} \left[ \mathbf{R} \mid \mathbf{t} \right] \begin{pmatrix} X \\ Y \\ Z \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{K} = \begin{pmatrix} f_x & 0 & c_x \\ 0 & f_y & c_y \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\tag{10.10}\]

where \(f_x, f_y\) are focal lengths in pixels, \((c_x, c_y)\) is the principal point, and \([\mathbf{R}|\mathbf{t}]\) is the extrinsic pose (rotation and translation from world to camera).

docs.title: 10.4.2 Classical Feature Descriptors
docs.text:
SIFT (Scale-Invariant Feature Transform): Detects keypoints at scale-space extrema of the DoG (Difference of Gaussians). Descriptor: 128-dimensional histogram of gradient orientations over \(4\times4\) sub-regions. SIFT is robust to scale and rotation but computationally expensive (patented until 2020, now free).

ORB (Oriented FAST and Rotated BRIEF): Combines FAST corner detector (intensity threshold comparison on a Bresenham circle) with BRIEF descriptor (binary comparison of pixel pairs at a learned sampling pattern). ORB is rotation-invariant (orientation computed from intensity centroid) and 100\(\times\) faster than SIFT at comparable matching precision, making it the standard for real-time mobile and UAV applications.

The optical flow (Lucas-Kanade) algorithm estimates pixel displacement \(\mathbf{v} = [v_x, v_y]^T\) between frames by solving the brightness constancy equation:

\[I_x v_x + I_y v_y + I_t = 0\tag{10.11}\]

In a local window of \(N\) pixels, the least-squares solution is:

\[\begin{pmatrix} v_x \\ v_y \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \sum I_x^2 & \sum I_x I_y \\ \sum I_x I_y & \sum I_y^2 \end{pmatrix}^{-1} \begin{pmatrix} -\sum I_x I_t \\ -\sum I_y I_t \end{pmatrix}\tag{10.12}\]

The \(2\times2\) matrix (the Harris matrix \(\mathbf{M}\)) must be well-conditioned — the minimum eigenvalue \(\lambda_\mathrm{min} > \tau\) ensures reliable flow (Harris corner condition).

docs.title: 10.4.3 Deep Learning Object Detection
docs.text:
The YOLO (You Only Look Once) family of detectors has become the default for onboard UAV inference due to its single-forward-pass architecture. YOLOv8 processes an input image in a single pass through a convolutional backbone (CSPDarknet), neck (PAN-FPN), and detection head.

The detection output for each grid cell \((i,j)\) and anchor \(k\) is a tensor:

\[\hat{\mathbf{y}}_{i,j,k} = \left[ \hat{t}_x, \hat{t}_y, \hat{t}_w, \hat{t}_h, \hat{p}_\mathrm{obj}, \hat{p}_1, …, \hat{p}_C \right]\tag{10.13}\]

where \((t_x, t_y)\) are box centre offsets relative to cell, \((t_w, t_h)\) are log-scale width/height relative to anchor, \(p_\mathrm{obj}\) is objectness score, and \(p_c\) are class probabilities. Decoded bounding box coordinates:

\[\begin{align*} b_x &= \sigma(\hat{t}_x) + c_x \\ b_y &= \sigma(\hat{t}_y) + c_y \\ b_w &= a_w \cdot e^{\hat{t}_w} \\ b_h &= a_h \cdot e^{\hat{t}_h} \end{align*}\]

where \((c_x, c_y)\) are grid cell offsets and \((a_w, a_h)\) are anchor dimensions.

The multi-task loss function:

\[\mathcal{L} = \lambda_\mathrm{coord} \mathcal{L}_\mathrm{box} + \lambda_\mathrm{obj} \mathcal{L}_\mathrm{obj} + \lambda_\mathrm{cls} \mathcal{L}_\mathrm{cls}\tag{10.18}\]

where \(\mathcal{L}_\mathrm{box}\) is CIoU (Complete IoU) loss, \(\mathcal{L}_\mathrm{obj}\) is binary cross-entropy on objectness, and \(\mathcal{L}_\mathrm{cls}\) is cross-entropy on class probabilities. Mean Average Precision (mAP) at IoU threshold 0.5 (mAP@0.5) is the standard benchmark metric.

Representative performance on VisDrone dataset (small object detection): YOLOv8-nano: 18.4 mAP@0.5, 3.2 ms inference (Jetson Orin); YOLOv8-x: 36.2 mAP@0.5, 28 ms inference (Jetson Orin).

docs.title: 10.4.4 Multi-Object Tracking
docs.text:
SORT (Simple Online and Real-time Tracking) combines Kalman filter prediction with IoU-based Hungarian assignment. The Kalman state for each track is \(\mathbf{x} = [u, v, s, r, \dot{u}, \dot{v}, \dot{s}]^T\) where \((u,v)\) is box centre, \(s\) is area, \(r = w/h\) is aspect ratio (assumed constant). Prediction:

\[\hat{\mathbf{x}}_k = \mathbf{F} \mathbf{x}_{k-1}, \quad \hat{\mathbf{P}}_k = \mathbf{F} \mathbf{P}_{k-1} \mathbf{F}^T + \mathbf{Q}\tag{10.19}\]

Update with detection \(\mathbf{z}_k\) (4-element bounding box vector):

\[\begin{align*} \mathbf{K}_k &= \hat{\mathbf{P}}_k \mathbf{H}^T (\mathbf{H} \hat{\mathbf{P}}_k \mathbf{H}^T + \mathbf{R})^{-1} \\ \mathbf{x}_k &= \hat{\mathbf{x}}_k + \mathbf{K}_k (\mathbf{z}_k - \mathbf{H}\hat{\mathbf{x}}_k) \\ \mathbf{P}_k &= (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{K}_k \mathbf{H}) \hat{\mathbf{P}}_k \end{align*}\]

The Hungarian algorithm solves the minimum-cost bipartite matching between \(M\) existing tracks and \(N\) detections in \(O(\max(M,N)^3)\) time. IoU is used as the cost (affinity) metric; tracks with IoU \(<0.3\) are rejected.

DeepSORT augments SORT with a CNN-based appearance descriptor (128-dimensional), using Mahalanobis distance for Kalman-gate filtering and cosine distance in appearance embedding space for track association, dramatically reducing ID switches in crowded scenes.

docs.title: 10.5.1 Feature-Based Visual SLAM: ORB-SLAM3
docs.text:
ORB-SLAM3 is the state-of-the-art monocular, stereo, and RGB-D visual SLAM system. Its architecture divides into three parallel threads:

  1. Tracking: Extracts ORB features; matches to local map; estimates camera pose using EPnP + RANSAC (Perspective-n-Point):

    \[\mathbf{T}_\mathrm{cw} = \arg\min_{\mathbf{T}} \sum_i \rho\!\left(\left\| \mathbf{p}_i - \pi\!\left(\mathbf{T} \mathbf{P}_i\right) \right\|^2\right)\tag{10.23}\]

    where \(\pi(\cdot)\) is the camera projection, \(\rho(\cdot)\) is a robust (Huber) loss.

  2. Local mapping: Triangulates new map points from new keyframes; runs local Bundle Adjustment (BA) optimising a window of recent keyframes and their observed map points.

  3. Loop closing: Detects revisited locations using DBoW2 (Bag-of-Words); performs global BA to correct accumulated drift.

Bundle Adjustment minimises the total reprojection error:

\[E_\mathrm{BA} = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{K}} \sum_{j \in \mathcal{P}_i} \rho\!\left(\left\| \mathbf{p}_{ij} - \pi\!\left(\mathbf{T}_i \mathbf{P}_j\right) \right\|_\mathbf{\Sigma}^2\right)\tag{10.24}\]

over all keyframes \(\mathcal{K}\) and their observed map points \(\mathcal{P}_i\). Gauss-Newton or Levenberg-Marquardt solves this large sparse nonlinear least-squares problem; g2o and Ceres Solver are the standard back-ends.

docs.title: 10.5.2 LiDAR SLAM: LIO-SAM
docs.text:
LIO-SAM (LiDAR-Inertial Odometry via Smoothing and Mapping) tightly couples LiDAR scan matching with IMU preintegration in a factor graph framework. The factor graph has four factor types:

  • IMU preintegration factors: Integrate IMU measurements between keyframes into a compact preintegrated measurement \(\Delta\mathbf{R}, \Delta\mathbf{v}, \Delta\mathbf{p}\) with associated covariance.

  • LiDAR odometry factors: Estimate relative pose between consecutive LiDAR scans using NDT (Normal Distribution Transform) or LOAM feature matching.

  • GPS factors: Absolute position constraints from RTK GPS.

  • Loop closure factors: Geometric verification of revisited locations using ICP.

The maximum-a-posteriori (MAP) estimate of the pose trajectory \(\mathcal{X} = \{T_0, T_1, …, T_n\}\) is found by minimising:

\[\mathcal{X}^* = \arg\min_\mathcal{X} \sum_k \left\| \mathbf{r}_k(\mathcal{X}) \right\|_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k^{-1}}^2\tag{10.25}\]

where \(\mathbf{r}_k\) are residuals and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_k\) are covariance matrices for each factor. GTSAM (Georgia Tech Smoothing and Mapping) solves this using iSAM2 (incremental smoothing), which maintains a Bayes tree and updates only affected nodes on each new measurement.

docs.title: 10.5.3 Visual-Inertial Odometry
docs.text:
VINS-Mono achieves metric-scale pose estimation from a monocular camera and IMU by exploiting the IMU for scale. The IMU preintegration between times \(t_i\) and \(t_j\) yields:

\[\Delta\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{ij} = \iint_{t_i}^{t_j} \left(\mathbf{R}_\tau \mathbf{a}_\tau - \mathbf{g}\right) d\tau^2\tag{10.26}\] \[\Delta\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{ij} = \int_{t_i}^{t_j} \left(\mathbf{R}_\tau \mathbf{a}_\tau - \mathbf{g}\right) d\tau\tag{10.27}\]

where \(\mathbf{a}_\tau\) is IMU accelerometer measurement (with bias subtracted) and \(\mathbf{g}\) is gravity. The residual of the IMU factor:

\[\mathbf{r}_{\mathcal{B}_{ij}} = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{R}_i^T (\mathbf{p}_j - \mathbf{p}_i - \mathbf{v}_i \Delta t_{ij} - \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{g}\Delta t_{ij}^2) - \Delta\hat{\mathbf{p}}_{ij} \\ \mathbf{R}_i^T (\mathbf{v}_j - \mathbf{v}_i - \mathbf{g}\Delta t_{ij}) - \Delta\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{ij} \\ 2[\mathbf{q}_i^{-1} \otimes \mathbf{q}_j \otimes \Delta\hat{\mathbf{q}}_{ij}^{-1}]_{xyz} \end{pmatrix}\tag{10.28}\]

is optimised jointly with visual reprojection residuals in a sliding window nonlinear optimiser.

docs.title: 10.6.1 Autonomy Level Frameworks
docs.text: STANAG 4586 defines ten levels of autonomy (LOA) for UAV human-machine interaction, from LOA 1 (remotely piloted) through LOA 10 (fully autonomous, no human in/on loop). The US Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL) Autonomous Control Levels (ACL) provide a parallel ten-level hierarchy focused on control functions. For a full taxonomy, see Chapter 2.

docs.title: 10.6.2 Behaviour Trees
docs.text:
Behaviour Trees (BTs) have emerged as the preferred architectural pattern for UAV mission logic, superseding hierarchical FSMs in most modern robotics systems (PX4 Navigator, Dronecode Mission BT, BT.cpp library). A BT is a rooted tree where:

  • Control flow nodes: Sequence (runs children left-to-right, returns SUCCESS only if all succeed), Fallback/Selector (runs children left-to-right, returns SUCCESS on first child success), Parallel (runs all children simultaneously).

  • Execution nodes: Condition (evaluates a predicate, SUCCESS/FAILURE), Action (executes a task, returns RUNNING/SUCCESS/FAILURE).

  • Decorator nodes: Modify the return status or control flow of a child (Retry, Inverter, ForceSuccess).

The BT is ticked at a fixed rate (10–50 Hz). Each tick traverses the tree from root. The status propagation follows:

\[\sigma_\mathrm{Sequence} = \begin{cases} \mathrm{SUCCESS} & \text{if } \forall i: \sigma_i = \mathrm{SUCCESS} \\ \mathrm{FAILURE} & \text{if } \exists i: \sigma_i = \mathrm{FAILURE} \\ \mathrm{RUNNING} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\tag{10.29}\]

The BT.cpp library (Davide Faconti, MIT licence) implements BTs with reactive event handling, blackboard memory, and XML tree loading, and is used in DJI, ArduPilot, and academic SLAM robots.

docs.title: 10.6.3 Reinforcement Learning for Drone Control
docs.text:
Reinforcement Learning (RL) trains a control policy \(\pi_\theta(\mathbf{a}|\mathbf{s})\) (parameterised by neural network weights \(\theta\)) to maximise cumulative discounted reward:

\[J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\tau \sim \pi_\theta}\!\left[\sum_{t=0}^{T} \gamma^t r(\mathbf{s}_t, \mathbf{a}_t)\right]\tag{10.30}\]

where \(\gamma \in (0,1)\) is the discount factor and \(r(\mathbf{s}_t, \mathbf{a}_t)\) is the reward at step \(t\). Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO) updates the policy using a clipped surrogate objective to limit step size:

\[\mathcal{L}^\mathrm{PPO}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_t\!\left[\min\!\left(r_t(\theta) \hat{A}_t,\; \mathrm{clip}(r_t(\theta), 1-\epsilon, 1+\epsilon) \hat{A}_t\right)\right]\tag{10.31}\]

where \(r_t(\theta) = \pi_\theta(\mathbf{a}_t|\mathbf{s}_t) / \pi_{\theta_\mathrm{old}}(\mathbf{a}_t|\mathbf{s}_t)\) is the probability ratio and \(\hat{A}_t\) is the generalised advantage estimate. PPO is used for quadrotor aggressive manoeuvre learning (Kaufmann et al., 2023 — RL policy exceeding human champion lap times in drone racing), agile perching, and wind-disturbance rejection.

The reward shaping for UAV navigation typically includes:

\[r_t = w_\mathrm{dist}(-\|\mathbf{p}_t - \mathbf{p}_\mathrm{goal}\|) + w_\mathrm{coll}(-c_t) + w_\mathrm{vel}(-\|\boldsymbol{\omega}_t\|) + w_\mathrm{prog}(d_\mathrm{progress})\tag{10.32}\]

where \(c_t = 1\) if collision occurred, \(\boldsymbol{\omega}_t\) is angular velocity (penalising aggressive attitude), and \(d_\mathrm{progress}\) is progress toward goal (sparse reward augmentation).

docs.title: 10.7.1 Neural Network Architectures for Onboard Inference
docs.text:
Airborne ML inference must balance accuracy against strict latency (\(<50\) ms for detection) and power (\(<15\) W) constraints. The dominant architecture families:

MobileNetV3 (Howard et al., 2019): depthwise separable convolutions reduce FLOPs by a factor \(\approx 1/(k^2)\) vs standard convolutions for kernel size \(k\). For a \(3\times3\) depthwise separable conv:

\[\frac{\mathrm{FLOPs}_\mathrm{DWS}}{\mathrm{FLOPs}_\mathrm{standard}} = \frac{1}{N} + \frac{1}{k^2} \approx \frac{1}{9} \text{ for } k=3\tag{10.33}\]

where \(N\) is the number of output channels (typically 256–512). MobileNetV3-Small achieves 67.4% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet at 56 ms on Cortex-A72, 0.60 B FLOPs.

EfficientNet scales width, depth, and resolution with compound coefficient \(\phi\):

\[\text{width} = \alpha^\phi, \quad \text{depth} = \beta^\phi, \quad \text{resolution} = \gamma^\phi, \quad \alpha\beta^2\gamma^2 \approx 2\tag{10.34}\]

Vision Transformer (ViT) and DeiT: For larger onboard processors (Jetson Orin), transformer-based backbones provide state-of-the-art accuracy. The self-attention operation for sequence length \(N\) has \(O(N^2)\) complexity, motivating efficient variants (Swin Transformer, DETR with spatial reduction).
