docs.title: 12.3.3 RF Power Amplifier
docs.text:
GDT transmit chains use solid-state power amplifiers (SSPA) or travelling-wave tube amplifiers (TWTA):

  • SSPA: 5–50 W; GaN HEMT on SiC substrate; efficiency \(\eta_{\text{PAE}} = 35\)–55% at P1dB; no warm-up; suitable for mobile GCS.

  • TWTA: 50–500 W; higher linearity for complex waveforms; \(\eta \approx 50\)–65%; warm-up 30 s; used on fixed ground stations and ship-based GCS.

Power-added efficiency:

\[\eta_{\text{PAE}} = \frac{P_{\text{out}} - P_{\text{in}}}{P_{\text{DC}}}\tag{12.7}\]

Thermal management: a 50 W SSPA at 40% PAE dissipates 75 W as heat; a heat sink of thermal resistance \(R_\theta \leq 0.8\) °C/W is required to keep junction temperature \(T_j < 125\)°C at ambient \(T_a = 55\)°C (MIL grade):

\[T_j = T_a + P_{\text{diss}} \cdot R_\theta = 55 + 75 \times 0.8 = 115~\text{°C}\tag{12.8}\]

docs.title: 12.3.4 Low-Noise Amplifier (LNA) on Receive
docs.text:
The receive chain LNA sets the system noise figure:

\[F_{\text{sys}} = F_{\text{LNA}} + \frac{F_{\text{next}} - 1}{G_{\text{LNA}}}\tag{12.9}\]

A typical C-band LNA: \(G_{\text{LNA}} = 20\) dB, \(F_{\text{LNA}} = 1.5\) dB (\(\text{NF} = 1.5\) dB, noise temperature \(T_n = 120\) K). With a subsequent mixer noise figure of 8 dB: \(F_{\text{sys}} = 1.41 + (6.31 - 1)/100 = 1.41 + 0.053 = 1.46\) (1.65 dB). This confirms that LNA gain \(\gg\) 10 dB effectively makes subsequent stage noise negligible.

docs.title: 12.3.5 Full-Duplex Operation
docs.text:
GDT must simultaneously transmit commands (uplink) and receive telemetry (downlink). Two approaches:

  • Frequency Division Duplex (FDD): separate uplink and downlink frequencies with sufficient guard band and a diplexer or circulator to isolate Tx from Rx. Typical isolation requirement: \(>\)80 dB from Tx port to Rx port (Tx power 50 W \(=\) +47 dBm; Rx noise floor \(\approx -100\) dBm; required isolation \(= 147\) dB; diplexer provides \(\approx\)80 dB, spatial separation and filtering provides the rest).

  • Time Division Duplex (TDD): share frequency; alternate Tx/Rx on a fixed schedule; simpler filtering; half-duplex in each slot; latency added by waiting for Rx slot.

docs.title: 12.4.1 Catapult Launch
docs.text:
Fixed-wing UAVs without runway access use catapult launchers. The launch system must accelerate the aircraft from rest to minimum flying speed \(V_{\min}\) over rail length \(L_r\).

Assuming uniform acceleration \(a\):

\[V_{\min}^2 = 2 a L_r \implies a = \frac{V_{\min}^2}{2 L_r}\tag{12.10}\]

For a 25 kg UAV with \(V_{\min} = 22\) m/s over \(L_r = 3\) m: \(a = 22^2 / (2 \times 3) = 80.7\) m/s\(^2 = 8.2~g\). Force on aircraft: \(F = m \cdot a = 25 \times 80.7 = 2{,}017\) N.

Bungee Cord Launcher.

Elastic potential energy stored in pre-stretched bungee:

\[E_{\text{bungee}} = \tfrac{1}{2} k_{\text{bungee}} x^2\tag{12.11}\]

where \(k_{\text{bungee}}\) is the cord stiffness and \(x\) is stretch. For \(E_{\text{bungee}} = \frac{1}{2}m V_{\min}^2 + m g L_r \sin\theta\) (kinetic energy plus potential energy against inclination \(\theta\)): at \(\theta = 10°\) and \(m = 25\) kg, \(V_{\min} = 22\) m/s: \(E_{\text{bungee}} = \frac{1}{2}(25)(484) + (25)(9.81)(3)(0.174) = 6{,}050 + 128 = 6{,}178\) J. With \(x = 2\) m stretch: \(k_{\text{bungee}} = 2 E / x^2 = 3{,}089\) N/m.

Pneumatic Launcher.

A pneumatic launcher stores energy in a pressure vessel (typical: 200–300 bar, 5 L bottle) and releases it through a piston/sled mechanism. More repeatable and adjustable than bungee; widely used in military tactical UAV systems (Insitu ScanEagle, MALE-class field launchers).

docs.title: 12.4.2 JATO (Jet Assisted Take Off)
docs.text:
Solid rocket boosters strapped to the airframe provide a 1–3 s burst of additional thrust for very short runway or obstacle-clearance scenarios. Typical JATO parameters for a 150 kg UAV:

  • Booster thrust: 2 kN (jettisoned after burnout)

  • Burn duration: 2 s

  • Velocity increment: \(\Delta V = F \cdot t / m = 2{,}000 \times 2 / 150 = 26.7\) m/s

  • Ground roll reduction: from 400 m to \(<\)50 m

docs.title: 12.4.3 Vertical Takeoff and Transition (Hybrid VTOL)
docs.text:
Hybrid VTOL-fixed-wing UAVs take off and land vertically like a multirotor, then transition to wing-borne flight for efficiency. Transition sequence:

  1. Vertical climb to 50–100 m AGL using lift rotors.

  2. Tilt or spin up pusher/puller motor; accelerate to \(V_{\text{trans}}\) (typically \(1.2 \times V_{\text{stall}}\)).

  3. Transition flag: lift rotors throttle down, elevons take over; pitch from \(+5°\) to \(-2°\) nose-down to prevent altitude excursion.

  4. Cruise on fixed wing; lift rotors stopped/folded.

Transition altitude and airspeed must ensure that total lift \(L \geq W\) is maintained continuously:

\[L = \tfrac{1}{2}\rho V^2 S C_L + T_{\text{lift-rotor}} \geq W\tag{12.12}\]

docs.title: 12.4.4 Net Recovery
docs.text:
Net recovery is used for ship-board or restricted-area recovery without a runway. A stretchable Kevlar/nylon net (4 m \(\times\) 8 m typical) is mounted on a frame. The aircraft approaches at low speed, stall \(+\) 5 kt, and engages the net with a hook or skids. Deceleration:

\[a_{\text{net}} = \frac{V_{\text{arr}}^2}{2\,\delta_{\text{net}}}\tag{12.13}\]

where \(\delta_{\text{net}}\) is net deflection (0.5–1.5 m). For \(V_{\text{arr}} = 20\) m/s, \(\delta = 1\) m: \(a = 200\) m/s\(^2 = 20.4~g\). Airframe bulkhead and hook attachment point are structural-tested to \(2.5 \times\) limit load (\(\approx\)50 g ultimate for \(m = 25\) kg; shear pin rated 125 kg minimum).

docs.title: 12.4.5 Parachute Recovery
docs.text:
Drogue + Main Sequence.

  1. Drogue chute (\(C_D S = 0.08\) m\(^2\)) deploys at \(H_{\text{deploy}}\); decelerates from \(V_0\) to \(V_d = 25\) m/s.

  2. Main canopy (\(C_D S = 2.5\) m\(^2\)) deploys at \(H_d = 200\) m AGL.

  3. Terminal descent rate:

    \[V_t = \sqrt{\frac{2W}{\rho\,C_D S}}\tag{12.14}\]

    For \(W = 250\) N, \(\rho = 1.225\) kg/m\(^3\), \(C_D S = 2.5\) m\(^2\): \(V_t = \sqrt{250/(1.225 \times 2.5 / 2)} = \sqrt{163.3} \approx 12.8\) m/s. This is above the 6 m/s limit for electronics survival without airbags; a larger canopy (\(C_D S = 6\) m\(^2\)) is needed: \(V_t = \sqrt{250 \times 2/(1.225 \times 6)} = \sqrt{68.0} = 8.2\) m/s.

Drift analysis: at \(V_t = 8\) m/s descent from 300 m with 5 m/s crosswind, horizontal drift \(= 5 \times (300/8) = 188\) m. Recovery zone must be sized accordingly.

docs.title: 12.4.6 Runway Landing
docs.text:
Conventional runway landing uses ILS-type GNSS-guided approaches. Crosswind correction angle (crab angle):

\[\beta_{\text{crab}} = \arcsin\!\left(\frac{V_w}{V_a}\right)\tag{12.15}\]

For \(V_w = 8\) m/s crosswind, \(V_a = 25\) m/s approach speed: \(\beta_{\text{crab}} = \arcsin(0.32) = 18.7°\). The autopilot must kick off the crab angle to wings-level in the flare; de-crab timing is a critical parameter for landing gear side-load limits.

docs.title: 12.4.7 Ship-Based Recovery: UCARS
docs.text:
The UAV Common Automatic Recovery System (UCARS) enables automated precision recovery of UAVs to ship decks. Key components:

  • Relative GPS: DGPS between ship and UAV; \(\pm\)0.3 m horizontal accuracy.

  • Deck motion compensation: ship accelerometers + gyros provide real-time heave, pitch, roll; the recovery window is defined when instantaneous deck position is in a safe zone.

  • Recovery modes: arrested landing (cable across deck); net capture; skyhook (UAV engages vertical cable lowered from a crane).

  • Wind-over-deck: carrier operations at 25 kt WOD; UAV approach corrected for ship wake turbulence.

Figure 12.2. GCS launch, mission, and recovery sequence flow diagram. The go/no-go decision point follows final system checks after climb to mission altitude.

docs.title: 12.5.1 Pre-Flight Workflow
docs.text:
A structured pre-flight checklist prevents avoidable incidents:

  1. Airspace authorisation: NOTAM check (FAA ATIS/DUAT, EUROCONTROL NM); UAS-specific NOTAMs; Temporary Flight Restrictions (TFRs); obtain authorisation via UAS Service Supplier (USS) in U-space / UTM framework.

  2. Weather: wind speed at multiple altitudes (upper-air sounding); visibility; precipitation; icing level; convective outlook.

  3. C2 link test: verify uplink/downlink on all frequencies; measure RSSI and BER at pre-set test distances.

  4. Battery/fuel: check charge state (%SOC); cell voltage balance (\(\Delta V_{\text{cell}} < 50\) mV); fuel quantity (weight or float sensor).

  5. Payload: camera boresight calibration; gimbal range of motion; sensor self-test.

docs.title: 12.5.2 Waypoint Mission Planning
docs.text:
The mission planner imports a Digital Elevation Model (DEM) (SRTM 1-arc-second; \(\approx\)30 m resolution) and calculates terrain-following altitude profiles. For a survey at fixed AGL height \(h\):

\[H_{\text{MSL},i} = \text{DEM}(E_i, N_i) + h + \Delta h_{\text{safety}}\tag{12.16}\]

where \(\Delta h_{\text{safety}} \geq 30\) m accounts for DEM error and vegetation height uncertainty.

Ground sample distance (GSD) for a camera with focal length \(f\) (mm), sensor width \(s_w\) (mm), image width \(n_w\) (pixels):

\[\text{GSD} = \frac{h \cdot s_w}{f \cdot n_w} \quad [\text{m/pixel}]\tag{12.17}\]

For \(h = 100\) m, \(f = 35\) mm, \(s_w = 23.5\) mm, \(n_w = 6{,}000\) pixels: GSD \(= 100 \times 23.5 / (35 \times 6{,}000) = 0.011\) m/px (\(= 1.1\) cm/px).

Overlap requirements: forward overlap \(\geq 70\%\), lateral overlap \(\geq 60\%\) for photogrammetry 3D reconstruction. This determines waypoint spacing:

\[\begin{align*} d_{\text{fwd}} &= \text{FOV}_{\text{fwd}} \times (1 - \text{OL}_{\text{fwd}}) = h \cdot \frac{s_h}{f} \cdot (1 - 0.70) \\ d_{\text{lat}} &= \text{FOV}_{\text{lat}} \times (1 - \text{OL}_{\text{lat}}) = h \cdot \frac{s_w}{f} \cdot (1 - 0.60) \end{align*}\]

docs.title: 12.5.3 Emergency Procedures and Contingency Zones
docs.text:
Every mission plan must define:

  • Lost-link timeout: if C2 link lost for \(>\)30 s, autopilot enters pre-programmed contingency (loiter at lost-link waypoint; after 3 min, descend to contingency landing zone).

  • Low-battery RTH threshold: return triggered at battery SOC sufficient to reach home + 20% reserve. Required SOC \(= E_{\text{fly\_home}} / E_{\text{total}} + 0.20\).

  • Geofence: hard boundary; autopilot refuses to cross even under operator command.

  • Alternate landing site: pre-surveyed clear area in the event primary landing zone is obstructed.

docs.title: 12.5.4 One Operator — Multiple UAS (1:N Ratio)
docs.text:
Advances in automation enable a single operator to supervise multiple UAVs simultaneously. The DoD goal is 1 operator : 8 aircraft (Group 3) and 1 : 50+ (small Group 1). Human factors research (Cummings, 2014) shows that operator performance (target detection probability, response to alerts) degrades with \(N\):

\[P_{\text{detect}} \approx P_0 \cdot e^{-\alpha(N-1)}\tag{12.20}\]

where \(P_0\) is single-aircraft performance and \(\alpha\) is a workload degradation coefficient (typically 0.08–0.15 depending on task complexity). Mitigations: automation of routine tasks; exception-based management (alert only on anomaly); graduated automation levels.

docs.title: 12.5.5 Air Traffic Management: UTM and U-Space
docs.text:
The FAA BEYOND programme and EASA U-Space Regulation (EU 2021/664) establish a framework for UAS traffic management:

  • UAS Service Supplier (USS): provides operational planning, conformance monitoring, and strategic deconfliction services.

  • FIMS (Flight Information Management System): central FAA/CAA data hub interfacing with USSs.

  • Remote ID: all UAVs broadcast ID, position, altitude, operator position via Wi-Fi or BLE in the clear; network-based Remote ID via cellular; mandatory in US (2023) and EU (2024).

  • Beyond Visual Line of Sight (BVLOS): requires demonstrated DAA (Detect and Avoid) capability; ASTM F3442 standard; Honeywell TCAS-UAS and ADS-B IN equipment.

docs.title: 12.6.1 Transport and Packaging
docs.text:
Military GCS systems must comply with MIL-STD-810H environmental categories: temperature (\(-46°\)C to \(+71°\)C storage; \(-32°\)C to \(+60°\)C operating), humidity (95% RH), salt fog (48 hr), and drop (1.2 m onto concrete). Packaging hierarchy:

  • Level 1: operational case (Pelican 1620, Zarges K470); foam-lined; \(<\)30 kg per case.

  • Level 2: standard military container (TRICON or QUADCON); forklift-compatible; air-portable on C-17/C-130.

  • Level 3: ISU-90 air freight pallet; NATO standard 4-way entry forklift.

docs.title: 12.6.2 Field Power Supply
docs.text: Table 12.2. Field power options for mobile GCS deployments. Source Power Duration Weight Notes Vehicle 24 V DC bus 2 kW Vehicle fuel 0 (integrated) Standard NATO 24 V Tactical generator 3 kW 24 hr on 10 L fuel 35 kg MEP-831A (3 kW) Solar panel array 1 kW Daylight only 12 kg (6 panels) Supplement/backup LiFePO4 battery pack — 4–8 hr (1 kW load) 25 kg (3 kWh) Silent operation Shore power (240 VAC) 10 kW Grid-dependent 0 Fixed site only

docs.title: 12.6.3 Battery Charging Infrastructure
docs.text:
A field charging station for a fleet of 20 drones equipped with 6S 22 Ah LiPo packs must deliver:

\[P_{\text{charge}} = N_{\text{parallel}} \cdot V_{\text{nominal}} \cdot I_{\text{charge}} = 10 \times 22.2 \times 20 = 4{,}440~\text{W}\tag{12.21}\]

(assuming 10 packs charging simultaneously at 1 C rate). A multi-bay charger (e.g., SkyRC Q200Neo: 4 channels \(\times\) 200 W) with 5 units provides the required 4 kW. Charge time at 1 C: \(\approx\)60 min full cycle; at 2 C: \(\approx\)35 min with BMS cell temperature monitoring (keep below 45°C during charge).

docs.title: 12.6.4 Maintenance: LRU Philosophy
docs.text:
The Line-Replaceable Unit (LRU) maintenance concept minimises downtime:

  • Level 1 (organisational): swap faulty LRU in \(<\)30 min; no tools beyond standard kit; trained operator/crew chief. LRUs: battery packs, motor/propeller assemblies, gimbal head, GDT antenna feed, control surfaces.

  • Level 2 (intermediate/direct support): bench repair of electronics; solder, oscilloscope, spectrum analyser; AVUM (Aviation Unit Maintenance) team.

  • Level 3 (depot): major structural repair, factory overhaul, software major-version upgrade.

Mean Time Between Maintenance (MTBM) and Mean Corrective Maintenance Time (MCMT) are key sustainment KPIs:

\[A_{\text{operational}} = \frac{\text{MTBM}}{\text{MTBM} + \text{MCMT}}\tag{12.22}\]

For MTBM = 40 hr, MCMT = 2 hr: \(A_o = 40/42 = 95.2\%\).

docs.title: 12.7.1 Pilot in Command (PIC) Responsibilities
docs.text:
Under CFR 14 Part 107 (USA), CAP 722 (UK), and NATO STANAG 4670, the PIC:

  • Has final authority over the airworthiness and safe conduct of the flight.

  • Must maintain situation awareness of the UAV and surrounding airspace.

  • Can hand control to the co-pilot/sensor operator but retains responsibility.

  • Is responsible for compliance with airspace authorisations and weather minima.

docs.title: 12.7.2 Crew Resource Management (CRM)
docs.text:
Multi-seat GCS operations (MALE/HALE class) involve a two- or three-person crew: PIC, Sensor Operator (SO), and optionally a Mission Commander (MC). CRM training addresses:

  • Task sharing: PIC manages flight, comms, and ATC; SO manages payload and data exploitation; MC manages mission objectives.

  • Sterile cockpit rule: non-essential conversation prohibited below 500 ft AGL during takeoff/approach.

  • Challenge-and-response checklists: critical steps read aloud and confirmed by a second crew member.

  • Incapacitation protocol: if PIC becomes incapacitated, SO takes immediate control and activates emergency RTH.

docs.title: 12.7.3 Situational Awareness: Endsley Model
docs.text:
Endsley’s (1995) three-level SA model is the standard framework for GCS display design:

  1. Level 1 — Perception: raw data; current UAV position, altitude, speed; link quality bar; battery percentage.

  2. Level 2 — Comprehension: integration; “aircraft is 5 km from waypoint 7, 15 min remaining, 40% battery — mission marginally achievable”.

  3. Level 3 — Projection: future state; “if wind increases 5 kt headwind, reserve will be \(<\)10% — abort recommended”.

Display design must support all three levels. Level 1 is well-served by raw telemetry; Level 2 and 3 require decision-support algorithms (range/endurance calculator with wind correction; auto-generated alert “RECOMMEND RTH IN 4 MIN”).

docs.title: 12.7.4 Display Design Principles
docs.text:
• Clutter reduction: show only operationally relevant parameters; use progressive disclosure (expanded view on click) for secondary data.

  • Colour coding: green = normal; amber = caution (action required soon); red = warning (immediate action); grey = unavailable. Adhere to RTCA DO-257A and MIL-STD-1787C for colour-coded displays.

  • Alarm management: ISA-18.2 alarm rationalisation; maximum 6 simultaneous alarms before operator saturation; priority queuing.

  • Ecological interface design: use configurable widgets that directly represent the system’s constraint space (e.g., a wind-corrected endurance ring on the map, not just a fuel number).

docs.title: 12.7.5 Training and Currency
docs.text: Table 12.3. Typical UAV operator qualification and currency requirements (military MALE-class reference). Phase Duration Method Milestone Ground school 40 hr Classroom Written examination (\(\geq\)80%) Simulator — basic 60 hr Full-mission sim Proficiency check Simulator — advanced 40 hr Emergency procs Check-ride Dual instruction (live) 20 hr Instructor PIC Solo authorisation Solo live hours 30 hr Supervised solo PIC qualification Currency 4 hr/90 days Live or sim Maintain rating

docs.title: 12.8.1 GCS Cyber Hardening
docs.text:
The GCS is a high-value target for adversary cyber operations. A hardened GCS implements:

  • Operating system: SELinux (Security-Enhanced Linux) with mandatory access control (MAC); principle of least privilege; all unnecessary services disabled.

  • Encrypted storage: LUKS2 full-disk encryption (AES-256-XTS); TPM 2.0 sealed key; prevents data extraction if GCS is captured.

  • VPN / IPSec to C2 server: IKEv2 with certificate authentication; AES-256-GCM transport; provides confidentiality and integrity for tactical intranet traffic.

  • Software updates: cryptographically signed firmware (ed25519 signature); update server identity verified by PKI chain.

  • USB and peripheral lockdown: only whitelisted devices (by USB hardware ID); BIOS USB boot disabled.

docs.title: 12.8.2 RF Emissions Control (EMCON)
docs.text:
In contested environments, GCS RF emissions constitute a signature:

  • Directional antenna (32 dBi parabolic dish) concentrates radiation toward the UAV, reducing side-lobe power by \(\geq\)20 dB compared to omnidirectional.

  • Minimum necessary power: adaptive power control reduces uplink EIRP to the minimum required for \(M_{\text{link}} \geq 10\) dB.

  • Frequency hopping: FHSS spread spectrum (MIL-STD-188-181B) hops across 1,000+ channels in a pseudo-random sequence; reduces probability of intercept/direction-finding.

  • Link budget for intercept: an adversary ESM receiver at range \(d_{\text{ESM}}\) requires:

    \[P_{\text{ESM}} = P_t + G_t(\theta_{\text{ESM}}) - L_{\text{FSPL}}(d_{\text{ESM}}) \geq P_{\text{min,ESM}}\tag{12.23}\]

    where \(G_t(\theta_{\text{ESM}})\) is the antenna gain toward the adversary (side-lobe, typically \(-20\) to \(-30\) dBi below boresight).

docs.title: 12.8.3 Physical Security and Anti-Tamper
docs.text:
• Access control: multi-factor authentication (CAC card + PIN + biometric fingerprint) required to unlock GCS.

  • Tamper detection: chassis intrusion switches; motion sensor in unattended mode triggers zeroisation of cryptographic keys.

  • Zeroisation: NSA/CSS EPL-listed zeroisation of cryptographic key material in \(<\)10 s on tamper detection; keys cannot be recovered.

  • Classification markings: GCS hardware labelled to highest classification of data handled; material accountability per DoD 5200.01 Vol. 3.

docs.title: 12.8.4 GPS Jamming Mitigation at the GCS Site
docs.text:
The GCS relies on GPS for its own position (used to compute antenna pointing angles and as the ground reference for DGPS corrections). GPS jamming mitigation:

  • Geodetic survey mark: GCS position pre-surveyed to \(\pm\)10 mm; stored in non-volatile memory; used when GPS is jammed.

  • CRPA (Controlled Reception Pattern Antenna): null-steered towards jammer direction; up to 30 dB jamming suppression.

  • Inertial-aided GPS: GNSS/INS integration; 100 s holdover at \(<\)10 m position error for tactical operations.

docs.title: 12.9.1 Ship Integration
docs.text:
A ship-mounted GCS faces three unique challenges not present in land-based operation:

Vibration and Shock.

MIL-STD-810H Method 514.8 specifies shipboard vibration profiles: broadband random vibration (10–500 Hz); gunfire shock (3,000 g peak, 0.3 ms); waterborne shock (from hull impacts). GCS electronics mount on vibration-isolated sub-racks (wire-rope isolators, \(f_n = 5\)–8 Hz); displays use anti-shock mounting with shock mounts rated \(>\)40 g SRS.

Salt Spray and Humidity.

External equipment (GDT antenna pedestal, waveguide runs, coaxial cables) must comply with MIL-STD-810H Method 509.6 (salt fog 48 hr; \(\geq\)95% concentration). Connector choice: MIL-DTL-38999 Series III with cadmium-plated shell and Viton O-ring seal; IP68 rating.

Antenna Motion Compensation.

Ship pitch (\(\pm\)10°) and roll (\(\pm\)20°) at sea state 4 introduce angular errors in the antenna pointing system. The pedestal incorporates a 3-axis IMU that provides roll and pitch compensation:

\[\theta_{\text{az,cmd}} = \theta_{\text{az,track}} + \psi_{\text{ship}}\tag{12.24}\] \[\theta_{\text{el,cmd}} = \theta_{\text{el,track}} + \phi_{\text{ship}} \cos(\theta_{\text{az,track}}) + \theta_{\text{ship}} \sin(\theta_{\text{az,track}})\tag{12.25}\]

where \(\psi_{\text{ship}}, \phi_{\text{ship}}, \theta_{\text{ship}}\) are ship yaw, roll, and pitch. Without compensation, a \(\pm\)20° roll at 10 km range causes a \(\pm\)3.5 km lateral pointing error on the aircraft (far outside a 3° antenna beamwidth).

docs.title: 12.9.2 Vehicle-Mounted GCS: HMMWV/JLTV
docs.text:
Vehicle integration requirements:

  • Shock/Vibration: MIL-STD-810H Methods 514.8 (vehicle vibration curves) and 516.8 (functional shock 20 g, 11 ms half-sine).

  • EMI: MIL-STD-461G CE102 (conducted emissions), CS114 (conducted susceptibility), RE102 (radiated emissions), RS103 (radiated susceptibility 200 V/m, 10 kHz–40 GHz).

  • Power conditioning: vehicle 24 VDC bus varies 18–32 V; GCS must accept full range; DC-DC converter with hold-up capacitor bridging 100 ms engine restart transient.

  • Antenna mounting: roof-mounted mast (3 m deployable mast for GDT) provides LOS clearance over vehicle body; lightning-protected (\(<\)0.1 ground bond).

docs.title: 12.9.3 Airborne GCS: Relay and BACN
docs.text:
In some architectures, a manned or unmanned relay aircraft serves as an airborne GCS or communications relay:

  • BACN (Battlefield Airborne Communications Node): E-11A (Bombardier Global Express) or High-Altitude Balloon; translates between diverse waveforms (LINK-16, SADL, VHF, UHF); extends coverage radius to \(>\)400 km line-of-sight at 65,000 ft.

  • Airborne relay for BVLOS: a relay UAV at 5,000 ft extends C-band LOS from ground GCS at 200 km to controlled UAV at 400 km separation.

  • JSTARS concept: battle management aircraft integrating ground surveillance radar, air-to-air datalink, and UAS control terminals.

docs.title: 12.11 Summary
docs.text:
The Ground Control System is far more than a joystick-and-screen. It is an integrated system of communication hardware, mission-planning software, launch and recovery equipment, human-machine interfaces, power infrastructure, and security measures that together determine whether an unmanned system can be operated reliably, safely, and legally.

The engineer responsible for GCS design must simultaneously satisfy requirements from RF link budget physics, avionics-grade software assurance (DO-178C), environmental robustness (MIL-STD-810H), human factors psychology (Endsley SA model), legal frameworks (UTM/U-Space), and cyber security (NIST SP 800-171). No single discipline dominates; the GCS is the archetype of a complex systems-of-systems engineering challenge.

Future GCS development trends include: AI-mediated exception-based management reducing operator workload in 1:\(N\) operations; AR headsets replacing traditional flat-panel displays; 5G/6G cellular serving as the primary C2 link for urban operations; and fully autonomous recovery systems eliminating the need for skilled pilot inputs during the most accident-prone phase of flight.

docs.title: 13.1 Introduction to Drone Manufacturing
docs.text:
The manufacture of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) spans an exceptionally wide range of production philosophies, from small-batch artisanal builds in university laboratories to high-rate defence production lines delivering hundreds of airframes per year. Regardless of scale, the engineering discipline of drone manufacturing integrates materials science, structural mechanics, electronics, software, and quality assurance into a coherent production system. This chapter provides a rigorous, end-to-end treatment of that system, covering composite fabrication, precision machining, additive processes, electronics assembly, quality control, and the emerging digital-factory paradigm.

A fundamental observation is that the choice of manufacturing route directly determines the achievable structural mass fraction, and therefore the payload-to-gross-weight ratio that defines mission utility. For a fixed-wing combat drone with a design gross weight \(W_0 = 500\,\mathrm{kg}\), a structural mass fraction \(f_s = m_s/W_0\) reduction from 0.32 to 0.27 frees 25 kg for additional fuel or payload — a 15% improvement achievable primarily through disciplined composite manufacturing.

docs.title: 13.2.1 Phase Gates from Concept to Production
docs.text:
The standard aerospace product lifecycle follows a phase-gate model aligned with the US DoD acquisition framework and the INCOSE systems engineering handbook. Each gate is a formal review at which the programme may proceed, loop back, or terminate.

Concept Phase encompasses market or mission analysis, operational requirements, and rough order-of-magnitude (ROM) cost estimation. The output is a System Requirements Document (SRD) and a business case with a return-on-investment projection.

Preliminary Design Review (PDR) validates that the selected design approach meets top-level requirements. Key deliverables include the preliminary 3-D model, initial weight budget, aerodynamic analysis (CFD or handbook methods), structural sizing, and power budget. Risk register is established with probability-impact matrices.

Critical Design Review (CDR) examines the detail design. All drawings are released to revision A. Finite-element models (FEM) are correlated with preliminary test data. Manufacturing plans and make-vs-buy decisions are finalised.

Prototype / Engineering Development Model (EDM) phase produces one to three flight articles built to production-intent processes. The EDM is used for flight-test envelope expansion and to validate manufacturing processes.

Qualification and First Article Inspection (FAI) formally verify that the production design and process yield hardware that meets specifications. AS9102 governs FAI for aerospace structures.

Low-Rate Initial Production (LRIP) ramps the production system while the qualification programme is completed. Typically 10–20% of the planned full rate.

Full-Rate Production (FRP) follows a successful production readiness review (PRR). The learning curve drives unit cost down as cumulative output increases.

docs.title: 13.2.2 Build-to-Print, Build-to-Spec, and COTS Integration
docs.text:
Three procurement and manufacturing paradigms coexist in UAV programmes:

Build-to-Print (BTP) The buyer provides fully dimensioned drawings; the supplier manufactures to those exact specifications. Intellectual property remains with the buyer. Used for structural components where geometry is performance-critical. Build-to-Spec (BTS) The buyer provides a performance specification; the supplier designs and manufactures to meet it. IP typically resides with the supplier. Common for motors, ESCs, and payload gimbals. COTS Integration Commercial off-the-shelf components are procured from catalogue and integrated without modification. Lowest NRE cost but supply-chain risk if the product is discontinued.

docs.title: 13.2.3 Make-vs-Buy Analysis
docs.text:
A rigorous make-vs-buy decision evaluates total cost of ownership (TCO), not merely unit price. The decision framework computes the net present value (NPV) of each option:

\[\mathrm{NPV}_{\mathrm{make}} = -C_{\mathrm{NRE}} + \sum_{t=1}^{T} \frac{(P_{\mathrm{buy},t} - C_{\mathrm{make},t})\,Q_t}{(1+r)^t}\tag{13.1}\]

where \(C_{\mathrm{NRE}}\) is the non-recurring engineering investment, \(P_{\mathrm{buy},t}\) is the per-unit buy price in period \(t\), \(C_{\mathrm{make},t}\) is the per-unit make cost, \(Q_t\) is the annual quantity, \(r\) is the discount rate, and \(T\) is the programme horizon in years. If \(\mathrm{NPV}_{\mathrm{make}} > 0\), internal manufacture is preferred on purely economic grounds, subject to strategic factors (IP retention, supply-chain security, export control).

Key cost drivers for the make option include tooling, floor space, capital equipment depreciation, direct labour, material scrap, and quality overhead. For composites, tooling amortised over the production run is often the dominant NRE term.

docs.title: 13.2.4 Quality Management: AS9100 and ISO 9001
docs.text:
AS9100 Rev D is the aerospace quality management system (QMS) standard, building upon ISO 9001:2015 with additional requirements for configuration management, first-article inspection, risk management, and key characteristics. Certification requires a third-party audit and is mandatory for suppliers to prime aerospace contractors.

Fundamental metrics within an AS9100 QMS include:

  • On-time delivery (OTD): target \(\geq 95\%\)

  • Incoming quality rate (IQR): incoming lots accepted / total lots

  • Defects per million opportunities (DPMO): Six Sigma target \(\leq 3.4\)

  • Cost of poor quality (CoPQ): internal failures + external failures + appraisal + prevention costs

docs.title: 13.3 Composite Manufacturing
docs.text: Fibre-reinforced polymers (FRPs) are the dominant structural material in modern UAVs, offering specific stiffness and specific strength superior to all structural metals. Carbon-fibre-reinforced polymer (CFRP) achieves specific tensile modulus \(E/\rho \approx 110\,\mathrm{GPa\cdot cm^3/g}\) versus \(26\,\mathrm{GPa\cdot cm^3/g}\) for 7075 aluminium.

docs.title: 13.3.1 Fibre and Matrix Systems
docs.text:
Reinforcing fibres are characterised by their tensile modulus and strength. Standard-modulus (SM) carbon fibre (e.g. Toray T700) has \(E_f = 230\,\mathrm{GPa}\), \(\sigma_{fu} = 4900\,\mathrm{MPa}\), \(\rho_f = 1.80\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}\). Intermediate-modulus (IM) fibre (T800) achieves \(E_f = 294\,\mathrm{GPa}\). High-modulus (HM) fibre (M55J) reaches \(E_f = 540\,\mathrm{GPa}\) at the cost of reduced failure strain (\(\varepsilon_{fu} \approx 0.8\%\)) and increased brittleness.

Epoxy matrices (e.g. Hexion EPON 862, Cytec 5320-1, Hexcel 8552) provide glass-transition temperatures \(T_g = 150\)–\(200\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) in the cured state. Toughened epoxy systems with thermoplastic interleaves (e.g. Hexcel M21) raise mode-I interlaminar fracture toughness from \(G_{Ic} \approx 150\,\mathrm{J/m^2}\) to \(\geq 600\,\mathrm{J/m^2}\).

The rule-of-mixtures longitudinal modulus of a unidirectional ply is:

\[E_1 = V_f E_f + (1-V_f) E_m\tag{13.2}\]

The transverse modulus is estimated by the Halpin-Tsai equation:

\[E_2 = E_m \frac{1 + \xi \eta V_f}{1 - \eta V_f},\quad \eta = \frac{E_f/E_m - 1}{E_f/E_m + \xi}\tag{13.3}\]

where \(\xi = 2\) for the transverse direction. Typical aerospace prepreg has fibre volume fraction \(V_f = 0.57\)–\(0.62\).

docs.title: 13.3.2 Prepreg Layup Process
docs.text:
Prepreg (pre-impregnated fabric or tape) is the highest-quality composite feedstock, with precisely controlled resin content (typically 34–38% by mass) and uniform fibre distribution. The process flow is:

  1. Tool preparation: Clean tool surface to \(Ra < 0.8\,\mu\mathrm{m}\). Apply release agent (Frekote 770-NC or Loctite Frekote 44-NC) in 3–5 coats, buffing each to a dry film. Apply peel ply if a bonding surface is required.

  2. Cutting: Automated ply cutting machine (Gerber, Lectra, Zund) cuts plies to nest patterns with \(<0.5\%\) material waste via optimisation algorithms. Manual cutting with template and rotary cutter is used for prototypes.

  3. Layup: Plies are applied sequentially. Each ply is consolidated by roller or squeegee to remove trapped air, particularly at ply drops and thickness transitions. Layup sequence follows laminate design code (e.g. \([0/\pm45/90]_s\) for quasi-isotropic laminates).

  4. Debulking: Every 4–6 plies, a vacuum of \(\geq 0.85\,\mathrm{bar}\) is drawn for 15–30 minutes to compact the laminate and remove interply voids.

  5. Vacuum bag assembly: Sequence from tool surface outward: release film / peel ply / breather cloth / vacuum bag / sealant tape. Bag leakage rate must be \(\leq 2.5\,\mathrm{mbar/min}\) before autoclave loading.

  6. Cure cycle: The standard two-dwell epoxy cure cycle for Hexcel 8552: ramp at \(1\)–\(3\,^\circ\mathrm{C/min}\) to \(110\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\), hold 60 min; ramp to \(180\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\), hold 120 min; cool at \(\leq 3\,^\circ\mathrm{C/min}\) to \(60\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) before pressure release. Autoclave pressure: 7 bar.

  7. Demould and trim: Part is extracted after cooling. Trimming to net shape by waterjet, CNC router, or diamond-coated abrasive wheel.

The degree of cure \(\alpha\) is tracked using an Arrhenius-based kinetic model:

\[\frac{d\alpha}{dt} = A\,e^{-E_a/(RT)}(1-\alpha)^n\tag{13.4}\]

where \(A\) is the pre-exponential factor, \(E_a\) the activation energy, \(R = 8.314\,\mathrm{J/(mol\cdot K)}\), and \(n\) the reaction order. Full cure (\(\alpha \geq 0.97\)) is verified by differential scanning calorimetry (DSC).

docs.title: 13.3.3 Vacuum-Assisted Resin Transfer Moulding (VARTM)
docs.text:
VARTM uses atmospheric pressure (one-sided vacuum) to drive resin through a dry preform. Darcy’s law describes the resin flow front velocity:

\[v = -\frac{K}{\mu} \frac{\partial P}{\partial x}\tag{13.5}\]

where \(K\) is the in-plane permeability (\(10^{-11}\)–\(10^{-9}\,\mathrm{m^2}\) for woven CF), \(\mu\) is the resin dynamic viscosity, and \(\partial P/\partial x\) is the pressure gradient. The flow front position for a constant-pressure one-dimensional case:

\[x_f(t) = \sqrt{\frac{2K \Delta P\,t}{\mu\,\phi}}\tag{13.6}\]

where \(\phi\) is the preform porosity and \(\Delta P\) is the driving pressure differential (\(\leq 1\,\mathrm{bar}\) for VARTM). Flow simulation tools (PAM-RTM, LIMS) optimise gate locations to prevent dry spots. Resin pot-life must exceed predicted fill time by a factor \(\geq 1.5\).

docs.title: 13.3.4 Filament Winding
docs.text:
Filament winding deposits continuous fibre tows over a rotating mandrel. The geodesic winding path satisfies Clairaut’s relation:

\[r\sin\phi = r_0\sin\phi_0 = \text{const}\tag{13.7}\]

For a cylindrical tube wound at angle \(\pm\phi\), the netting-theory hoop stress capacity is:

\[\sigma_\theta = \frac{p r}{t} = \frac{n_f \sigma_{fu}}{2}\left(\sin^2\phi + \nu_{12}\cos^2\phi\right)\tag{13.8}\]

Wet winding impregnates rovings in a resin bath immediately before deposition (\(V_f = 50\)–\(55\%\)); dry winding uses pre-towpreg (\(V_f = 58\)–\(62\%\), higher quality). Fibre tension \(T_f = 5\)–\(25\,\mathrm{N/roving}\) must be maintained \(\pm5\%\) across the winding cycle to avoid fibre waviness.

docs.title: 13.3.5 Resin Transfer Moulding (RTM)
docs.text:
RTM uses matched tooling with resin injected under pressure. The fill time equation for a rectangular cavity:

\[t_{\mathrm{fill}} = \frac{\phi L^2 \mu}{2 K P_{\mathrm{inj}}}\tag{13.9}\]

Injection pressures of 1–10 bar are typical for conventional RTM. High-pressure RTM (HP-RTM, \(>30\,\mathrm{bar}\)) enables cycle times of 3–10 minutes, increasingly applied to UAV production at volumes \(>1000\)/year.

docs.title: 13.3.6 Automated Fibre Placement (AFP)
docs.text:
AFP machines deposit slit tapes (3.175–12.7 mm wide) over complex double-curved surfaces. Each tow is cut, clamped, and restarted individually, allowing curvilinear “steered” fibre paths. The compaction roller applies \(100\)–\(400\,\mathrm{N}\) normal force.

Common AFP defect types:

Gaps Spaces between adjacent tows; limit \(<0.8\,\mathrm{mm}\), max 3 gaps/ply. Overlaps Tow overlap \(>0.3\,\mathrm{mm}\) creates thickness variation. Fibre waviness Tow steering radius \(<600\,\mathrm{mm}\) risks tow buckling. Twisted tows Tow twist \(>5^\circ/100\,\mathrm{mm}\) reduces compressive strength.

docs.title: 13.3.7 Composite Tooling
docs.text:
CTE mismatch between tool and part induces spring-in at cured corners:

\[\Delta\theta = \theta_0\left[\frac{(\alpha_\perp - \alpha_\parallel) (1+\nu_{12})}{\cos^2\theta_0} \Delta T\right]\tag{13.10}\]

where \(\theta_0\) is the nominal corner angle, \(\alpha_\parallel\) and \(\alpha_\perp\) are in-plane and through-thickness CTE values.

Table 13.2. Composite tooling material comparison Material CTE (\(10^{-6}\)/K) Max Service (\(^\circ\)C) Mass Index Cost Index Parts/Tool Invar 36 steel 1.5 200 High High \(>5000\) CFRP tooling 2–3 180 Low Medium 500–2000 Aluminium 6061 23 150 Medium Low 100–500 Epoxy board 30 80 Low Low 50–200

docs.title: 13.4.1 Material Stock and Selection
docs.text: Aluminium alloy 7075-T651 is the workhorse machined structural material in UAV production: \(\sigma_{yt} = 503\,\mathrm{MPa}\), \(E = 71.7\,\mathrm{GPa}\), \(\rho = 2.81\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}\), machinability rating 8/10. Titanium Ti-6Al-4V (Grade 5) is used for highly loaded fittings and fastener bosses (\(\sigma_{yt} = 880\,\mathrm{MPa}\), \(\rho = 4.43\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}\)) despite higher cost and lower machinability rating 3/10. Engineering plastics (Delrin/POM, PEEK, UHMWPE) are machined for lightweight brackets, bushings, and fairings where structural loads are modest.

docs.title: 13.4.2 Multi-Axis Machining Capabilities
docs.text: 3-axis Tool moves in \(X\), \(Y\), \(Z\); suitable for prismatic parts with features on one face. Achieves tolerances \(\pm 0.05\,\mathrm{mm}\). 4-axis Adds rotary axis \(A\) (rotation about \(X\)). Enables cylindrical parts. 5-axis simultaneous Continuously varying tool orientation vector. Required for complex aerodynamic surfaces and undercut features. Tolerances \(\pm 0.01\)–\(0.02\,\mathrm{mm}\). Collision avoidance verified by CAM simulation (Mastercam, NX CAM, Hypermill).

docs.title: 13.4.3 Cutting Parameters and Tool Wear
docs.text:
The Taylor tool-life equation:

\[V_c\,T_{\mathrm{tool}}^n = C\tag{13.11}\]

where \(n \approx 0.25\) for uncoated HSS, \(n \approx 0.35\) for coated carbide. Recommended parameters for 7075 aluminium: \(V_c = 250\)–\(500\,\mathrm{m/min}\), feed per tooth \(f_z = 0.05\)–\(0.15\,\mathrm{mm}\), axial depth \(a_p = 0.5\)–\(5\,\mathrm{mm}\). For Ti-6Al-4V: \(V_c = 40\)–\(80\,\mathrm{m/min}\), \(f_z = 0.03\)–\(0.08\,\mathrm{mm}\), flood coolant mandatory, TiAlN-coated carbide.

The material removal rate is:

\[\dot{V} = a_p \cdot a_e \cdot f_z \cdot z \cdot n_{\mathrm{spindle}}\tag{13.12}\]

where \(z\) is the number of cutter flutes and \(n_{\mathrm{spindle}}\) is spindle speed (rpm).

docs.title: 13.4.4 Surface Finish and Post-Processing
docs.text: Aerodynamic external surfaces require \(Ra \leq 1.6\,\mu\mathrm{m}\); bearing surfaces \(Ra \leq 0.4\,\mu\mathrm{m}\). Hard anodising (MIL-A-8625 Type III) deposits an Al\(_2\)O\(_3\) layer 25–75 \(\mu\)m thick, hardness 400–600 HV. Type II anodising (5–25 \(\mu\)m) provides corrosion protection only. Alodine (MIL-C-5541 chromate conversion coating) is applied in thin film (\(<2\,\mu\mathrm{m}\)) for electrical conductivity continuity at bonding interfaces.

docs.title: 13.4.5 Electrical Discharge Machining (EDM)
docs.text:
Wire EDM uses a continuously moving brass wire (0.10–0.33 mm diameter) to erode material via spark discharge in deionised water. Material removal rate:

\[\dot{m}_{\mathrm{EDM}} = \frac{E_d \cdot f_p}{H_w}\tag{13.13}\]

where \(E_d\) is energy per discharge pulse, \(f_p\) is pulse frequency, and \(H_w\) is the specific erosion enthalpy. Achieves tolerances \(\pm 0.003\,\mathrm{mm}\); ideal for hard-metal spars, Ti landing-gear brackets, and airfoil templates.

docs.title: 13.4.6 Waterjet Cutting
docs.text: Abrasive waterjet (AWJ) cutting uses a water-garnet slurry at 350–690 MPa through a 0.25–1.0 mm orifice. No heat-affected zone: critical for CFRP where heat causes delamination. Kerf width \(0.8\)–\(1.2\,\mathrm{mm}\); burr-free on metals. CFRP panel (3 mm thick) cutting speed: \(1500\)–\(3000\,\mathrm{mm/min}\) at 420 MPa.

docs.title: 13.5.1 Technology Overview
docs.text:
Additive manufacturing (AM) enables rapid iteration, complex geometry without tooling, and on-demand production of replacement parts in deployed environments.

Table 13.3. Additive manufacturing processes for UAV components Process Materials Layer (\(\mu\)m) Accuracy (mm) Strength vs Bulk (%) Cost Index FDM/FFF PLA, PETG, PA, CF-PA 100–300 \(\pm 0.30\) 60–80 1.0 SLA/DLP Photopolymer resin 25–100 \(\pm 0.10\) 40–70 2.5 SLS/MJF PA12, PA11, TPU 80–120 \(\pm 0.20\) 80–95 3.5 DMLS/SLM (metal) AlSi10Mg, Ti-6Al-4V 20–60 \(\pm 0.10\) 95–105 10–25 Cont. fibre (MFX) CF/Kevlar in nylon 100–200 \(\pm 0.20\) 110–130 8 Binder jetting 316L SS, Inconel 35–50 \(\pm 0.05\) 98–100 12

docs.title: 13.5.2 Fused Deposition Modelling (FDM/FFF)
docs.text:
Interlayer bond strength is governed by the degree of polymer inter-diffusion, modelled by the reptation theory:

\[\frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{weld}}}{\sigma_\infty} \propto \left(\frac{t_c}{\tau_r}\right)^{1/4}\tag{13.14}\]

where \(t_c\) is the contact time above \(T_g\) and \(\tau_r\) is the reptation time. Faster printing (shorter \(t_c\)) yields weaker layer adhesion, explaining the empirical 60–80% bulk strength reported for FDM parts. Carbon-fibre-filled PETG (15–20% short fibre by mass) increases tensile modulus from 3.5 GPa to 8–12 GPa. Nylon PA12 and PA6 offer better ductility and environmental resistance than PLA for operational hardware.

Warping of large FDM parts is controlled by a heated build platform (\(T_{\mathrm{bed}} = 60\)–\(110\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\)), a heated enclosure (\(T \approx 45\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\)), and brim/raft adhesion layers.

docs.title: 13.5.3 Selective Laser Sintering (SLS) and Multi-Jet Fusion (MJF)
docs.text: SLS fuses nylon powder with a CO\(_2\) laser. PA12 properties: \(\sigma_{ut} = 48\,\mathrm{MPa}\), \(E = 1.7\,\mathrm{GPa}\), elongation 20%, \(\rho = 0.95\,\mathrm{g/cm^3}\). Parts are isotropic (\(\pm 5\%\) in XYZ) unlike FDM. MJF (HP) achieves surface finish \(Ra \approx 8\,\mu\mathrm{m}\) vs \(12\,\mu\mathrm{m}\) for SLS and faster throughput. Applications: flight control mounts, access panels, sensor housings, duct sections.

docs.title: 13.5.4 Metal Selective Laser Melting (SLM/DMLS)
docs.text:
Powder is fully melted by a focused laser (\(P = 200\)–\(1000\,\mathrm{W}\), \(d_{\mathrm{beam}} = 70\)–\(200\,\mu\mathrm{m}\), layer thickness 30–60 \(\mu\)m). The volumetric energy density governs densification:

\[E_v = \frac{P}{v_s \cdot h_s \cdot t_l}\tag{13.15}\]

where \(v_s\) is scan speed, \(h_s\) is hatch spacing, and \(t_l\) is layer thickness. Optimal \(E_v\) for AlSi10Mg: \(40\)–\(80\,\mathrm{J/mm^3}\). Mechanical properties of SLM AlSi10Mg (as-built): \(\sigma_{ut} = 400\)–\(430\,\mathrm{MPa}\), \(\sigma_{y0.2} = 230\)–\(270\,\mathrm{MPa}\), \(E = 70\,\mathrm{GPa}\), elongation 4–8%.

Post-processing:

  • Stress relief anneal: \(300\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\)/2 h (AlSi10Mg); \(800\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\)/2 h (Ti-6Al-4V).

  • HIP (hot isostatic pressing): 150 MPa argon at \(920\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) for Ti-6Al-4V; reduces residual porosity from \(<0.5\%\) to \(<0.1\%\); fatigue life improvement 20–50%.

  • Machining of critical interfaces to tolerance.

  • Surface finishing: bead blast \(Ra 4\)–\(6\,\mu\)m; electropolish to \(Ra 0.5\,\mu\)m.

docs.title: 13.5.5 Continuous Fibre Reinforced AM (Markforged Process)
docs.text: The Markforged process co-extrudes a continuous fibre tow (carbon fibre, Kevlar, HSHT fibreglass) within a nylon matrix. Fibre volume fraction \(V_f \approx 35\)–\(40\%\). Predicted longitudinal modulus by ROM (Eq. (13.2)): \(E_1 \approx 0.38 \times 70 + 0.62 \times 2.5 \approx 28\,\mathrm{GPa}\). Measured \(E_1 = 54\,\mathrm{GPa}\) for CF-reinforced nylon, \(\sigma_{ut,1} = 800\,\mathrm{MPa}\), approaching aluminium in specific strength. Applications: structural ribs, wing spar inserts, and load-bearing brackets.

docs.title: 13.5.6 Design for Additive Manufacture (DfAM)
docs.text:
Key DfAM rules for UAV structural parts:

  • Self-supporting overhangs: angle from horizontal \(\geq 45^\circ\) for FDM/SLS; \(\geq 35^\circ\) for SLM.

  • Minimum wall thickness: 0.8 mm (FDM), 0.5 mm (SLS), 0.3 mm (SLM).

  • Lattice structures: gyroid, BCC, FCC unit cells reduce mass 30–60% at equal stiffness vs solid.

  • Topology optimisation (SIMP method):

    \[\min_\rho\; \mathbf{f}^T\mathbf{u}\quad \text{s.t.}\; V(\rho)/V_0 \leq f,\; 0 < \rho_{\min} \leq \rho_i \leq 1\tag{13.16}\]

  • Trapped powder: provide \(\geq 2\) mm drain holes in SLM internal cavities.

Quality assurance for AM parts uses X-ray CT to map internal porosity; minimum detectable void \(\approx 100\,\mu\mathrm{m}\) at standard scan resolutions. Porosity limit for structural applications: \(<0.5\%\) by volume.

docs.title: 13.6.1 PCB Design for UAV Applications
docs.text:
Flight controller, motor controller, and communications PCBs must survive vibration, thermal cycling, and humidity of UAV operation.

  • Layer count: 4-layer minimum for digital logic; 6–16 layer for high-speed interfaces (PCIe, USB 3.0, MIPI CSI-2).

  • Controlled impedance: single-ended \(50\,\Omega\); differential pairs \(100\,\Omega\) (LVDS, USB 3.0) or \(90\,\Omega\) (USB 2.0); tolerance \(\pm 10\%\).

  • Dielectric: FR4 (\(\varepsilon_r = 4.2\)–\(4.8\)) for general digital; Rogers RO4003C (\(\varepsilon_r = 3.55 \pm 0.05\), \(\tan\delta = 0.0021\)) for RF traces at 2.4 GHz and above.

  • Thermal management: 2 oz copper planes; thermal vias (via-in-pad for QFN/BGA); aluminium-base PCBs for high-power motor controllers.

  • Trace current capacity per IPC-2152:

    \[I = k_1 (\Delta T)^{k_2} A^{k_3}\tag{13.17}\]

    where \(A\) is trace cross-sectional area, \(\Delta T\) is allowable temperature rise, \(k_1\), \(k_2\), \(k_3\) are empirical constants from IPC-2152 Table 6-1.

IPC-6012 classification: Class 2 for general electronics; Class 3 (minimum annular ring 0.075 mm) mandatory for flight-critical avionics. Surface finishes: ENIG for BGA and fine-pitch pads; HASL for general through-hole; OSP for low-cost production.

docs.title: 13.6.2 SMT Assembly
docs.text:
The SMT assembly process:

  1. Solder paste print: Stainless steel stencil (100–150 \(\mu\)m thick); squeegee at \(60^\circ\), speed \(25\)–\(75\,\mathrm{mm/s}\). Solder paste SAC305 (96.5Sn/3.0Ag/0.5Cu), Type 4 powder (20–38 \(\mu\)m). Aperture area ratio \(> 0.66\) for clean paste release.

  2. Pick and place: Multi-head gantry machine (Yamaha, Fuji NXT, Juki); placement accuracy \(\pm 0.025\)–\(0.05\,\mathrm{mm}\); throughput 10,000–80,000 cph.

  3. Reflow: SAC305 profile: preheat ramp \(1.0\)–\(2.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C/s}\) to \(150\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\), soak 60–90 s, ramp to peak \(245\)–\(250\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\), time above liquidus (\(217\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\)) 30–60 s, cool-down \(<4\,^\circ\mathrm{C/s}\).

  4. AOI: Automated optical inspection checks solder bridges, missing components, and misalignment.

  5. X-ray: BGA and QFN solder joints; void content \(<25\%\) by area.

docs.title: 13.6.3 Conformal Coating
docs.text:
Conformal coating protects PCBs from humidity, salt fog, and contamination per MIL-I-46058C:

AR (acrylic) Easy rework; \(-65\) to \(+130\,^\circ\)C; good humidity resistance. SR (silicone) \(-65\) to \(+200\,^\circ\)C; preferred for motor controllers. UR (polyurethane) Very good chemical resistance; harder than acrylic. XY (parylene) Vacuum-deposited, 5–30 \(\mu\)m, pinhole-free; best moisture barrier; requires specialised stripping for rework.

Coating thickness: 25–130 \(\mu\)m single coat. IPC-A-610 Class 3: 100% coverage verified by UV fluorescence inspection.

docs.title: 13.6.4 ESD Control
docs.text:
ESD can destroy sensitive devices at voltages as low as 100 V (HBM). ANSI/ESD S20.20 ESD protection programme:

  • Wrist straps: resistance \(1\,\mathrm{M}\Omega \pm 10\%\) to ground; tested before each use.

  • Conductive flooring: \(10^6\)–\(10^9\,\Omega\) surface resistance.

  • ESD packaging: static-shielding bags (\(<10\,\mathrm{nJ}\) energy on contact).

  • Ionisers to neutralise insulator surfaces.

docs.title: 13.7.1 Assembly Sequence Planning
docs.text:
The master assembly sequence (MAS) is developed using CAPP tools linked to the digital CAD model under a model-based definition (MBD) philosophy. A typical small-UAV assembly sequence:

  1. Structural sub-assemblies: fuselage shells bonded; cured under pressure fixture.

  2. Main spar installed; shear pins inserted and secured.

  3. Wing skins bonded to rib/spar skeleton; vacuum-bagged overnight.

  4. Landing gear and motor mounts installed; torqued per fastener schedule.

  5. Wire harness routed and secured; connector backshells torqued.

  6. Avionics bay populated: FC, GPS, IMU, radio, power distribution board.

  7. Propulsion: motor mounted, ESC installed, propeller balanced and attached.

  8. Final weight measurement and functional test.

docs.title: 13.7.2 Fastener Installation
docs.text:
Torque specifications use the nut-factor (K-factor) method:

\[T = K \cdot F_i \cdot d\tag{13.18}\]

where \(K = 0.15\)–\(0.25\) depending on thread finish and lubrication. Thread-locking compound (Loctite 243, medium strength) is applied to vibration-exposed fasteners. Safety wiring used on flight-critical fasteners per MS33540.

docs.title: 13.7.3 Structural Bonding
docs.text:
The peel stress at the adhesive bondline edge must satisfy:

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{peel}} = \frac{M_e}{b\,t_a} \leq \frac{\sigma_{a,\mathrm{allow}}}{\mathrm{SF}}\tag{13.19}\]

Surface preparation for aluminium: chromic acid anodise (CAA) or phosphoric acid anodise (PAA) + BR127 primer; bond strength \(>30\,\mathrm{MPa}\) lap shear. For CFRP: peel-ply removal immediately before bonding; light grit-blast (120 grit); wipe with acetone. Bondline thickness controlled by glass beads or shims (0.1–0.3 mm).

docs.title: 13.7.4 Wire Harness Fabrication
docs.text:
• Wire specification: MIL-DTL-22759 (PTFE-insulated, rated \(-65\) to \(+200\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\)); 30–40% lighter than PVC equivalent.

  • Connectors: MIL-C-26482 Series 1 (bayonet); MIL-DTL-38999 (environmental seal).

  • Shielded twisted pair for analogue signals; shield grounded at one end.

  • Minimum bend radius \(10\times\) conductor diameter; tie wraps at max 50 mm intervals.

Voltage drop along a power run:

\[\Delta V = I \cdot R = I \cdot \frac{\rho_e\,L}{A_w}\tag{13.20}\]

where \(\rho_e = 1.72\times10^{-8}\,\Omega\cdot\mathrm{m}\) for copper, \(L\) is wire length, \(A_w\) is cross-sectional area. Maximum allowable \(\Delta V \leq 2\%\) of supply voltage at full load.

docs.title: 13.7.5 Potting and Environmental Sealing
docs.text:
Electronics are potted with two-part polyurethane (Dow Sylgard 170) or rigid epoxy (Emerson & Cuming Stycast 2651). Potting process:

  1. Pre-bake PCB at \(80\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) for 2 h to remove absorbed moisture.

  2. Mix resin/hardener; vacuum degas (\(<1\,\mathrm{mbar}\), 5 min).

  3. Pour at \(5\)–\(10\,\mathrm{mm/min}\) to allow air escape.

  4. Cure at RT 24 h; post-cure \(80\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\)/2 h.

Maximum operating temperature range: \(-55\) to \(+125\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\).

docs.title: 13.7.6 Weight Budgeting and Mass Reduction
docs.text:
The structural mass fraction:

\[f_s = \frac{m_{\mathrm{structure}}}{m_{\mathrm{MTOM}}}\tag{13.21}\]

Typical values: small multi-rotor \(f_s = 0.15\)–\(0.25\); medium fixed-wing \(f_s = 0.25\)–\(0.35\). Mass reduction techniques: replace aluminium brackets with CFRP (density 2.8 \(\to\) 1.6 g/cm\(^3\)), hollow titanium fasteners (HiLok), mouse-holing of non-load-path regions, and honeycomb sandwich panels in place of solid composite shear webs.

docs.title: 13.8.1 Receiving Inspection and Traceability
docs.text: All incoming structural materials are accompanied by a certificate of conformance (CoC) and a certificate of test (CoT) traceable to a test batch. Prepreg is stored at \(-18\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\); cumulative out-time at room temperature tracked against a 30-day limit. Incoming lot sample plan: 10% per MIL-STD-1916.

docs.title: 13.8.2 First Article Inspection (FAI) per AS9102
docs.text:
AS9102 Rev B governs FAI for aerospace parts. Required documentation:

  1. Design documentation review (drawings, specs, deviations).

  2. Material and process certification review.

  3. 100% dimensional inspection of all drawing callouts.

  4. Functional test results.

  5. As-built weight.

  6. FAI report signed by QA and customer.

Partial FAI (PFAI) required after any engineering change affecting form, fit, or function, and after a production break of more than 24 months.

docs.title: 13.8.3 Non-Destructive Testing Methods
docs.text:
UT C-scan Focused transducer scans the part in water immersion or squirter coupling. Maps disbonds, delaminations, and porosity. Lateral resolution \(1\)–\(3\,\mathrm{mm}\); sensitivity \(<0.5\%\) void volume. X-radiography Detects density variations (porosity, inclusions, solder voids). Real-time radioscopy for production screening. Flash thermography IR camera records thermal response after flash excitation. Disbonds (air cavities) appear as warm regions. Coverage rate \(0.5\,\mathrm{m^2/min}\). Dye penetrant (DP) Detects surface-breaking cracks in metal parts. Process: clean \(\to\) penetrant (15 min dwell) \(\to\) remove \(\to\) developer \(\to\) UV inspection. Eddy current (ET)

Detects subsurface cracks and corrosion. Probe frequency \(f\) determines skin depth:

\[\delta = \sqrt{\frac{1}{\pi f \mu \sigma}}\tag{13.22}\]

Higher frequency = shallower penetration, higher surface resolution.

docs.title: 13.8.4 Coordinate Measuring Machine (CMM)
docs.text: CMM probing with ruby-tipped probe (\(\varnothing\,1\)–\(5\,\mathrm{mm}\)) measures 3-D coordinates to \(\pm 1\)–\(3\,\mu\mathrm{m}\) (bridge CMM). GD&T callouts evaluated: flatness, circularity, true position, angularity, perpendicularity. Calibration traceable to national standards per ISO 14253-1.

docs.title: 13.8.5 Functional Testing Protocol
docs.text:
Prior to delivery each UAV undergoes:

  1. Motor run-in: 10%, 50%, 100% throttle for 2 min each; vibration and current monitored.

  2. ESC calibration: throttle range programmed; current limiting verified.

  3. IMU calibration: accelerometer, gyroscope, magnetometer.

  4. GPS lock verification: \(\geq 6\) satellites, PDOP \(< 3.0\).

  5. Control surface travel check: actuation angles and direction.

  6. Datalink check: uplink/downlink verified at maximum design range.

docs.title: 13.8.6 Environmental Qualification (HALT and HASS)
docs.text: HALT (Highly Accelerated Life Test) applies stepped stress beyond specification limits: cold step stress \(-40\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) to \(-80\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) in \(10\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) steps; hot step stress \(+60\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) to \(+100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) in \(5\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) steps; vibration step stress 5 Grms to 40 Grms in 5 Grms steps; combined temperature and vibration stress. HALT identifies design margins; HASS (Highly Accelerated Stress Screening) at reduced levels is used as a production screen.

docs.title: 13.9.1 Lean Manufacturing Principles
docs.text:
5S Sort, Set in order, Shine, Standardise, Sustain: organises the workspace to eliminate waste and reduce errors. Value Stream Mapping (VSM) Identifies all value-adding and non-value-adding steps. Target: reduce non-value-added time from 80–90% (batch) to \(<50\%\) (lean). Takt time

The pace of customer demand:

\[T_{\mathrm{takt}} = \frac{T_{\mathrm{available}}}{Q_{\mathrm{demand}}}\tag{13.23}\]

Production cycle time at each station must \(\leq T_{\mathrm{takt}}\).

Kanban Pull-based inventory control; eliminates excess WIP. Poka-yoke Error-proofing via asymmetric connectors, colour-coded wire insulation.

docs.title: 13.9.2 Jigs and Fixtures
docs.text: Datum scheme per ASME Y14.5: primary (3 points), secondary (2 points), tertiary (1 point) datums uniquely locate the part. Jig accuracy \(\leq 1/3\) of the part tolerance: for \(\pm 0.5\,\mathrm{mm}\) wing attachment tolerance, jig accuracy \(\leq \pm 0.17\,\mathrm{mm}\). Modular fixturing systems (Bluco, Siegmund) allow rapid reconfiguration between variants.

docs.title: 13.9.3 Supply Chain Management
docs.text: UAV supply chains: Tier 1 (system integrators, major sub-systems), Tier 2 (component suppliers: motor winders, PCB fabricators, composite houses), Tier 3 (raw material suppliers). ITAR/EAR compliance is mandatory; State Department licences required for ITAR-controlled items. Sole-source risk mitigated by qualifying \(\geq 2\) sources for each critical component.

docs.title: 13.9.4 Learning Curve and Cost Estimation
docs.text:
The Wright learning curve:

\[C_N = C_1 N^{\log_2(p)}\tag{13.24}\]

where \(C_1\) is first-unit cost, \(N\) is cumulative unit number, and \(p\) is the learning curve percentage (80% curve = 20% cost reduction per doubling of quantity). For UAV airframe assembly, \(p = 0.80\)–\(0.85\) is typical.

The DAPCA IV manufacturing labour equation:

\[H_{\mathrm{mfg}} = F_{\mathrm{diff}} \cdot 7.37 \cdot W_e^{0.82} \cdot V_{\max}^{0.484} \cdot Q^{0.641}\tag{13.25}\]

where \(H_{\mathrm{mfg}}\) is total manufacturing hours, \(W_e\) is empty weight (lb), \(V_{\max}\) is maximum speed (knots), \(Q\) is production quantity, and \(F_{\mathrm{diff}}\) is a difficulty factor (\(1.0\) for aluminium, \(1.5\)–\(2.0\) for composite-primary structures).

docs.text:
