docs.title: 17.7.1 Sea-Skimming Flight Dynamics
docs.text:
A sea-skimming missile flying at altitude \(h\) exploits the Earth’s curvature to minimise radar detection range. The radar line-of-sight (LOS) horizon from a ship radar antenna at height \(H_{radar}\):

\[R_{hor} = \sqrt{2k_e R_E H_{radar}} + \sqrt{2k_e R_E h}\tag{17.25}\]

where \(k_e \approx 1.333\) is the effective Earth radius factor (4/3 Earth model for standard atmosphere). For \(H_{radar} = 20\) m and \(h = 3\) m: \(R_{hor} \approx 24\) km, providing warning time of:

\[t_{warn} = \frac{R_{hor}}{V_{missile}}\tag{17.26}\]

At Mach 0.9 (\(V \approx 308\) m/s): \(t_{warn} \approx 78\) s; at Mach 3 (\(\approx 1{,}020\) m/s): \(t_{warn} \approx 24\) s; at Mach 9 (\(\approx 3{,}060\) m/s): \(t_{warn} \approx 8\) s — less than CIWS engagement time.

Altitude maintenance uses a closed-loop radar altimeter:

\[\dot{h}_{cmd} = K_h(h_{ref} - h_{meas}) + K_{dh}\,\dot{h}_{meas}\tag{17.27}\]

Minimum achievable sea-skim altitude in Sea State 4 (significant wave height \(\approx\)2.5 m): \(h_{min} \approx 3\)–\(5\) m.

docs.title: 17.7.2 Subsonic AShM Systems
docs.text:
AGM-84D/L Harpoon.

Range 315 km (Block II+); speed Mach 0.85; cruise altitude 15–30 m; terminal sea-skim 2 m; warhead 221 kg PBXN-103 blast/penetrator; Williams F112 turbofan; active radar seeker (frequency-agile ECCM); four fold-out strakes; launch mass 691 kg. Decommissioning altitude from 300 m cruise, pull-down to sea-skim at 15 km from target.

Exocet AM39 (Air-Launched).

Length 4.69 m; diameter 0.35 m; mass 655 kg; speed Mach 0.93; range 70 km; warhead 165 kg (semi-armour-piercing charge detonates inside the ship); active monopulse radar seeker; sea-state-adaptive altitude control. The Exocet sank HMS Sheffield (Falklands, 4 May 1982) and MV Atlantic Conveyor with a single hit each, demonstrating decisive AShM lethality.

NSM (Naval Strike Missile / JSM).

Norwegian; range 185 km; speed Mach 0.95; mass 407 kg; warhead 125 kg semi-AP; IIR imaging seeker with autonomous target classification; stealth shaping (RCS \(<\)0.1 m\(^2\)); terrain-following capability for coastal-defence mode. Joint Strike Missile (JSM) variant fits internally in F-35A weapons bay.

docs.title: 17.7.3 Supersonic AShM Systems
docs.text:
P-800 Oniks (SS-N-26 Strobile).

Range 600 km; cruise speed Mach 2.5 at 14 km altitude, terminal sea-skim Mach 2.0; mass 3,000 kg; warhead 250 kg; liquid-fuel ramjet sustainer with solid-rocket booster; active radar seeker (ISAR mode for ship target selection); can engage from multiple simultaneous azimuths in ripple-fire mode; submarine, ship, and truck-launched.

BrahMos Block III.

Terminal dive mode from 14 km altitude at Mach 3.5; active ISAR radar seeker for target-type discrimination; see Section 17.3.

docs.title: 17.7.4 Hypersonic AShM
docs.text:
3M22 Zircon (SS-N-33).

Mach 8–9 cruise; range \(\approx 1{,}000\) km; 300 kg warhead; generates plasma sheath at terminal velocities that theoretically defeats conventional CIWS radar tracking. Kinetic energy on impact: for \(m = 300\) kg travelling at \(V = 2{,}500\) m/s (Mach 7 at sea level): \(E_k = \frac{1}{2}(300)(2500)^2 = 937.5\) MJ — equivalent to 224 kg TNT purely from kinetic energy, before warhead detonation.

DF-17 HGV Anti-Ship Concept.

DF-17 carries the DF-ZF HGV; manoeuvring at Mach 5–10 at 30–80 km altitude; warhead reportedly includes conventional penetrator; engagement of carrier-sized targets from \(>\)2,000 km. Terminal radar seeker must track a 300 m\(\times\)40 m carrier at Mach 10 re-entry; ISAR resolution of \(\approx\)1 m requires 1 GHz radar bandwidth.

docs.title: 17.7.5 Saturation Attack Tactics and Ship Vulnerability
docs.text:
A saturation raid is designed to overwhelm layered ship defences. The critical rate equation for defence:

\[R_{max} = \frac{1}{t_{engage}} \quad [\text{targets/second per weapon}]\tag{17.28}\]

Phalanx Block 1B: \(t_{engage} \approx 2\) s; \(R_{max} = 0.5\) target/s. A 4-missile salvo arriving in a 3 s window from two azimuths saturates a single Phalanx. Coordinated tactics: (1) separate missile arrivals to \(\Delta t < 1\) s; (2) one decoy missile (large RCS) plus one stealth attacker; (3) mix of high sea-skim plus diving attacker to present two elevation layers simultaneously.

Ship vulnerability zones:

  • Magazine hit: detonation of own ordnance; catastrophic (\(>\)90% probability of loss).

  • Waterline penetration: flooding; loss of buoyancy; ship may survive with damage control.

  • Superstructure hit: fires, radar/comms damage; combat capability degraded.

  • Engineering spaces: loss of propulsion; ship disabled but may survive.

Countermeasure hierarchy: outer layer (SM-2/6 at 100–150 km), middle layer (ESSM at 50 km), inner layer (RAM/SeaRAM at 9 km), last-ditch (Phalanx at 2 km), passive (chaff, towed decoys, IR flares, jamming).

docs.title: 17.8.1 Direct-Ascent ASAT
docs.text:
Direct-ascent systems launch a KKV on a modified ballistic trajectory to the target satellite’s orbital altitude. The PL-19 Nudol (Russia) demonstrated ASAT capability against Cosmos 1408 (November 2021), creating \(>\)1,500 trackable debris fragments (\(>\)10 cm) and estimated \(>\)15,000 fragments \(>\)1 cm at altitudes 450–650 km.

Intercept closing velocity for a counter-orbit (retrograde) intercept:

\[V_c = V_{orbit} + V_{KKV,z} = \sqrt{\frac{\mu}{r}} + V_{ascent,z}\tag{17.29}\]

For LEO at 500 km: \(V_{orbit} = 7.61\) km/s; \(V_{KKV,z} \approx 1\) km/s; \(V_c \approx 8.5\)–\(9\) km/s. Kinetic energy at impact (\(m_{KKV} = 60\) kg, \(V_c = 8{,}500\) m/s):

\[E_k = \frac{1}{2}\,m_{KKV}\,V_c^2 = \frac{1}{2}(60)(8500)^2 = 2.17\text{ GJ}\tag{17.30}\]

Equivalent to 519 kg TNT — no conventional warhead required; the debris field IS the kill mechanism.

docs.title: 17.8.2 Kessler Syndrome and Orbital Debris
docs.text:
The self-sustaining cascade criterion compares collision generation rate with debris decay rate:

\[\frac{dN}{dt} = \alpha N^2 - \beta N\tag{17.31}\]

where \(\alpha\) is the collision rate coefficient (proportional to orbital flux and mean cross-section) and \(\beta\) is the decay rate constant (atmospheric drag, predominantly above 200 km). For 400 km altitude, \(\beta \gg \alpha N\): benign, self-cleansing. For 700 km altitude, \(\alpha N \approx \beta\): marginal stability. Above 800 km: \(\alpha N > \beta\) — an existing debris population can self-sustain even without new launches.

docs.title: 17.8.3 Co-Orbital ASAT
docs.text:
A manoeuvring “inspector satellite” approaches a target in the same orbital plane. Rendezvous \(\Delta V\) using the Clohessy–Wiltshire equations for in-plane manoeuvre:

\[\ddot{x} - 2n\dot{y} - 3n^2 x = f_x;\qquad \ddot{y} + 2n\dot{x} = f_y\tag{17.32}\]

where \((x, y)\) are radial/in-track relative positions, \(n = \sqrt{\mu/r^3}\) is mean motion, and \((f_x, f_y)\) are specific thrust components. Russian Cosmos 2542/2543 manoeuvred to within \(\approx\)150 km of USA-245 in January 2020, demonstrating proximity operations.

docs.title: 17.8.4 Directed-Energy ASAT
docs.text:
Ground-based HEL irradiance at satellite altitude \(R\):

\[I_{sat} = \frac{P_{laser}\,\eta_{atm}\,D_{ap}^2}{(1.22\,\lambda\,R)^2\,\pi}\tag{17.33}\]

where \(P_{laser}\) is beam power, \(\eta_{atm}\) is atmospheric transmission (\(\sim\)0.5–0.8), \(\lambda\) is wavelength, and \(D_{ap}\) is aperture diameter. Dazzle threshold \(I_{dazzle} \approx 10\) W/cm\(^2\); damage threshold \(I_{damage} \approx 10\)–\(100\) kW/cm\(^2\). For \(P_{laser} = 1\) MW, \(D_{ap} = 1.5\) m, \(\lambda = 1.06~\mu\)m, \(R = 500\) km, \(\eta_{atm} = 0.6\):

\[I_{sat} = \frac{10^6 \times 0.6 \times 1.5^2}{(1.22 \times 1.06\times10^{-6}\times 5\times10^5)^2 \pi} \approx 3.1\text{ kW/cm}^2\]

This marginally achieves damage threshold; adaptive optics (AO) correction of atmospheric turbulence increases \(I_{sat}\) by a factor of 2–5.

docs.title: 17.9.1 Concept and Design Philosophy
docs.text:
Loitering munitions (LM), also termed kamikaze drones or suicide UAS, combine the persistent area-surveillance capability of a UAS with the precision-lethality of a guided munition. Defining characteristics:

  • Dual-phase mission: loiter (reconnaissance/target-acquisition mode) then strike (munition mode).

  • Operator-in-the-loop (OITL): human authorises final attack — legally necessary under LOAC for autonomous lethal engagement.

  • Wave-off capability: operator can abort attack; missile continues loitering or returns to pre-programmed abort waypoint.

  • Low unit cost ($10,000–$100,000) enabling expendable mass-attrition operations and cost-asymmetric warfare.

  • Tube-launched or canister-launched for minimal logistical footprint; man-portable.

docs.title: 17.9.2 Propulsion and Endurance
docs.text:
Electric brushless-DC motor with folding propeller dominates small LM (\(<\)10 kg). Endurance:

\[t_{endurance} = \frac{\eta_{mot}\,\eta_{prop}\,E_{batt}}{P_{req,cruise}}\tag{17.34}\]

where cruise power:

\[P_{req} = \frac{1}{2}\rho V_c^3 C_D A_{ref} + \frac{2\,W^2}{\rho V_c A_{wing} \pi e \mathcal{AR}}\tag{17.35}\]

(parasite + induced power; \(e\) = Oswald efficiency; \(\mathcal{AR}\) = aspect ratio). Worked example (Switchblade 300): \(V_c = 35\) m/s; \(C_D = 0.055\); \(A_{ref} = 0.008\) m\(^2\); \(W = 25\) N; \(A_{wing} = 0.12\) m\(^2\); \(\mathcal{AR} = 4\); \(e = 0.8\); \(\rho = 1.225\) kg/m\(^3\): \(P_{parasite} \approx 18\) W; \(P_{induced} \approx 5\) W; \(P_{req} \approx 23\) W. Battery: \(E_{batt} = 6\) Ah\(\times\)22.2 V\(\times\)0.85 = 113 Wh; \(\eta_{mot}\eta_{prop} = 0.80\); \(t = 113 \times 3600 \times 0.80 / (23 \times 3600) \approx 4.0\) hr. Actual endurance \(\approx\)10 min (accounting for terminal dive \(\approx\)full throttle and a conservative usable battery fraction of 0.12 at low temperature).

docs.title: 17.9.3 Seeker and Terminal Guidance
docs.text:
EO/IR gimballed camera provides imagery to the remote operator via encrypted RF data-link. Uncooled microbolometer (320\(\times\)256 pixels, 17 \(\mu\)m pitch) for night operation; EO for day. Terminal guidance:

\[\dot{\gamma}_m = N_{PNG}\,V_c\,\dot{\sigma}\tag{17.36}\]

Impact precision: CEP \(<\)1 m at ranges \(<\)10 km under calm wind. Cross-wind correction required at final approach:

\[\delta_{aileron} = K_{cw}\,\frac{V_{wind}}{V_m}\cos(\psi_{wind} - \psi_m)\tag{17.37}\]

docs.title: 17.9.4 Key Loitering Munition Systems
docs.text:
Switchblade 300.

AeroVironment (US); tube-launched; diameter 38 mm (canister); folded length 600 mm; missile mass 2.5 kg; warhead 0.3 kg HEAT or blast-frag; range 10 km; endurance 10 min; speed up to 157 km/h terminal; EO+IR seeker; man-in-the-loop authorisation; wave-off capability; backpack-portable system (6 tubes).

Switchblade 600.

23 kg total system; anti-armour warhead (estimated Javelin-equivalent HEAT); range 40 km; endurance 40 min; speed 185 km/h terminal; mmW seeker option. Engages IFV, MBT (thin-roof attack).

Lancet-3 (ZALA Aero / Kalashnikov).

12 kg; electric pusher propulsion; EO seeker with target-tracking algorithm; HEAT warhead; range 40 km; extensively used in Russo-Ukraine war (2022–2025) against artillery systems, air-defence radars, armoured vehicles. Estimated unit cost \(\approx\)$35,000.

Harop (IAI).

135 kg; 3.0 m span; 6+ hr endurance; range 1,000 km; 23 kg warhead; Williams TJ-150 turbojet; dual-mode: anti-radiation (homes on enemy radar emission via passive radar seeker) or electro-optical (operator selects target via downlink video); used by Azerbaijan (Nagorno-Karabakh 2020) to destroy S-300 and Buk batteries.

HERO Series (UVision).

HERO-30: 4 kg, 30 min, HEAT; HERO-120: 18 kg, 60 min, 120 mm HEAT, effective vs. MBT; HERO-400: 40 kg anti-armour penetrator.

docs.title: 17.9.5 Swarm Effectiveness
docs.text:
Coordinated swarm probability of kill against a single defended target:

\[P_{k,swarm} = 1 - \prod_{i=1}^{N}(1 - P_{k,i})\tag{17.38}\]

For \(N = 10\) LMs, each \(P_{k,i} = 0.30\): \(P_{k,swarm} = 1 - 0.70^{10} = 0.972\). This mathematical basis drives the shift toward high-volume, low-cost munitions over exquisite low-density precision weapons.

docs.title: 17.10.1 Submarine-Launched Cruise Missiles (SLCM)
docs.text:
The BGM-109 Tomahawk SLCM can be launched from the 533 mm torpedo tube of any US SSN/SSBN or from the Virginia Payload Module (VPM): 28 additional VLS cells added to Virginia Block V giving total of 40 SLCM. Launch from torpedo tube: capsule ejects; missile emerges from water; booster ignites; wings deploy.

BrahMos SLCM.

Sealed underwater launch canister; solid booster ignites above water; Mach 3 cruise; range 500 km; available for Akula and Yasen-class SSNs.

docs.title: 17.10.2 Anti-Submarine Weapons
docs.text:
RUR-5 ASROC.

Standard US surface-ship weapon: rockets the Mk 54 LWT (Light Weight Torpedo, 274 kg) to 22 km; torpedo enters water on parachute; active sonar seeker homes on submarine. ASROC effectively bypasses the acoustic-advantage of the submarine by shortening closing time from \(>\)30 min (helicopter delivery) to \(<\)60 s.

VL-ASROC.

VLS-launched ASROC; same Mk 54 payload; fully compatible with Mk 41 cells.

docs.title: 17.10.3 Vertical Launch System Integration
docs.text:
The Mk 41 VLS is the backbone of US and allied surface-combatant armament. Specifications: 8 cells per module; cell cross-section 0.625 m \(\times\) 0.625 m; depth 7.72 m; compatible missiles: SM-2/3/6, Tomahawk, ASROC, ESSM (4:1 quad-pack). A DDG-51 Flight III carries 96 VLS cells; an Ticonderoga-class cruiser 122 cells.

SM-6 (RIM-174).

Dual-role AAW + surface strike; range 240 km; Mach 3.5; active radar seeker (AIM-120 seeker head); BMD capability; 64 kg warhead. At Mach 3.5, SM-6 intercepts Mach 2–3 AShM at \(>\)100 km standoff.

docs.title: 17.10.4 Close-In Weapon Systems
docs.text:
RAM Block II (RIM-116C).

21-round launcher; speed Mach 2; range 9 km; passive RF + dual IIR seeker; rolling-airframe single-control-fin design; 11 kg blast-frag warhead; 400 ms reaction time; effective against sea-skimmers and supersonic AShM.

Phalanx Block 1B (reference only).

M61A1 20 mm Vulcan; 4,500 rd/min; effective range 2 km; autonomous close-in last-ditch defence; complements SeaRAM in layered architecture.

docs.title: 17.11.1 The Kill Chain
docs.text:
The BMD kill chain involves five sequential, time-critical functions:

\[t_{total} = t_{detect} + t_{track} + t_{discrim} + t_{intercept} + t_{assess}\tag{17.39}\]

For a 1,000 km SRBM (\(t_{flight} \approx 5\) min): \(t_{decision} < 90\) s available for commit-to-fire. DSP/SBIRS satellites detect ICBM boost-phase plume within 30 s of launch; AN/TPY-2 X-band GBR provides tracking accuracy \(<\)50 m at 5,000 km range (\(\sigma_{track} < 0.01\) mrad). Debris discrimination (separating warhead RV from decoys and bus fragments) remains the most technically challenging function:

\[P_{discrim} = f\!\left(\frac{\Delta\beta_{decoy}}{\sigma_{\beta}}\right)\tag{17.40}\]

where \(\Delta\beta_{decoy}\) is the ballistic coefficient difference between the RV and decoy, and \(\sigma_\beta\) is measurement uncertainty.

docs.title: 17.11.2 Hit-to-Kill KKV Physics
docs.text:
Modern KKVs destroy their targets by direct hypervelocity impact. Energy at impact:

\[E_{impact} = \frac{1}{2}(m_{KKV} + m_{RV})\,V_c^2\tag{17.41}\]

For \(m_{KKV} = 70\) kg, \(m_{RV} = 800\) kg, \(V_c = 10\) km/s: \(E_{impact} = \frac{1}{2}(870)(10^4)^2 = 4.35 \times 10^{10}\) J = 10.4 kton TNT equivalent — sufficient to completely disintegrate the RV. The KKV terminal guidance closing-error budget:

\[\sigma_{miss} = \sqrt{\sigma_{nav}^2 + \sigma_{seeker}^2 + \sigma_{dacs}^2}\tag{17.42}\]

DACS (Divert and Attitude Control System): cold-gas or hydrazine thrusters; specific impulse \(\approx\)220 s; \(\Delta V_{dacs} \approx 200\) m/s for terminal correction.

docs.title: 17.11.3 THAAD — Terminal High Altitude Area Defense
docs.text: Intercept altitude 40–150 km (upper endo/lower exo-atmosphere); missile speed \(>\) Mach 8.2 (\(\approx\)2.8 km/s); kill mechanism: direct KKV with no explosive warhead; seeker: cryogenically cooled long-wave IIR FPA with autonomous guidance; DACS thruster package; 8 missiles per launcher; AN/TPY-2 X-band AESA radar (2.4 m aperture; 1,000+ km tracking range); deployed OCONUS and CONUS; single-shot \(P_k\) vs. Scud-class \(\approx\)0.84 (14/17 intercept tests through 2022).

docs.title: 17.11.4 SM-3 Block IIA Midcourse Interceptor
docs.text:
Three stages: Mk 72 solid booster (1.557 m diameter); Mk 104 dual-thrust solid sustainer; Mk 142 DACS stage with KKV. Total length 6.55 m; diameter 0.533 m; weight 1,500 kg; intercept altitude \(>\)180 km; closing speed \(>\)10 km/s. The KKV has \(\approx\)7 kg mass; IIR seeker with 128\(\times\)128 FLIR array; 3-axis divert thrusters (\(\pm\)60 m/s \(\Delta V\) budget).

Table 17.7. Ballistic Missile Defence System Comparison System Intercept Layer Altitude (km) Range (km) Speed Target Class Patriot PAC-3 MSE Terminal endo 0–40 35 M4.5 SRBM, aircraft THAAD Terminal endo/exo 40–150 200 M8.2 SRBM, MRBM, IRBM Arrow-3 Exo-atmospheric 100–200 2,400 M9+ MRBM, IRBM SM-3 Block IIA Midcourse exo 70–500+ 2,500 M13+ MRBM, IRBM, limited ICBM GBI (EKV) Midcourse exo 200+ 5,000 M25 ICBM

docs.title: 17.12.1 Hypersonic Weapons
docs.text:
The proliferation of HGVs and hypersonic cruise missiles (Ma \(>\) 5) represents the most significant shift in missile technology since the ICBM era. Key integration challenges:

  1. Thermal management: sustained Mach 5+ flight generates stagnation temperatures \(T_s = T_\infty\!\left(1 + \frac{\gamma-1}{2}Ma^2\right)\) at Mach 10, \(T_s \approx 19{,}000\) K (equilibrium air); actual wall temperature (with ablation/radiation cooling) \(T_{wall} \approx 2{,}000\)–\(2{,}500\) K. C–C composites and UHTCs (ZrB\(_2\), HfC, TaC; \(T_{melt} > 3{,}000\)°C) are required.

  2. Plasma sheath communication blackout: electron number density \(n_e > 10^{18}\) m\(^{-3}\) at Mach 15 creates plasma frequency \(f_p = \frac{1}{2\pi}\!\sqrt{n_e e^2/m_e \varepsilon_0} > 10\) GHz, blocking conventional RF. Trailing-wire antenna, HF windows, or in-band transmission protocols are solutions.

  3. Seeker window: SiC, ALON, spinel, or sapphire domes at Mach 5–10; \(T_{surface} > 1{,}000\)°C; transmissivity degrades in mid-wave IR. Active cooling of seeker dome required above Mach 8.

  4. Manufacturing tolerances: leading-edge radius variation of \(\pm\)0.5 mm causes \(>\)200% variation in peak heat flux at Mach 15; tolerance stack-up becomes a primary design constraint.

docs.title: 17.12.2 Directed Energy Adjuncts
docs.text:
Cost exchange ratio (CER) drives transition to HEL and HPM:

\[\text{CER} = \frac{C_{interceptor}}{C_{threat}}\tag{17.43}\]

Iron Dome vs. Qassam rocket: CER \(\approx 50{,}000/500 = 100:1\). Iron Beam (Rafael, 100 kW HEL): \(\approx \$3.50\) per engagement (electricity cost) vs. \(>\$50{,}000\) per Tamir kinetic interceptor. HEL is most effective against slow, unarmoured threats (UAS, mortar, unguided rockets); kinetic interceptors remain necessary for fast manoeuvring missiles.

docs.title: 17.12.3 Artificial Intelligence Integration
docs.text:
LRASM employs autonomous multi-target discrimination using computer vision:

  • Object detection (YOLOv8-equivalent on embedded GPU) at 30 Hz, classifying vessel type from IIR imagery.

  • Cooperative target-deconfliction: swarm of 4 LRASM shares target tracks via TDMA datalink; one missile attacks, others reassign or continue surveillance.

  • Cognitive ECCM: seeker adapts frequency-hop pattern in response to detected jamming spectrum; machine-learning classifier distinguishes jamming from clutter.

docs.title: 17.12.4 Modular Design and Mass Production
docs.text: The Ukraine conflict (2022–present) demonstrated the operational primacy of production rate over peak capability. Industrial bottlenecks: ammonium perchlorate (solid rocket oxidiser, concentrated supply); TSMC-class ICs for guidance; PBXN/IMX energetic formulations (limited US capacity \(\approx\)30,000 precision munitions/yr vs. demand). Modular design philosophy (common seeker + variable warhead + common motor + variable airframe) reduces non-recurring engineering cost and enables rapid capability insertion.

docs.title: 17.13 Summary and Design Trade-Off Matrix
docs.text:
Table 17.8. Missile Category Design Trade-Off Matrix Category Range Speed CEP Survivability Cost Primary Design Constraint ICBM 10,000+ km M20–25 terminal 100 m High (silo/SSBN) Very high MIRV payload; MIRV bus nav accuracy SLBM 11,300 km M20+ terminal 90 m Very high (SSBN) Very high Undersea launch; stellar-inertial nav Cruise (subsonic) 500–2,500 km M0.7–0.9 \(<\)10 m Med (low RCS) High Turbofan endurance; terrain mapping Cruise (supersonic) 300–1,000 km M2–9 1–10 m High (speed) High Thermal mgmt; propulsion integration SAM (long-range) 100–400 km M4–6 N/A (\(P_k\)) Fixed/TEL High Radar discrimination; engagement capacity AAM (BVRAAM) 50–400 km M4–6 N/A (\(P_k\)) Aircraft-carried Med-high No-escape zone; energy at intercept ATGM 0.5–16 km M1–3 \(<\)1 m Manpack Low Armour defeat; tandem warhead mass AShM 50–1,000 km M0.85–9 5–10 m Low RCS + speed Medium Sea-skim altitude; seeker ECCM Loitering Munition 10–1,000 km M0.2–0.5 \(<\)1 m Low cost/attrition Low Endurance; warhead yield; OITL law ASAT (direct) LEO alts M25+ terminal \(<\)1 m Single-use High Discrimination; debris avoidance

The optimal missile design is invariably a system-of-systems solution: no single weapon dominates all parameters simultaneously. The central recurring trade is between speed (thermal complexity, propulsion integration, cost) and stealth plus guidance precision (low signature, low-altitude flight, sophisticated GNC, small radar cross-section). Hypersonic cruise missiles attempt to achieve both speed and precision simultaneously, at the cost of extreme technical, manufacturing, and materials challenges that represent the frontier of contemporary weapons engineering.

Future directions include: multi-domain strike packages coordinating ballistic, cruise, and loitering munitions in timed simultaneous strikes; AI-enabled autonomous retargeting with legal OITL constraints; modular seeker-warhead-motor payload interfaces enabling hot-swap capability; directed energy as primary lethality mechanism for UAS and rocket threats; quantum inertial navigation (cold-atom interferometry) eliminating GPS dependency at \(<\)1 cm/hr drift; and 3D-additive-manufactured rocket motors and airframes reducing production lead time from 24 months to \(<\)6 months.

docs.title: 18.1 Introduction to Missile Aerodynamics
docs.text:
Missile aerodynamics sits at the intersection of classical fluid mechanics, structural dynamics, and flight-control engineering. Unlike aircraft aerodynamics—which is dominated by near-subsonic, quasi-steady regimes with well-characterised stall behaviour—missiles must operate reliably across Mach 0.3 to Mach 25, spanning subsonic, transonic, supersonic, and hypersonic regimes in a single flight trajectory. Each regime introduces qualitatively different flow physics: separated low-speed laminar flow, transonic shock formation, oblique shock–expansion fan systems, and chemically reacting real-gas hypersonic flows.

The aerodynamic force and moment system on a missile uses a body-fixed coordinate frame: axial force \(X\) (along body axis, positive rearward), normal force \(Z\) (positive upward in pitch plane), and side force \(Y\) (positive starboard). Corresponding moments: pitching moment \(M\) (positive nose-up), yawing moment \(N\) (positive nose-right), rolling moment \(L\) (positive starboard-wing-down). Non-dimensional coefficients are formed with dynamic pressure \(q_\infty = \frac{1}{2}\rho_\infty V_\infty^2\), reference area \(S_{ref} = \pi D^2/4\) (body cross-section), and reference length \(D\) (body diameter) for moments:

\[\begin{align*} C_N &= \frac{Z}{q_\infty S_{ref}} & C_A &= \frac{X}{q_\infty S_{ref}} & C_m &= \frac{M}{q_\infty S_{ref} D} \end{align*}\]

docs.title: 18.2.1 Nose Geometry
docs.text: The nose cone geometry determines zero-lift wave drag and the nose contribution to normal force. Principal nose shapes used in missile design:

docs.title: Conical Nose
docs.text:
A cone of half-angle \(\theta_c\) has wave-drag coefficient at supersonic speeds (linearised theory):

\[C_{D,cone} = \frac{2\theta_c^2}{\sqrt{Ma^2 - 1}}\bigl(1 + \text{correction terms}\bigr)\tag{18.2}\]

Conical noses are simple to manufacture and have low wave drag at Mach \(>\)3 but higher drag than optimised shapes at Mach 1–3.

docs.title: Ogive Nose
docs.text:
The tangent ogive is the circular-arc profile whose arc is tangent to the body cylinder at the shoulder. Nose radius \(R_{ogive}\), calibre \(D\), and nose length \(L_n\) are related by:

\[R_{ogive} = \frac{(L_n/D)^2 + 0.25}{1}\cdot\frac{D}{2}\tag{18.3}\]

The cross-sectional radius at axial station \(x\) (measured from nose tip):

\[r(x) = \sqrt{R_{ogive}^2 - (L_n - x)^2} - (R_{ogive} - D/2)\tag{18.4}\]

Optimum fineness ratio \(L_n/D \approx 3\)–\(4\) for minimum wave drag at Mach 1.5–3; increasing \(L_n/D\) beyond 5 gives diminishing drag reduction while reducing internal volume.

docs.title: Von Kármán (LD-Haack) Nose
docs.text:
Derived by minimising wave drag for a fixed enclosed volume (von Kármán, 1947):

\[r(x) = \frac{R}{\sqrt{\pi}}\bigl[\theta - \tfrac{1}{2}\sin(2\theta)\bigr]^{1/2}, \quad \theta = \arccos\!\left(1 - \frac{2x}{L_n}\right)\tag{18.5}\]

where \(R\) is the base radius and \(L_n\) is nose length. The LD-Haack profile has 20–30% lower wave drag than a tangent ogive of equal fineness ratio at Mach 1.5–3.

docs.title: Parabolic Nose
docs.text: A parabolic profile \(r(x) = R(x/L_n)^n\) where \(n = 0.5\)–\(0.75\); simple to define; drag intermediate between conical and von Kármán.

docs.title: 18.2.2 Normal Force on the Body
docs.text:
Slender-body theory (Allen and Perkins, 1951) separates body normal force into a potential (linear) term and a crossflow viscous (nonlinear) term:

\[C_{N,body} = C_{N,body}^{linear}(\alpha) + C_{N,body}^{nonlinear}(\alpha)\tag{18.6}\]

The linear (potential flow) term from slender-body theory:

\[\frac{dC_N}{d\alpha}\bigg|_{linear} = \frac{2}{D}\left(\frac{A_{base}}{S_{ref}} - \frac{A_{nose}}{S_{ref}}\right)\tag{18.7}\]

For a body of revolution with no nose cut-off: \(dC_N/d\alpha \approx 2 \times A_{base}/S_{ref} = 2\) (per radian) where \(S_{ref} = A_{base}\).

The nonlinear crossflow term at angle of attack \(\alpha > 10°\):

\[C_{N,body}^{NL} = \eta\,C_{d,cf}\,\frac{A_{plan}}{S_{ref}}\sin^2\alpha\tag{18.8}\]

where \(C_{d,cf} \approx 1.2\) is the crossflow drag coefficient of a cylinder, \(A_{plan}\) is the planform area of the body (projected side area), and \(\eta \approx 0.8\)–\(1.0\) is an empirical correction factor. The centre of pressure of the crossflow term is located at mid-body; this moves \(x_{cp}\) aft as \(\alpha\) increases, potentially destabilising a marginally stable missile.

docs.title: 18.2.3 Body Drag Components
docs.text:
Total zero-lift drag coefficient of a missile body:

\[C_{D0,body} = C_{D,friction} + C_{D,wave} + C_{D,base}\tag{18.9}\]

Skin friction.

For turbulent flow (transition at \(Re_x \approx 5\times10^5\)), the compressible turbulent skin friction using the van Driest II method:

\[C_f = \frac{0.455}{(\log_{10} Re_L)^{2.58} (1 + 0.21 Ma_\infty^2)^{0.467}}\tag{18.10}\]

Wetted area correction: \(C_{D,friction} = C_f \cdot (S_{wet}/S_{ref})\). For \(Ma = 2\), \(Re_L = 10^7\): \(C_f \approx 0.0027\); \(S_{wet}/S_{ref} \approx 4 L/D\); \(C_{D,friction} \approx 0.054\) for \(L/D = 5\).

Wave drag.

At supersonic speeds, linear wave drag of a smooth body of revolution (linearised theory):

\[C_{D,wave} = \frac{4}{\pi S_{ref}}\int_0^L\!\int_0^L \frac{d^2A}{dx^2}\frac{d^2A}{d\xi^2}\ln|x-\xi|\,dx\,d\xi\tag{18.11}\]

For the Sears–Haack body (minimum wave drag for fixed volume \(V\) and length \(L\)):

\[C_{D,wave,min} = \frac{24\pi V}{L^2 S_{ref}} = \frac{9\pi^2}{2}\left(\frac{A_{max}}{L^2}\right)\tag{18.12}\]

Base drag.

Base drag arises from the low-pressure region aft of a blunt base. The empirical Platou formula:

\[C_{D,base} = \frac{0.25}{1 + 0.4\,Ma_\infty^2}\cdot\frac{A_{base}}{S_{ref}}\tag{18.13}\]

Base drag is reduced by a boattail (reducing \(A_{base}\)), a nozzle plume (which acts as an aerodynamic boat-tail), or a base-bleed device. At Mach 2, a boattail of 10° half-angle reducing base area by 50% cuts base drag by \(\approx\)60%.

docs.title: 18.2.4 Centre of Pressure of the Body
docs.text:
From slender-body theory, the axial location of the body CP (linear term only):

\[x_{cp,body} = \frac{\int_0^L x\,\frac{d(dC_N/dx)}{dx}\,dx}{\int_0^L \frac{d(dC_N/dx)}{dx}\,dx} = x_{centroid,A(x)}\tag{18.14}\]

For a tangent ogive + cylinder configuration, \(x_{cp,body} \approx 0.67\,L_n\) (located within the ogive).

docs.title: 18.3.1 Fin Planform Selection
docs.text: Fin planforms in order of decreasing subsonic normal-force slope (per unit aspect ratio): rectangular \(>\) trapezoidal \(>\) delta \(\approx\) cropped delta. The fin aspect ratio: \(AR = b^2/S_{fin}\) where \(b\) is fin span and \(S_{fin}\) is fin area. For a delta fin: \(AR = 4/(C_{root}/b + C_{tip}/b) = 4/\bar{c}/b\) where \(\bar{c}\) is mean chord.

docs.title: 18.3.2 Fin Normal-Force Slope
docs.text:
For a single fin at angle of attack \(\alpha\), the subsonic normal-force slope per unit \(\alpha\) (Prandtl–Glauert corrected):

\[C_{N\alpha,fin} = \frac{2\pi AR}{2 + \sqrt{4 + AR^2(1 + \tan^2\Lambda_{c/2}/\beta^2)}}\tag{18.15}\]

where \(\beta = \sqrt{1 - Ma^2}\) (subsonic), \(\Lambda_{c/2}\) is quarter-chord sweep. For \(AR = 2\), \(Ma = 0.5\), \(\Lambda_{c/2} = 45°\): \(C_{N\alpha,fin} \approx 2.1\) rad\(^{-1}\).

At supersonic speeds (Ackeret 2D linear theory, thin fin):

\[C_{N\alpha,fin,sup} = \frac{4}{\sqrt{Ma^2 - 1}}\tag{18.16}\]

For 3D fins a correction factor \(K\) (typically 0.8–0.95 for practical AR) applies.

docs.title: 18.3.3 Body–Fin Interference: Carryover Factors
docs.text:
The total normal-force coefficient of a body–fin combination exceeds the sum of isolated components due to mutual interference. The Nielsen interference factors:

\[\begin{align*} K_{W(B)} &= \text{ratio of fin lift in presence of body to isolated fin lift} \\ K_{B(W)} &= \text{ratio of body lift (carryover from fin) to isolated fin lift} \end{align*}\]

These are functions of \(d/(d+s)\) where \(d\) is body diameter and \(s\) is fin semi-span. For \(d/(d+s) = 0.5\): \(K_{W(B)} \approx 1.37\); \(K_{B(W)} \approx 0.87\). Total fin + carryover contribution:

\[C_{N,fins+carryover} = n_{fins} \cdot [K_{W(B)} + K_{B(W)}]\,C_{N\alpha,fin}\,\alpha\,\frac{S_{fin}}{S_{ref}}\tag{18.19}\]

where \(n_{fins}\) is the number of fins (typically 3 or 4).

docs.title: 18.3.4 Fin Flutter
docs.text:
Panel flutter velocity (simplified Theodorsen approach for a rectangular panel):

\[V_F = \sqrt{\frac{2\pi E t^3 \beta_F}{3(1-\nu^2) \rho_\infty c^4}}\tag{18.20}\]

where \(E\) is panel Young’s modulus, \(t\) is panel thickness, \(\nu\) is Poisson’s ratio, \(c\) is chord, and \(\beta_F\) is a non-dimensional flutter parameter (\(\approx 0.07\) for an aspect-ratio-1 panel). Structural damping ratio \(\zeta > 0.01\) increases \(V_F\) by 10–15%. Titanium alloy fins (Ti-6Al-4V: \(E = 114\) GPa, \(\rho = 4{,}430\) kg/m\(^3\)) vs. aluminium 7075 (\(E = 72\) GPa, \(\rho = 2{,}810\) kg/m\(^3\)): Ti provides \(\approx 2.0\times\) higher specific stiffness, increasing \(V_F\) by \(\approx 40\%\) at the same geometry.

docs.title: 18.3.5 Roll Stabilisation and Spin Rate
docs.text:
Fin cant angle \(\phi_{cant}\) induces a rolling moment:

\[C_{l,cant} = n_{fins}\,C_{N\alpha,fin}\,\phi_{cant}\,\frac{S_{fin}}{S_{ref}}\,\frac{y_{fin}}{D}\tag{18.21}\]

Steady-state roll rate for a free-rolling missile:

\[p = \frac{C_{l,cant}\,q_\infty\,S_{ref}\,D}{I_{xx}\,|C_{l\delta}|\,q_\infty\,S_{ref}\,D\,D/(2V_m)}\tag{18.22}\]

Spinning stabilisation is used in unguided rockets; guided missiles typically require low roll rate (\(<\)5 rad/s) to prevent seeker gimbal saturation and cross-coupling between pitch and yaw axes. Roll rate induced by cant angle of 1° (\(\phi_{cant} \approx 0.0175\) rad) on a Mach 2 missile at sea level (HIMARS GMLRS geometry): \(p \approx 12\) rad/s.

docs.title: 18.4.1 Normal Force Coefficient
docs.text:
The total normal force coefficient by additive interference method:

\[C_N = C_{N,body} + C_{N,fins+carryover} + C_{N,canard}\bigl(\text{if present}\bigr)\tag{18.23}\]

For a tail-controlled missile at \(\alpha = 5°\), \(Ma = 2\), \(n = 4\) fins of \(S_{fin}/S_{ref} = 0.8\):

  • \(C_{N,body} = 2.0\,\alpha_{rad} = 2.0 \times 0.0873 = 0.175\)

  • \(K_{W(B)} + K_{B(W)} = 2.0\) (typical)

  • \(C_{N\alpha,fin} = 4/\sqrt{4-1} = 2.31\) rad\(^{-1}\)

  • \(C_{N,fins} = 4 \times 2.0 \times 2.31 \times 0.0873 \times 0.8 = 1.29\)

  • \(C_N = 0.175 + 1.29 = 1.47\)

docs.title: 18.4.2 Pitching Moment Coefficient and Stability
docs.text:
Pitching moment coefficient about the nose (reference point \(x_{ref} = 0\)):

\[C_m = C_{m,body} + C_{m,fins} = -C_{N,body}\frac{x_{cp,body}}{D} - C_{N,fins}\frac{x_{cp,fins}}{D}\tag{18.24}\]

Pitching moment slope about the CG:

\[C_{m\alpha} = C_{N\alpha}\,\frac{x_{CG} - x_{CP}}{D}\tag{18.25}\]

Static stability criterion: \(C_{m\alpha} < 0\) (restoring moment for positive AoA). This requires \(x_{CG} < x_{CP}\) (CG ahead of CP), i.e. positive static margin:

\[SM = \frac{x_{CP} - x_{CG}}{D} > 0\tag{18.26}\]

Typical design target: \(SM \approx 0.5\)–\(2.0\) calibres. Insufficient SM \(\to\) instability; excessive SM \(\to\) sluggish response, high control surface deflections required, aerodynamic heating of tail concentrated.

docs.title: 18.4.3 Centre of Pressure Calculation
docs.text:
Weighted-average CP location:

\[x_{CP} = \frac{\sum_i C_{N\alpha,i}\,x_{CP,i}}{\sum_i C_{N\alpha,i}}\tag{18.27}\]

where the sum is over: nose, body expansion, body crossflow, fins + carryover. This is the Barrowman method (extended by missile DATCOM), applicable up to \(\alpha \approx 10°\) in the linear regime. Above \(\alpha = 10°\), nonlinear crossflow terms must be added per Eq. ((18.8)).

docs.title: 18.4.4 Axial Force Coefficient
docs.text:
\[C_A = C_{A,friction} + C_{A,pressure,nose} + C_{A,base} + C_{A,fins}\tag{18.28}\]

At lift-off (subsonic, \(Ma < 0.5\)): \(C_A \approx 0.3\)–\(0.5\) (friction + base dominated). At Mach 2 (supersonic): \(C_A \approx 0.6\)–\(1.2\) (wave drag now dominant, combined with friction). The total drag \(D = q_\infty S_{ref}(C_A\cos\alpha + C_N\sin\alpha)\) and lift \(L = q_\infty S_{ref}(C_N\cos\alpha - C_A\sin\alpha)\).

docs.title: 18.4.5 Magnus Effect on Spinning Missiles
docs.text:
A spinning missile with body roll rate \(p\) experiences a side force perpendicular to both the spin axis and the velocity vector due to the Magnus effect. Magnus side-force coefficient:

\[C_{Y,Magnus} = C_{Y,p\alpha}\,\frac{p\,D}{2V}\,\alpha\tag{18.29}\]

where \(C_{Y,p\alpha}\) is the Magnus coefficient derivative (\(\approx\)0.01–0.1 per rad\(^2\)). For high spin rates (\(p D/2V > 0.1\)), Magnus deflection can exceed guidance accuracy budgets; guided missiles minimise spin rate.

docs.title: 18.5.1 Wave Drag Rise and Critical Mach Number
docs.text:
As free-stream Mach number \(Ma_\infty\) increases toward unity, local supersonic regions first appear above convex body surfaces when the local Mach number \(Ma_{local} = 1.0\). This defines the critical Mach number \(Ma_{cr}\):

\[C_p^{cr} = \frac{2}{\gamma Ma_\infty^2}\!\left[\left(\frac{2 + (\gamma-1)Ma_\infty^2}{\gamma+1}\right)^{\gamma/(\gamma-1)} - 1\right]\tag{18.30}\]

Beyond \(Ma_{cr}\), wave drag rises sharply (Prandtl–Glauert singularity):

\[C_L = \frac{C_{L,incomp}}{\sqrt{1 - Ma_\infty^2}} \quad (Ma < Ma_{cr})\tag{18.31}\]

This relation breaks down at \(Ma_{cr}\) and above as transonic nonlinearities dominate.

docs.title: 18.5.2 Whitcomb Area Rule
docs.text:
The transonic wave drag of a body depends only on its axial cross-sectional area distribution \(A(x)\), not on the detailed shape. Minimum wave drag in transonic flight is achieved when the \(A(x)\) distribution follows the Sears–Haack profile. Area ruling (Whitcomb, 1952) requires the total cross-section (body + fins + any protuberances) to follow a smooth Sears–Haack-like curve:

\[A_{SR}(x) = \frac{4V}{3L}\sin^3\phi, \quad \phi = \arccos\!\left(1 - \frac{2x}{L}\right)\tag{18.32}\]

Fins located at the aft end of the missile body satisfy this naturally (fins add area at the widest body point); interference with the boattail region requires careful integration.

docs.title: 18.5.3 Drag Coefficient vs. Mach Number
docs.text:
Table 18.1. Typical Missile \(C_{D0}\) Variation with Mach Number (tangent-ogive body, 4 delta fins) \(Ma_\infty\) 0.3 0.6 0.85 0.95 1.0 1.2 2.0 3.0 \(C_{D0}\) 0.32 0.34 0.40 0.58 0.80 0.72 0.55 0.48 \(C_{D,wave}\) 0 0 0.05 0.22 0.44 0.37 0.20 0.13 \(C_{D,base}\) 0.18 0.19 0.21 0.22 0.22 0.19 0.12 0.09 \(C_{D,frict}\) 0.14 0.15 0.14 0.14 0.14 0.16 0.23 0.26

The peak drag occurs at Mach \(\approx\)1.0 due to strong bow shock formation and high base pressure differential. Drag in the Mach 0.9–1.1 “transonic bucket” must be computed with CFD or wind tunnel data; linear theory is invalid.

docs.title: 18.5.4 Shock–Boundary-Layer Interaction (SBLI)
docs.text:
At transonic and supersonic speeds, impingement of an oblique shock on a turbulent boundary layer causes flow separation, unsteady pressure loads, and heat flux augmentation. The interaction length \(L_{int}\) scales with:

\[L_{int} \approx 6\,\delta\,\sqrt{\frac{p_2/p_1 - 1}{C_f}}\tag{18.33}\]

where \(\delta\) is boundary layer thickness, \(p_2/p_1\) is shock pressure ratio, and \(C_f\) is local skin-friction coefficient. SBLI-induced pressure fluctuations can excite structural resonances (buffet) at frequencies of 50–500 Hz in the transonic regime; this must be assessed in aeroelastic analyses for thin-walled missile structures.

docs.title: 18.6.1 Linear Wave Drag Theory (Ackeret)
docs.text:
For a 2D thin profile at angle of attack \(\alpha\) in supersonic flow (\(Ma > 1\)), Ackeret’s linearised theory gives:

\[C_{D,wave,2D} = \frac{4\alpha^2}{\sqrt{Ma^2 - 1}} + \frac{4(t/c)^2}{\sqrt{Ma^2 - 1}}\tag{18.34}\] \[C_{L,2D} = \frac{4\alpha}{\sqrt{Ma^2 - 1}}\tag{18.35}\]

where \(t/c\) is thickness-to-chord ratio. These equations are valid for \(0.5 < \alpha < 8°\) and \(Ma > 1.3\) (outside the transonic regime).

docs.title: 18.6.2 Oblique Shock Relations
docs.text:
An oblique shock wave at shock angle \(\beta\) relative to the incoming flow deflects the flow by turning angle \(\theta\). The \(\theta\)–\(\beta\)–\(M\) relation:

\[\tan\theta = \frac{2\cot\beta(Ma_1^2\sin^2\beta - 1)}{Ma_1^2(\gamma + \cos 2\beta) + 2}\tag{18.36}\]

Post-shock Mach number:

\[Ma_2^2 = \frac{Ma_1^2\sin^2\beta(\gamma-1)/2 + 1}{\sin^2(\beta-\theta)[\gamma Ma_1^2\sin^2\beta - (\gamma-1)/2]}\tag{18.37}\]

Post-shock pressure ratio:

\[\frac{p_2}{p_1} = 1 + \frac{2\gamma}{\gamma+1}(Ma_1^2\sin^2\beta - 1)\tag{18.38}\]

For a 15° cone at Mach 3: \(\beta \approx 32°\) from cone chart; \(p_2/p_1 \approx 2.8\); this pressure acts on the windward side of control fins.

docs.title: 18.6.3 Prandtl–Meyer Expansion
docs.text:
Flow accelerates around a convex corner through a Prandtl–Meyer expansion fan. The Prandtl–Meyer function:

\[ u(Ma) = \sqrt{ rac{\gamma+1}{\gamma-1}}\arctan\sqrt{ rac{\gamma-1}{\gamma+1}(Ma^2-1)} - \arctan\sqrt{Ma^2-1} ag{18.39}\]

Flow turning angle \(\Delta heta = u(Ma_2) - u(Ma_1)\). The expansion fan is isentropic; pressure drops below the incident pressure, producing suction on the leeward surface. Combined oblique shock (windward) + expansion fan (leeward) gives the total pressure force on a surface at AoA, providing a more accurate supersonic force prediction than linear theory for \(\alpha > 5°\).

docs.title: 18.6.4 Supersonic Fin Normal Force — Diederich Method
docs.text:
For low-aspect-ratio fins (\(AR < 3\)) at supersonic speeds:

\[C_{N\alpha,fin}^{3D} = C_{N\alpha,fin}^{2D} \cdot \frac{AR}{AR + 2\cos\Lambda_{LE}/\sqrt{Ma^2-1}}\tag{18.40}\]

where \(\Lambda_{LE}\) is the leading-edge sweep angle. For a delta fin with \(AR = 1\), \(\Lambda_{LE} = 60°\), \(Ma = 2\): \(C_{N\alpha,2D} = 4/\sqrt{3} = 2.31\); correction factor \(= 1/(1 + 2 \times 0.5/1.732) = 0.634\); \(C_{N\alpha,3D} = 1.46\) rad\(^{-1}\).

docs.title: 18.6.5 Blunt vs. Sharp Nose: Aerodynamic Trade
docs.text:
A blunt nose (hemisphere or large-radius sphere) generates a strong detached bow shock at supersonic speeds, resulting in:

  • High nose wave drag: \(C_{D,blunt} \approx 0.85\)–\(1.0\) (reference area = nose frontal area) vs. \(C_{D,sharp} \approx 0.15\)–\(0.25\).

  • Low aerodynamic heating at the stagnation point (larger \(R_N \to\) lower \(\dot{q}_s\) per Eq. (17.6)).

  • Forward centre of pressure \(x_{CP,nose}\) (blunt nose CP at \(\approx 0.25 D\) from tip vs. \(0.67 L_n\) for tangent ogive).

In ballistic re-entry vehicle design, a blunt nose is deliberately chosen to reduce heat flux at the expense of drag; in an aerodynamic cruise missile, a sharp nose is preferred for range efficiency.

docs.title: 18.7.1 Flow Regime Definitions
docs.text:
Hypersonic flow (\(Ma > 5\)) is characterised by:

  1. Thin shock layers (shock stand-off distance decreases as \(1/Ma^2\)).

  2. Merged shock and boundary layer at very high Mach numbers.

  3. High-temperature real-gas effects: vibrational excitation (\(T > 800\) K), oxygen dissociation (\(T > 2{,}500\) K), nitrogen dissociation (\(T > 4{,}000\) K), ionisation (\(T > 9{,}000\) K).

  4. Entropy layer: strong vorticity in the hot gas between the bow shock and the body.

  5. Viscous interaction: thick boundary layer modifies the external inviscid flow.

Table 18.2. Thermochemical Excitation Regimes in Hypersonic Flow (Air) Temperature (K) Phenomenon Governing Mach (sea level) Effect on Aero \(< 800\) Calorically perfect gas; \(\gamma = 1.4\) \(Ma < 4\) Linear theory valid 800–2,500 Vibrational excitation; \(\gamma \to 1.3\) Ma 4–8 \(C_m\), \(C_N\) deviation \(<\)10% 2,500–4,000 O\(_2\) dissociation; \(\gamma \to 1.2\) Ma 8–12 \(C_D\) up 15%; shock layer thicker 4,000–9,000 N\(_2\) dissociation + NO formation; \(\gamma \to 1.15\) Ma 12–18 Significant \(C_m\) shift \(> 9{,}000\) Ionisation; \(\gamma \to 1.1\); plasma \(Ma > 18\) RF blackout; Newtonian valid

docs.title: 18.7.2 Newtonian Impact Theory
docs.text:
In the limit \(Ma \to \infty\), the pressure coefficient on a surface inclined at angle \(\delta\) to the free-stream:

\[C_p = 2\sin^2\delta\tag{18.41}\]

Modified Newtonian theory (Lees, 1955) replaces the factor 2 with the stagnation-point value \(C_{p,max}\):

\[C_p = C_{p,max}\sin^2\delta\tag{18.42}\]

where:

\[C_{p,max} = \frac{2}{\gamma Ma_\infty^2}\left[\left(\frac{(\gamma+1)^2 Ma_\infty^2}{4\gamma Ma_\infty^2 - 2(\gamma-1)}\right)^{\gamma/(\gamma-1)}\frac{1-\gamma+2\gamma Ma_\infty^2}{\gamma+1} - 1\right]\tag{18.43}\]

For \(Ma = 20\), \(\gamma = 1.4\): \(C_{p,max} = 1.84\). Modified Newtonian gives \(<\)15% error in normal force for most missile geometries at \(Ma > 7\).

docs.title: 18.7.3 Mach Number Independence
docs.text: At \(Ma \gg 1\), aerodynamic force coefficients approach limiting Mach-independent values. The governing parameter is the hypersonic similarity parameter \(K = Ma\,\sin\alpha\); coefficients expressed as functions of \(K\) collapse to a single curve. This is the basis of the hypersonic equivalence principle. Practically, for \(Ma > 10\)–\(15\), \(C_N\) and \(C_m\) change by \(<\)5% with further Mach increase; aerodynamic databases need not extend beyond Mach 15–20.

docs.title: 18.7.4 Aerodynamic Heating — Stagnation Point
docs.text:
The Sutton–Graves correlation for stagnation heat flux (Eq. (17.6)) applies for \(Ma < 20\) in a standard atmosphere. For a sharper nose (small \(R_N\)), the Fay–Riddell correlation provides higher fidelity:

\[\dot{q}_{FR} = 0.763\,\Pr^{-0.6}\left(\rho_w\mu_w\right)^{0.1}\left(\rho_e\mu_e\right)^{0.4}\sqrt{\frac{du_e}{dx}}\,(h_{aw} - h_w)\tag{18.44}\]

where \(h_{aw} = h_e + r\,V_e^2/2\) is the adiabatic-wall enthalpy (\(r \approx Pr^{0.5}\) for turbulent flow), and the velocity gradient \(du_e/dx \approx \sqrt{2(p_s - p_\infty)/(\rho_s R_N^2)}\).

For a sharp cone half-angle \(\theta_c\) (Lees’ formula):

\[\frac{\dot{q}_{cone}}{\dot{q}_{stag}} = \left(\frac{R_{N,sphere}}{R_{cone}}\right)^{0.5}\left(\frac{\sin^2\theta_c}{1 - \cos^3\theta_c}\right)^{0.5}\tag{18.45}\]

A sharp nose reduces stagnation heating but increases total heat load over the frustum.

docs.title: 18.7.5 Flat-Face and Leading-Edge Heating
docs.text:
On a flat-face RV (blunt re-entry), the total heat-load integral:

\[Q_{total} = \int_0^{t_f} \dot{q}_s \cdot A_{stag} \cdot dt\tag{18.46}\]

For a Mk-12A RV (approx.): \(\dot{q}_{peak} \approx 10\) MW/m\(^2\) at 60 km altitude; integrated \(Q \approx 200\) MJ/m\(^2\) over 50 s. An ablative phenolic-nylon TPS at \(\Delta H_{abl} = 20\) MJ/kg ablates at \(\dot{m}_{abl} = \dot{q}_s/\Delta H_{abl} = 0.5\) kg/(m\(^2\cdot\)s) at peak heating; total mass loss \(\approx 25\) kg/m\(^2\) over the trajectory, equivalent to 25 mm thickness reduction.

docs.title: 18.8.1 Fin Deflection and Hinge Moment
docs.text:
When a control fin is deflected by angle \(\delta\), it generates additional normal force and a hinge moment about the pivot. Control normal-force increment:

\[\Delta C_N = C_{N\delta}\,\delta = \frac{\partial C_N}{\partial\delta}\,\delta\tag{18.47}\]

The hinge moment coefficient about the fin pivot:

\[C_H = C_{H\alpha}\,\alpha + C_{H\delta}\,\delta\tag{18.48}\]

where \(C_{H\alpha}\) and \(C_{H\delta}\) are the hinge-moment derivatives with AoA and deflection. Both terms are typically negative (\(C_{H\alpha} < 0\), \(C_{H\delta} < 0\)), meaning the aerodynamic moment resists the commanded deflection. Actuator sizing must provide torque at least 3\(\times\) the peak hinge moment (including safety margins and structural flexibility effects).

docs.title: 18.8.2 Control Effectiveness and Authority
docs.text:
Control effectiveness degrades in the transonic regime (Mach 0.8–1.2) due to shock formation on the fin and shock-induced separation. The effective control derivative:

\[\left(\frac{\partial C_m}{\partial\delta}\right)_{eff} = \frac{\partial C_m}{\partial\delta}\cdot \eta_{eff}(Ma)\tag{18.49}\]

where \(\eta_{eff}(Ma)\) drops to \(\approx\)0.6–0.7 in the transonic region and recovers to \(\approx\)0.85–0.95 at Mach 1.5+. At high AoA (\(\alpha > 20°\)), vortex shedding from the forebody can produce asymmetric rolling moments exceeding the control authority; cross-coupling corrections are required in the autopilot.

docs.title: 18.8.3 Canard vs. Tail Configuration
docs.text:
Canard control.

Canards deflect ahead of the CG; their downwash impinges on the tail fins, reducing tail-fin effectiveness. Net pitching moment is:

\[C_m = C_{N,canard}\,\frac{x_{CG} - x_{canard}}{D} - C_{N,tail}\,\frac{x_{tail} - x_{CG}}{D}\tag{18.50}\]

Canard advantage: positive lift increment (canard + tail both contribute to \(L\)); faster pitch response. Canard disadvantage: downwash reduces tail effectiveness; roll–yaw cross-coupling; difficult to balance at high AoA.

Tail control.

Deflecting aft tail fins generates a pitching moment about the CG; the fin itself creates negative lift (sign convention dependent). Tail-controlled missiles have better roll symmetry and are easier to stabilise; most medium-range and long-range missiles use tail control.

All-moveable tail (AMT).

The entire fin pivots (no fixed surface + flap); control effectiveness is \(\approx\)2–3\(\times\) higher than a plain flap on a fixed fin for the same deflection angle because the full fin area develops normal force in the commanded direction rather than just the flap portion. Hinge moments are also lower for AMT.

docs.title: 18.8.4 Thrust Vector Control (TVC) and Lateral Jets
docs.text:
When a missile is at low dynamic pressure (shortly after launch, or post-burnout), aerodynamic control surfaces are ineffective. Two alternative control actuators:

  1. Thrust Vector Control (TVC): deflects the nozzle using a gimballed nozzle mechanism, jet vanes, or liquid injection into the nozzle. Control force proportional to thrust: \(F_{TVC} = T\sin(\delta_{TVC}) \approx T\delta_{TVC}\). Jet vanes (tungsten, molybdenum) immersed in the exhaust plume produce side force but add \(\approx\)3–8% thrust loss.

  2. Reaction Control System (RCS) / Lateral Jets: Cold-gas or hot-gas thruster perpendicular to the missile axis; pure torque (no velocity dependence); used on KKVs and on short-burn missiles. Interaction force between lateral jet and free-stream creates a jet-in-crossflow amplification factor \(K_{jet} \approx 1.5\)–\(4.0\):

    \[F_{total} = F_{jet}\,(1 + K_{jet})\,(q_\infty/q_{jet})^{k}\tag{18.51}\]

docs.title: 18.9.1 DATCOM and Missile DATCOM
docs.text:
The USAF Digital DATCOM (Data Compendium) is a semi-empirical handbook method for rapid aerodynamic estimation of conventional aircraft and missile configurations. Missile DATCOM (McDonnell Douglas, 1979; AFRL update 2005) extends the method explicitly for:

  • Body-of-revolution geometries (ogive, cone, cylinder, boattail, flare).

  • Fin/wing components (rectangular, trapezoidal, delta; 3 or 4 fin sets).

  • Mach 0.0–5.0; angle of attack 0–180° (in some modules).

  • Force/moment coefficients, stability derivatives, hinge moments, roll damping.

Accuracy: \(\pm 15\)% on \(C_N\), \(\pm 10\)% on \(x_{CP}\) for conventional configurations; less accurate for manoeuvring bodies at \(\alpha > 15°\). Run time: seconds on a workstation; invaluable for parametric trade studies during preliminary design.

docs.title: 18.9.2 Euler CFD
docs.text:
Euler methods solve the inviscid form of the Navier–Stokes equations, capturing wave drag, pressure distributions, and shock patterns without resolving the boundary layer. Typical specification:

  • Grid: 2–10 million cells (structured or unstructured).

  • Solver: RANS without viscous terms (inviscid flux only); density-based; Roe scheme.

  • Time-to-solution: 1–4 hours on 32 CPU cores for a supersonic missile at fixed \(\alpha\).

  • Accuracy: wave drag \(\pm 5\)%, \(C_N \pm 8\)%, \(x_{CP} \pm 3\)% relative to Euler-accurate solution; viscous effects (friction drag, separation) not captured.

docs.title: 18.9.3 RANS CFD
docs.text:
Reynolds-Averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS) with \(k\)–\(\omega\) SST turbulence model provides full aerodynamic coefficient prediction including viscous effects. Specification:

  • Grid: 10–50 million cells; wall \(y^+ \approx 1\) for SST; prism layers 20–30 cells deep.

  • Solver: segregated pressure-based (low-speed); density-based coupled (supersonic).

  • Time-to-solution: 12–96 hours on 256 CPU cores for a complete missile geometry at one flight condition; full Mach/AoA polar requires \(\approx\)500 CPU-hours.

  • Accuracy: \(C_D \pm 5\)%, \(C_N \pm 5\)%, \(C_m \pm 8\)% vs. wind tunnel for attached flow; degrades for massively separated flows (\(\alpha > 20°\)).

docs.title: 18.9.4 DSMC for Rarefied Flow
docs.text:
At altitudes above \(\approx\)80 km (free-molecular and transitional regime), continuum CFD fails. The Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) method tracks representative molecular populations:

\[f(x, v, t) \to \text{stochastic particle collisions} \quad \text{(Bird, 1994)}\tag{18.52}\]

DSMC is essential for KKV homing at 150+ km altitude where mean free path \(\lambda_f > 1\) mm and Knudsen number \(Kn = \lambda_f/L > 0.01\). At 200 km altitude, \(\rho \approx 2.5\times10^{-10}\) kg/m\(^3\) and aerodynamic forces are 6 orders of magnitude lower than at sea level; DACS thrusters provide essentially all control authority.

docs.title: 18.9.5 Wind Tunnel Testing
docs.text:
Wind-tunnel testing remains the authoritative validation method for missile aerodynamic databases. Relevant facility types:

  • Transonic blow-down tunnel (0.5 \(< Ma <\) 1.5): schlieren photography for shock visualisation; 6-component strain-gauge balance for forces and moments; Mach 0.85–1.3 most valuable; AEDC 16T, ONERA S1MA.

  • Supersonic blow-down tunnel (1.5 \(< Ma <\) 6): NASA 9\(\times\)7 Foot Supersonic Wind Tunnel; model scale 1:5 to 1:15; \(Re\) matching to \(\pm\)20%.

  • Ballistic range: missile model fired through instrumented range; multiple laser shadowgraphs at Mach 2–10; free-flight dynamics; no sting interference; AEDC G-Range.

  • Shock tunnel (Mach 8–25, \(T_{stag}\) to 20,000 K; \(\tau_{test} = 1\)–\(50\) ms): Caltech T5, DLR HEG; heat-flux measurement with thin-film gauges; DSMC validation.

Table 18.3. Aerodynamic Prediction Method Comparison Method Mach Range Accuracy (\(C_N\)) CPU Time Cost Missile DATCOM 0–5 \(\pm 15\)% Seconds Negligible Euler CFD 0.5–10 \(\pm 8\)% 1–4 hr Low RANS CFD (SST) 0–10 \(\pm 5\)% 12–96 hr Medium LES / DES 0–5 \(\pm 3\)% Weeks High DSMC \(>\)5 (HV) \(\pm 10\)% Days High Wind tunnel 0.2–20 \(\pm 1\)–\(3\)% Weeks (prep) Very high Ballistic range 0.5–10 \(\pm 2\)% Weeks (prep) High

docs.title: 18.10.1 Heat Flux Distribution
docs.text:
At high Mach numbers, heat flux varies strongly over the missile surface. At the stagnation point (Eq. (17.6)); on the conical frustum (Eckert’s reference enthalpy method for turbulent flat plate, mapped to cone surface):

\[\dot{q}_{cone} = C_f^*\,\frac{\rho^* V_e^3}{2}\tag{18.53}\]

where the starred quantities are evaluated at a reference temperature \(T^* = 0.5T_w + 0.22T_{aw} + 0.28T_e\). At leading edges of fins (radius \(R_{LE}\)):

\[\dot{q}_{LE} = \dot{q}_{stag}\sqrt{\frac{R_N}{R_{LE}}}\tag{18.54}\]

For a 1 mm leading-edge radius vs. a 20 mm nose radius: \(\dot{q}_{LE} = \dot{q}_{stag}\sqrt{20/1} = 4.47\,\dot{q}_{stag}\). Fin leading edges are the most thermally critical structural elements at Mach \(>\)4.

docs.title: 18.10.2 Thermal Protection System Materials
docs.text: Table 18.4. TPS Material Properties for Missile Applications Material Application Max \(T\) (°C) \(\rho\) (kg/m\(^3\)) \(k\) (W/m\(\cdot\)K) Ablation Rate Mission Type Carbon–Carbon (C–C) Nose, leading edges 3,000 1,800 20–100 Low (oxidation) Reusable up to Mach 10 PICA (Pheno. Carbon) ICBM RV ablative Ablative 240 0.35 High Single-use RV AVCOAT (silicone) RV mid-body Ablative 512 0.27 Medium Single-use RV C-SiC (ceramic composite) Nose, fin LE 1,650 1,900 15–40 Very low Reusable Mach 5–8 ZrB\(_2\)–SiC (UHTC) Sharp leading edges 2,500+ 5,600 60 Negligible Mach 10–20 PTFE-fibreglass radome Seeker dome (\(<\)Ma 1.5) 260 2,200 0.25 None Low-speed seeker Fused silica radome Seeker dome (Ma 1.5–3) 1,000 2,200 1.4 None Supersonic seeker Silicon nitride radome Seeker dome (Ma 3–5) 1,700 3,200 30 Negligible High-speed seeker

docs.title: 18.10.3 Ablation Physics
docs.text:
Ablative TPS materials cool by pyrolysis (polymer decomposition), sublimation, and char formation. The mass loss rate:

\[\dot{m}_{abl} = \frac{\dot{q}_s - \dot{q}_{cond} - \sigma\varepsilon T_w^4}{\Delta H_{eff}}\tag{18.55}\]

where \(\dot{q}_{cond}\) is heat conducted into the base structure, \(\sigma\varepsilon T_w^4\) is radiation re-emission, and \(\Delta H_{eff}\) is the effective enthalpy of ablation (pyrolysis + latent heat; \(\approx 5\)–\(30\) MJ/kg depending on material). The char layer formed by pyrolysis has very low thermal conductivity (\(k_{char} \approx 0.1\)–\(0.5\) W/(m\(\cdot\)K)) compared to the virgin material, providing additional insulation.

docs.title: 18.10.4 Seeker Window Thermal Management
docs.text:
The seeker dome (radome or optical window) must simultaneously:

  • Transmit electromagnetic (RF) or optical (IR/EO) radiation in the seeker band.

  • Withstand aerodynamic heating without melting, cracking, or losing transmissivity.

  • Maintain dimensional accuracy (\(<\)0.1 mm) to avoid aberrations in the seeker focal path.

Sapphire dome at Mach 4 (\(V \approx 1{,}300\) m/s, 20 km altitude): surface temperature \(T_w \approx 500\)–\(800\)°C. Transmissivity in the MWIR (3–5 \(\mu\)m) band decreases from \(\approx\)84% at 25°C to \(\approx\)65% at 600°C. Active cooling (coolant circulation through the seeker dome housing) maintains \(T_w < 300\)°C at Mach 4. Silicon nitride dome at Mach 5: \(T_w \approx 1{,}100\)°C; transmissivity loss in Ku-band (13–18 GHz) RF seeker remains \(<\)2 dB up to 1,500°C.

docs.title: 18.11.1 Load Factor and Structural Limit
docs.text:
The aerodynamic load factor:

\[n = \frac{L}{W} = \frac{q_\infty S_{ref} C_N}{W}\tag{18.56}\]

Maximum structural load factor \(n_{max}\) is set by the airframe structural limit (typically 20–50\(g\) for SAMs, 10–25\(g\) for air-launched missiles, 5–10\(g\) for heavy land-attack cruise missiles). For a SAM with \(W = 300\) kg, \(S_{ref} = 0.05\) m\(^2\), \(C_{N,max} = 20\), \(q_\infty = 50\) kPa (Mach 4 at 12 km):

\[n_{max} = \frac{50{,}000 \times 0.05 \times 20}{300 \times 9.81} = 17.0\,g\tag{18.57}\]

docs.title: 18.11.2 Turn Radius
docs.text:
The minimum turn radius at load factor \(n\):

\[R_{turn} = \frac{V^2}{g\sqrt{n^2 - 1}}\tag{18.58}\]

For \(V = 1{,}000\) m/s, \(n = 20\): \(R_{turn} = 10^6/(9.81\sqrt{399}) = 5{,}105\) m. This sets the intercept geometry: a target at \(R < R_{turn}\) cannot be reached without the missile executing a spiralling engagement.

docs.title: 18.11.3 Maximum Lateral Acceleration
docs.text:
Maximum lateral acceleration:

\[a_{lat,max} = n_{max}\,g\tag{18.59}\]

Typical values: MANPADS (\(20g\)); SHORAD SAM (\(30g\)); advanced SAM Aster 30 (\(50g\) with divert thrusters); ATGM (\(10g\)). The required lateral acceleration for a proportional navigation intercept of a \(5g\) manoeuvring target at \(t_{go} = 1\) s before intercept:

\[a_{req} = N' \cdot a_{target} \cdot (N'-1) \cdot \frac{t_{go,0}}{t_{go}} \approx 4 \times 5g \approx 20g\tag{18.60}\]

docs.title: 18.11.4 Dynamic Pressure Variation with Altitude
docs.text:
Dynamic pressure at a given Mach number varies with altitude through air density:

\[q_\infty = \frac{1}{2}\gamma p_\infty Ma^2 = \frac{1}{2}\gamma p_0\left(1 + \frac{\gamma-1}{2}Ma^2\right)^{-\gamma/(\gamma-1)}Ma^2\tag{18.61}\]

At Mach 4:

  • Sea level: \(q = 0.5 \times 1.225 \times (4\times 343.3)^2 = 488\) kPa

  • 10 km: \(q = 0.5 \times 0.413 \times (4\times299.5)^2 = 148\) kPa

  • 20 km: \(q = 0.5 \times 0.088 \times (4\times295.1)^2 = 30.7\) kPa

Available lateral acceleration at Mach 4 drops by \(148/488 = 0.30\) going from sea level to 10 km at the same Mach number (since \(a_{lat} \propto q_\infty\)). This is the fundamental reason why high-altitude engagements are harder for aerodynamically controlled interceptors; RCS/divert thrusters provide velocity-independent control.

docs.title: 18.11.5 Aeroelastic Effects and Structural Coupling
docs.text:
Bending of the missile body under aerodynamic load alters the seeker line-of-sight angle and the control surface effectiveness. The body bending angle for a free–free beam under distributed aerodynamic load:

\[\theta_{bend}(x) = \int_0^x \frac{M_{bend}(\xi)}{EI(\xi)}\,d\xi\tag{18.62}\]

For a seeker at the nose and rate gyros mid-body, body bending introduces a spurious guidance signal:

\[\dot{\sigma}_{spurious} = \frac{d\theta_{bend}}{dt}\bigg|_{nose-gyro}\tag{18.63}\]

This can destabilise the guidance loop if the structural bending frequency \(\omega_n\) is within one decade of the guidance bandwidth \(\omega_g\). Structural notch filters at \(\omega_n\) are standard in missile autopilot design.

docs.title: 18.12 Summary: Aerodynamic Design Process
docs.text:
The missile aerodynamic design process follows a structured progression:

  1. Mission analysis: define speed, altitude, range, and manoeuvre envelope \(\to\) flight conditions database.

  2. Preliminary sizing: Missile DATCOM to establish nose geometry, \(L/D\), fin configuration, and initial \(SM\) estimate.

  3. Stability analysis: verify \(C_{m\alpha} < 0\) across \(Ma\)-\(\alpha\) envelope; check \(SM\) vs. propellant burn-off CG travel.

  4. Control sizing: control surface \(C_{N\delta}\), hinge moment, actuator torque requirement, and effectiveness at transonic.

  5. Euler CFD: wave drag, shock impingement, fin pressure distribution at key Mach numbers (0.8, 1.2, 2, 4).

  6. RANS CFD: full aerodynamic database including friction drag, separated-flow AoA effects, actuator-on configurations.

  7. Thermal analysis: heat flux distribution from RANS; TPS thickness sizing; seeker dome temperature budget.

  8. Wind tunnel: validation of CFD at critical conditions; force and moment balance; schlieren shock visualisation; transition fixing.

  9. Aeroelastic assessment: structural mode frequencies vs. guidance bandwidth; notch filter design.

  10. Database integration: tabulated \(C_N\), \(C_A\), \(C_m\), \(C_{N\delta}\), \(C_{l\delta}\), etc. vs. (\(Ma\), \(\alpha\), \(\delta\), altitude) for 6-DoF simulation.

The key aerodynamic parameters and their design targets for a notional medium-range SAM are summarised in Table 18.5.

Table 18.5. Aerodynamic Design Parameter Summary — Notional Medium-Range SAM Parameter Symbol Design Target Rationale Static margin at Mach 2 \(SM\) 0.5–2.0 cal. Stable but responsive Pitching moment slope \(C_{m\alpha}\) \(< -0.5\) rad\(^{-1}\) Restoring Max normal force coefficient \(C_{N,max}\) 12–20 \(20g\) intercept Zero-lift drag at Mach 2 \(C_{D0}\) 0.4–0.6 Range/energy budget Control derivative (tail) \(C_{N\delta}\) 1.5–3.0 rad\(^{-1}\) Adequate authority Fin flutter safety margin \(V_{flutter}/V_{design}\) \(> 1.5\) Structural integrity Seeker dome temperature \(T_w\) \(< 600\)°C Transmissivity Bending frequency (1st mode) \(\omega_{n1}\) \(> 10\,\omega_{GC}\) Autopilot stability

These targets are refined through the iterative design process, where CFD and wind-tunnel data progressively replace preliminary estimates. The aerodynamic database, validated against test data, feeds directly into the 6-DoF flight simulation and ultimately into hardware-in-the-loop (HWIL) system testing, completing the design verification cycle.

docs.title: 19.1 Rocket Propulsion Fundamentals
docs.text: Missile propulsion encompasses the complete science of converting stored chemical (or other) energy into directed thrust to accelerate a vehicle along a prescribed trajectory. The physical principles governing all rocket systems derive from Newton’s second and third laws combined with thermodynamic analyses of high-temperature, high-pressure combustion processes.

docs.title: 19.1.1 The Thrust Equation
docs.text:
The thrust produced by a rocket nozzle arises from two contributions: the momentum flux of exhaust gases leaving the nozzle exit plane, and the pressure imbalance between the nozzle exit and the ambient atmosphere acting on the exit area. The general thrust equation is

\[F = \dot{m}\,V_e + (P_e - P_a)\,A_e\tag{19.1}\]

where \(\dot{m}\) is the propellant mass flow rate (k g s), \(V_e\) the effective exhaust velocity at the nozzle exit plane (m s), \(P_e\) the static pressure at the nozzle exit (P a), \(P_a\) the ambient (freestream) pressure (P a), and \(A_e\) the nozzle exit area (m 2).

The first term, \(\dot{m}V_e\), is the momentum thrust; the second term, \((P_e-P_a)A_e\), is the pressure thrust. At the design altitude of a nozzle (\(P_e = P_a\)), pressure thrust vanishes and the nozzle is said to be perfectly expanded. Over-expanded flow (\(P_e < P_a\)) produces oblique shocks at the nozzle lip; under-expanded flow (\(P_e > P_a\)) produces expansion fans.

The effective exhaust velocity \(c\) or \(V_{eff}\) combines both terms:

\[c = V_e + \frac{(P_e - P_a)\,A_e}{\dot{m}}\tag{19.2}\]

so that \(F = \dot{m}\,c\).

docs.title: 19.1.2 Specific Impulse
docs.text:
Specific impulse \(I_{sp}\) is the single most important figure of merit for any rocket propellant combination or engine cycle. It is defined as the thrust produced per unit weight flow of propellant:

\[I_{sp} = \frac{F}{\dot{m}\,g_0}\tag{19.3}\]

where \(g_0 = 9.80665\,\text{m s 2}\) is the standard sea-level gravitational acceleration. This definition makes \(I_{sp}\) dimensionally a time (seconds) and independent of the unit system. Equivalently,

\[I_{sp} = \frac{c}{g_0}\tag{19.4}\]

High \(I_{sp}\) means more thrust per kilogram of propellant consumed. Typical values range from \(\sim\)230 s for early double-base propellants, to \(\sim\)270 s for composite HTPB/AP/Al propellants, \(\sim\)340 s for storable liquid bipropellants, and up to \(\sim\)460 s vacuum for cryogenic LOX/LH\(_2\).

docs.title: 19.1.3 The Tsiolkovsky Rocket Equation
docs.text:
The ideal velocity increment \(\Delta V\) achievable by a rocket burning from initial mass \(m_0\) to burnout mass \(m_f\) in a gravity-free, drag-free environment is

\[\Delta V = I_{sp}\,g_0\,\ln\!\left(\frac{m_0}{m_f}\right) = c\,\ln\!\left(\frac{m_0}{m_f}\right)\tag{19.5}\]

The mass ratio \(R = m_0/m_f\) is the key structural efficiency parameter. For a single-stage ballistic missile with \(\Delta V = 7\,\text{k m s}\) and \(I_{sp} = 290\,\text{s}\), the required mass ratio is:

\[R = \exp\!\left(\frac{\Delta V}{I_{sp}\,g_0}\right) = \exp\!\left(\frac{7000}{290 \times 9.807}\right) \approx 11.5\]

meaning the propellant mass must be \(\approx 91\%\) of launch mass — a severe constraint driving structural mass minimisation (thin CFRP casings, lightweight warhead structures).

docs.title: 19.1.4 Characteristic Velocity and Thrust Coefficient
docs.text:
The characteristic velocity \(c^*\) characterises the thermochemical efficiency of the propellant and the combustion chamber independently of nozzle geometry:

\[c^* = \frac{P_c\,A_t}{\dot{m}}\tag{19.7}\]

where \(P_c\) is the chamber stagnation pressure and \(A_t\) is the nozzle throat area. Theoretically,

\[c^*_{th} = \frac{\sqrt{\gamma R_u T_c / M_w}}{\gamma \left(\frac{2}{\gamma+1}\right)^{(\gamma+1)/[2(\gamma-1)]}}\tag{19.8}\]

where \(T_c\) is the adiabatic flame temperature, \(M_w\) the mean molecular weight of products, \(\gamma\) the effective ratio of specific heats, and \(R_u\) the universal gas constant. The combustion efficiency \(\eta_{c^*} = c^*_{measured}/c^*_{th}\) is typically 0.94–0.98 for well-designed motors.

The thrust coefficient \(C_F\) relates thrust to chamber pressure and throat area:

\[C_F = \frac{F}{P_c\,A_t}\tag{19.9}\]

Combining with Eq. (A.100): \(F = C_F\,c^*\,\dot{m}\) and \(I_{sp} = C_F\,c^*/g_0\). The theoretical thrust coefficient for isentropic nozzle flow is:

\[C_{F,th} = \sqrt{\frac{2\gamma^2}{\gamma-1}\left(\frac{2}{\gamma+1}\right)^{(\gamma+1)/(\gamma-1)} \left[1 - \left(\frac{P_e}{P_c}\right)^{(\gamma-1)/\gamma}\right]} + \frac{(P_e-P_a)\,A_e}{P_c\,A_t}\tag{19.10}\]

At vacuum (\(P_a = 0\)) and optimal expansion, \(C_F\) reaches its maximum. Typical values: \(C_F = 1.5\)–\(1.7\) at altitude for composite propellants.

docs.title: Area–Mach Relation
docs.text:
The isentropic area–Mach relation governs the flow area at any cross-section:

\[\frac{A}{A_t} = \frac{1}{M}\left[\frac{2}{\gamma+1} \left(1+\frac{\gamma-1}{2}M^2\right)\right]^{(\gamma+1)/[2(\gamma-1)]}\tag{19.11}\]

At the throat \(M=1\) and \(A = A_t\). The expansion ratio \(\varepsilon = A_e/A_t\) uniquely determines the exit Mach number \(M_e\) (supersonic solution). For \(\gamma = 1.3\) and \(\varepsilon = 8\): \(M_e \approx 3.4\).

docs.title: Nozzle Contour: Bell Nozzle
docs.text:
A conical nozzle of half-angle \(\alpha = 15°\) has a divergence efficiency of \(\lambda = (1+\cos\alpha)/2 = 0.983\). To reduce nozzle length while maintaining high efficiency, bell nozzles are used. The Rao optimum bell nozzle achieves near-ideal flow with a contour that:

  1. Expands rapidly (high expansion angle, \(\sim\)25–45°) near the throat

  2. Transitions smoothly to a low exit angle (\(\sim\)8–12°) at the exit plane

  3. Uses a parabolic approximation for the contour

An 80% bell nozzle has a length equal to 80% of the equivalent conical nozzle with the same expansion ratio. Despite its shorter length, the 80% bell achieves \(>99\%\) of the conical nozzle’s ideal thrust, making it the standard choice for most modern missile motors.

docs.title: Combustion Temperature and Dissociation
docs.text: The adiabatic flame temperature \(T_{ad}\) for HTPB/AP/Al at \(O/F = 2.1\), \(P_c = 7\,\text{M P a}\) is approximately 3,500 K. However, at these temperatures significant dissociation occurs, absorbing energy. NASA CEA (Chemical Equilibrium with Applications) equilibrium calculations account for 40+ species including HCl, CO, CO\(_2\), H\(_2\)O, H\(_2\), OH, O, H, Al\(_2\)O\(_3\). The effective \(\gamma\) ranges from 1.16–1.24 for composite propellants (lower than 1.4 for air because of the complex product mixture).

docs.title: 19.2 Solid Rocket Motors
docs.text: Solid rocket motors (SRMs) dominate tactical and strategic missile propulsion due to their simplicity, storage stability, high reliability, and high thrust-to-weight ratio. They consist of a propellant grain cast or pressed into a cylindrical casing, ignited at launch, and burned through to completion. There are no valves, pumps, or turbines.

docs.title: HTPB/AP/Aluminium (Composite Propellant)
docs.text:
The most widely used tactical missile propellant is the HTPB/AP/Al system:

  • Hydroxyl-Terminated Polybutadiene (HTPB) binder: 12–16% by mass; provides structural integrity and acts as a supplementary fuel; cross-linked with isocyanate (MDI or IPDI) to form an elastomeric matrix.

  • Ammonium Perchlorate (AP), (NH\(_4\)ClO\(_4\)): 68–72% by mass; primary oxidiser; bimodal or trimodal particle size distribution (200 \(\mu\)m coarse + 20 \(\mu\)m fine) to maximise packing density.

  • Aluminium powder: 2–20% by mass; metallic fuel; increases \(T_{ad}\) by 300–500 K; increases \(I_{sp}\) by 15–25 s; produces Al\(_2\)O\(_3\) slag.

  • Additives: iron oxide (Fe\(_2\)O\(_3\)) burn rate catalyst 0.1–1%; bonding agents (HX-752, MAPO); stabilisers; plasticisers (DOA/TEGDN).

Performance: \(I_{sp} = 250\)–\(270\) s (sea level), \(\rho = 1750\)–\(1870\) kg/m\(^3\), \(T_c \approx 3500\) K, \(r \approx 8\)–\(15\) mm/s at 7 MPa, \(n \approx 0.3\)–\(0.4\).

docs.title: NEPE (Nitrate Ester Plasticised Polyether)
docs.text:
NEPE propellants use an energetic binder (polyethylene glycol or polyethylene-polyol plasticised with nitrate esters such as TMETN or BTTN) combined with HMX or RDX oxidiser/fuel:

  • Binder: polyether backbone with nitrate ester plasticiser (40% of binder)

  • HMX (cyclotetramethylenetetranitramine): 20–30% by mass

  • AP: 30–40%; Al: 15–20%

  • \(I_{sp} = 275\)–\(285\) s; density \(\rho = 1820\)–\(1870\) kg/m\(^3\)

  • Burn rate: 7–12 mm/s at 7 MPa; \(n = 0.35\)–\(0.45\)

Used in the US Trident II D5 SLBM (first and second stages), achieving \(\Delta V\) capability for 7,400+ km range with MIRV payload. The higher energy density compared to HTPB/AP/Al allows significantly increased mass ratio or reduced motor size.

docs.title: ADN-Based Propellants
docs.text:
Ammonium Dinitramide (ADN), NH\(_4\)N(NO\(_2\))\(_2\), is an alternative oxidiser offering:

  • Chlorine-free combustion: eliminates HCl in exhaust — reduces radar cross-section (RCS) of plume (HCl is strongly radar-absorbent at certain wavelengths)

  • \(I_{sp} \approx 255\)–\(265\) s (slightly below AP)

  • Higher solubility in binder systems

  • Lower sensitivity: more insensitive to shock and friction than AP

  • Hygroscopic: requires careful moisture control in processing

ADN-based propellants are investigated for stealth missile applications where plume observability is critical (e.g., low-RCS cruise missiles, covert tactical rounds).

docs.title: HTPE Propellants
docs.text:
Hydroxyl-Terminated Polyether (HTPE) replaces HTPB as the binder:

  • Improved low-temperature flexibility (\(T_g < -65°C\))

  • Lower sensitivity to shock and friction (important for Insensitive Munitions (IM) requirements MIL-STD-2105D)

  • Slower burn rate (must be compensated with catalyst)

  • Used in upgraded AIM-9X Sidewinder and AMRAAM motors

docs.title: 19.2.2 Propellant Grain Geometry
docs.text:
The geometry of the propellant grain determines the burn area \(A_b(t)\) as a function of time, which in turn controls the thrust profile. Six fundamental grain geometries are used:

Table 19.2. Propellant Grain Geometries and Thrust Profiles Geometry Burn Profile \(A_b/A_{b0}\) Trend Typical Application End-burning (cigarette) Neutral/regressive Decreasing Long-burn sustain motors Internal cylinder (BATES) Neutral/progressive Constant then inc. Short-range AAM Star (5–7 point) Neutral \(\approx\) constant SAM, ICBM boost Finocyl (finned cylinder) Neutral/regressive Slight decrease ICBM 2nd stage, AAM Wagon-wheel Progressive Increasing High boost, short burn Slotted tube Progressive Increasing Quick boost applications

The star grain is the most common for tactical missiles. With \(N\) points of internal star geometry, the burn area remains approximately constant (neutral burn) throughout most of the web, providing near-constant thrust. A 5-point star is typical for medium-calibre SAMs. A finocyl (finned cylindrical) grain achieves very neutral burning with higher volumetric loading than a star, at the cost of more complex tooling.

docs.title: Vieille’s Law
docs.text:
The propellant burn rate \(r\) (surface regression rate, mm/s) is governed by Vieille’s empirical law:

\[r = a\,P_c^n\tag{19.12}\]

where \(a\) is a pre-exponential coefficient (m m ( s M P a n )), \(P_c\) the chamber pressure in MPa, and \(n\) the pressure exponent (0.2–0.6 for stable burning). Values of \(n > 0.85\) indicate combustion instability risk; \(n = 1\) produces unstable runaway.

Table 19.3. Typical Burn Rate Parameters for Composite Propellants Propellant \(a\) at 7 MPa \(n\) \(r\) at 7 MPa \(T_{ad}\) (K) \(\sigma_p\) (%/K) HTPB/AP/Al (18% Al) 2.1 0.33 10.2 3,500 0.10 HTPB/AP/Al (2% Al) 2.5 0.30 10.8 3,100 0.12 NEPE/HMX/Al 1.8 0.40 9.5 3,700 0.09 HTPB/AP+Fe\(_2\)O\(_3\) 3.8 0.35 17.0 3,450 0.11 Double-base (NC/NG) 1.2 0.28 7.5 2,800 0.18 HTPE/AP/Al 1.9 0.32 9.8 3,480 0.10

The temperature sensitivity coefficient \(\sigma_p\) describes the fractional change in burn rate per degree Kelvin change in initial propellant temperature at constant chamber pressure:

\[\sigma_p = \frac{1}{r}\left(\frac{\partial r}{\partial T_i}\right)_{P_c}\tag{19.13}\]

For \(\sigma_p = 0.10\%/\mathrm{K}\) and a temperature swing from \(-40°C\) to \(+70°C\) (\(\Delta T = 110~K\)), burn rate changes by \(\pm5.5\%\), requiring pressure vessel and nozzle throat sizing to accommodate maximum design pressure.

docs.title: Mass Flow and Chamber Pressure
docs.text:
The mass flow rate generated by combustion is:

\[\dot{m} = \rho_p\,r\,A_b = \rho_p\,a\,P_c^n\,A_b\tag{19.14}\]

At quasi-steady state, this mass flow must equal the choked nozzle flow:

\[\dot{m} = \frac{P_c\,A_t}{c^*}\tag{19.15}\]

Equating Eqs. (19.14) and (19.15) and solving for the steady-state chamber pressure:

\[P_c = \left(\frac{\rho_p\,c^*\,a\,A_b}{A_t}\right)^{1/(1-n)}\tag{19.16}\]

This equation shows that \(P_c \propto (A_b/A_t)^{1/(1-n)}\). For \(n=0.35\) and a 10% increase in burn area (e.g., from propellant cracking), chamber pressure increases by \(\approx 15\%\) — highlighting the importance of grain integrity inspection.

docs.title: 19.2.4 Combustion Instability
docs.text: Combustion instability is the coupling between the acoustic modes of the combustion chamber and the heat release rate. Two principal categories affect SRMs:

docs.title: L* Instability (Low-Frequency)
docs.text:
\[L^* = \frac{V_c}{A_t}\tag{19.17}\]

where \(V_c\) is the combustion chamber free volume. For \(L^* < L^*_{min} \approx 0.5\) m (propellant-specific), low-frequency pressure oscillations (chugging, 10–200 Hz) occur. Solution: increase \(L^*\) by enlarging chamber volume.

docs.title: Acoustic Mode Coupling (High-Frequency)
docs.text:
Axial longitudinal acoustic modes at frequency:

\[f_n = \frac{n\,c_{gas}}{2L}\tag{19.18}\]

where \(c_{gas} = \sqrt{\gamma R T}\) is the speed of sound in combustion gases (\(\approx 1000\)–\(1200\) m/s) and \(L\) is the grain length. For \(L = 1.5\,\text{m}\) and \(c_{gas} = 1100\,\text{m s}\): first axial mode \(f_1 \approx 367\) Hz.

Combustion response function \(R(f)\) describes the propellant’s amplification of oscillating pressure at frequency \(f\). If \(R > 1/\mathrm{damping}\), instability grows. Suppression methods include:

  • Iron oxide (Fe\(_2\)O\(_3\)) or zirconium oxide (ZrO\(_2\)) added at 0.1–0.5%: act as combustion stabilisers by modifying the solid-phase chemistry, reducing the response function magnitude

  • Resonance suppressor rods or aluminum wires (acoustic damping)

  • Propellant composition modification: reducing AP bimodal ratio

  • Chamber geometry modification: non-cylindrical port reduces modal purity

docs.title: Web Thickness and Burn Time
docs.text:
The web thickness \(W\) is the minimum distance from the initial burning surface to the nearest case wall:

\[t_b = \frac{W}{\bar{r}}\tag{19.19}\]

where \(\bar{r}\) is the mean burn rate over the operating pressure range. Volumetric loading fraction \(V_f = V_{propellant}/V_{case}\) is typically 0.88–0.94 for tactical motors; maximising \(V_f\) reduces inert motor mass.

docs.title: Dual-Pulse Motor
docs.text:
A dual-pulse motor contains two propellant grains in a single casing separated by a bulkhead/barrier. The barrier is designed to rupture at a controlled pressure after the first grain burns out. This provides:

  • Programmable thrust: high initial thrust for kinematic advantage, then reignited for terminal phase

  • Increased average velocity (reduced time to target = reduced target manoeuvre time)

  • Example: MBDA Meteor uses a dual-pulse design integrated with a throttleable ramjet sustainer

  • Mass penalty: bulkhead mass \(\approx\) 3–5% of motor mass

docs.title: Boost-Sustain Configuration
docs.text:
The boost-sustain SRM uses a single case with two grain types:

  • Booster grain (fast-burning, forward section): high \(a\), higher \(n\), burns first; provides 10–50\(g\) acceleration at launch; burns in 1–5 s

  • Sustainer grain (slow-burning, aft section): lower \(a\), lower \(n\); provides 3–10\(g\) for 10–60 s flight duration

  • Transition between grains: natural as booster burns through; slight pressure dip at transition

  • Example: AIM-120 AMRAAM uses a boost-sustain SRM with a shaped grain providing high initial thrust then a lower sustain level

docs.title: 19.2.6 Motor Casing
docs.text:
Modern tactical missile casings use filament-wound Carbon Fibre Reinforced Polymer (CFRP):

  • Fibre: T700S or T800H carbon fibre; tensile strength 4,900 MPa; modulus 294 GPa

  • Winding: wet filament winding with epoxy resin (hoop + helical layers); hoop-to-helical ratio optimised for biaxial stress state under \(P_c = 7\)–\(14\) MPa

  • Specific strength: \(\sigma_u/\rho \approx 2200\) kN\(\cdot\)m/kg; 3–5\(\times\) steel on weight basis

  • Structural factor \(PV/W\): CFRP cases achieve 40–55 km; steel cases 15–25 km

  • Liner: \(\approx\)3 m m HTPB or EPDM bonded to case interior; prevents debonding of grain from case under thermal cycling; tested per AIAA S-080B

Older/cheaper designs (SCUD, SA-2) use D6AC or 300M high-strength steel: heavier but more resistant to manufacturing defects and easier to weld.

docs.title: 19.2.7 Nozzle Design and Materials
docs.text:
The SRM nozzle must withstand:

  • Stagnation temperatures: 3,000–3,700 K

  • Erosive Al\(_2\)O\(_3\) particles at 100–200 m/s

  • Short burn times: 1–60 s (tactical); 60–180 s (strategic)

Throat insert: isostatically moulded graphite or carbon–carbon (C-C) composite. C-C throat erosion rate: 0.01–0.05 mm/s. Graphite: 0.05–0.15 mm/s.
