The IFM receiver uses a microwave delay line and phase comparator to measure the frequency of any signal present at its input within nanoseconds. The fundamental relationship is:

\[\phi = 2\pi f \tau_d\tag{31.13}\]

where \(\phi\) is the measured phase difference (rad) and \(\tau_d\) is the delay line length (s). Multiple delay lines with lengths in ratio 1:2:4:8 provide ambiguity-free frequency measurement. The IFM offers:

  • Frequency measurement latency \(<\)20 ns.

  • Frequency accuracy: 1–5 MHz across 2–18 GHz.

  • Bandwidth: simultaneous measurement possible only for single-signal environments.

  • Limitation: fails with simultaneous signals (two emitters cause false frequency readings).

docs.title: Channelised Receiver
docs.text:
The channelised receiver divides the frequency band into parallel sub-bands, each processed simultaneously by a dedicated filter, amplifier, and detector chain. A 2–18 GHz receiver may use 128 or more contiguous channels. The channelised architecture achieves:

  • Instantaneous frequency measurement without scanning.

  • Sensitivity approaching the superheterodyne in each channel: \(-80\) to \(-90\) dBm.

  • Simultaneous signal capability (each channel is independent).

  • Frequency resolution equal to channel bandwidth (typically 100–500 MHz per channel).

The channelised receiver is the preferred architecture for modern high-performance RWRs. Digital implementations using fast Fourier transforms (FFT) approach arbitrary channelisation:

\[\Delta f_{FFT} = \frac{f_s}{N_{FFT}}\tag{31.14}\]

where \(f_s\) is the ADC sample rate and \(N_{FFT}\) is the FFT size. A 4 GHz ADC with \(N_{FFT} = 4096\) achieves \(\Delta f = 976\) kHz frequency resolution.

docs.title: 31.4.2 Emitter Identification
docs.text:
RWR emitter identification (EID) matches measured pulse parameters against a threat library. The key parameters extracted from each intercept are:

  • Radio frequency (RF): Carrier frequency; may be agile — measured via IFM or channelised receiver.

  • Pulse width (PW): Duration of individual pulse; 0.1–100 \(\mu\)s typical.

  • Pulse repetition interval (PRI): Time between successive pulses; staggered, jittered, or dwell-and-switch waveforms complicate measurement.

  • Scan period/type: Antenna rotation; sector scan; track-while-scan; conical scan modulates pulse amplitude with scan frequency.

  • Intra-pulse modulation: LFM chirp; phase coding; detected by baseband digitiser.

The emitter identification score function is typically a weighted Mahalanobis distance in parameter space:

\[d_M = \sqrt{(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_i)^T \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_i)}\tag{31.15}\]

where \(\mathbf{x}\) is the measured parameter vector, \(\boldsymbol{\mu}_i\) is the library centroid for emitter \(i\), and \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_i\) is the covariance matrix capturing measurement uncertainty and emitter variability. The identity assigned is \(\hat{i} = \arg\min_i d_M\).

docs.title: Time Difference of Arrival (TDOA)
docs.text:
Two ES receivers at known positions \(\mathbf{r}_1\) and \(\mathbf{r}_2\) measure the arrival time of the same emitter pulse with times \(t_1\) and \(t_2\). The time difference \(\Delta t = t_1 - t_2\) constrains the emitter to a hyperbola:

\[\|\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_1\| - \|\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_2\| = c\,\Delta t\tag{31.16}\]

Three receivers produce two hyperbolas whose intersection yields a position fix. TDOA accuracy is governed by the timing resolution:

\[\sigma_{pos} \approx \frac{c\,\sigma_{\Delta t}}{2\sin(\theta/2)}\tag{31.17}\]

where \(\sigma_{\Delta t}\) is the timing measurement noise and \(\theta\) is the baseline-to-target subtended angle. Modern TDOA systems achieve \(<\)10 ns timing resolution, yielding \(<\)1 km position accuracy at 100 km range.

docs.title: Angle of Arrival Interferometry
docs.text:
Phase interferometry measures the phase difference between two antenna elements separated by baseline \(d\):

\[\Delta\phi = \frac{2\pi d \sin\theta}{\lambda}\tag{31.18}\]

where \(\theta\) is the angle of arrival. Ambiguity-free angle measurement requires \(d < \lambda/2\), but accuracy improves with longer baselines. Multi-baseline interferometers resolve ambiguities while achieving angle accuracy of \(\sigma_\theta \approx \lambda / (2\pi d \cdot \mathrm{SNR}^{1/2})\).

docs.title: 31.5.1 Noise Jamming
docs.text: Noise jamming degrades radar detection by raising the noise floor at the radar receiver. Three variants are in common use:

docs.title: Barrage Noise Jamming
docs.text:
Barrage jamming spreads power across a wide bandwidth \(B_{barrage}\) simultaneously, ensuring coverage regardless of threat radar frequency. The noise spectral density injected into the threat radar is:

\[N_0^{(j)} = \frac{P_j G_j}{B_{barrage}} \cdot \frac{G_{r,j} \lambda^2}{(4\pi)^2 R_j^2} \quad [\text{W/Hz}]\tag{31.19}\]

The J/S penalty for barrage relative to spot jamming is:

\[\Delta_{JS}\,[\text{dB}] = 10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{B_{barrage}}{B_{radar}}\right)\tag{31.20}\]

A barrage jammer covering 8–12 GHz (4 GHz) against a 10 MHz-bandwidth fire control radar wastes \(10\log(400) = 26\) dB of jamming effectiveness.

docs.title: Spot Noise Jamming
docs.text:
Spot jamming concentrates all available power into the radar’s operating bandwidth, maximising J/S. However, it requires precise knowledge of the threat frequency and an agile tuner fast enough to track frequency-hopping emitters. The frequency tracking residual introduces a J/S degradation:

\[J/S_{effective} = J/S_{peak} - \Delta f_{error}^2 \cdot \left(\frac{\partial(J/S)}{\partial f}\right)^2\tag{31.21}\]

where \(\Delta f_{error}\) is the frequency tracking error. Modern threat radars with frequency agility at pulse-to-pulse rates of 1–10 GHz/s can defeat slow-tuning spot jammers.

docs.title: Swept Noise Jamming
docs.text:
Swept jamming represents a compromise: a narrow jammer bandwidth sweeps across the threat band at rate \(\dot{f}\), spending dwell time \(t_{dwell} = B_{radar}/\dot{f}\) per radar frequency. The duty cycle against a specific radar frequency determines the effective J/S:

\[J/S_{swept} = J/S_{spot} \cdot \frac{B_{radar}}{\dot{f} \cdot T_{return}}\tag{31.22}\]

docs.title: 31.5.2 Digital Radio Frequency Memory (DRFM) Deceptive Jamming
docs.text:
The DRFM is the enabling technology for modern deceptive electronic attack. It digitises the intercepted radar pulse at the carrier frequency, stores it in a high-speed RAM, and retransmits the stored waveform with controlled modifications to produce false targets. The key DRFM performance parameters are:

\[f_{ADC} \geq 2 \cdot B_{IF} \quad \text{(Nyquist criterion)}\tag{31.23}\] \[\text{SFDR} = 6.02 N_{bits} + 1.76 \quad [\text{dBc}] \quad \text{(ideal ADC spurious-free dynamic range)}\tag{31.24}\]

A 12-bit DRFM achieves \(\sim\)74 dBc SFDR, sufficient to generate false targets that are indistinguishable in amplitude from real targets.

docs.title: Range Gate Pull-Off (RGPO)
docs.text:
RGPO exploits the range-tracking loop of a pulse Doppler or range-gated radar. The DRFM first retransmits the intercepted pulse synchronously with the received pulse (zero delay), creating a false target at the true range. It then progressively increases the retransmission delay \(\Delta\tau\):

\[R_{false}(t) = R_{true} + \frac{c}{2}\Delta\tau(t)\tag{31.25}\]

The delay ramp rate is matched to the radar tracking loop bandwidth \(B_{TL}\) to ensure capture:

\[\dot{R}_{false} = \frac{c}{2}\dot{\Delta\tau} \leq \frac{c}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{\pi B_{TL} \tau_{PW}}\tag{31.26}\]

Once the range gate has been pulled far enough from the true range, the DRFM cuts transmission, leaving the radar tracker tracking empty space. The aircraft manoeuvres during this window.

docs.title: Velocity Gate Pull-Off (VGPO)
docs.text:
VGPO operates analogously in the Doppler domain. The DRFM introduces a frequency offset \(\Delta f_D\) to the retransmitted pulse, mimicking a Doppler shift corresponding to a false velocity. The false radial velocity is:

\[v_{false} = v_{true} + \frac{\lambda \Delta f_D}{2}\tag{31.27}\]

The DRFM sweeps \(\Delta f_D\) at a rate just within the Doppler tracking loop bandwidth, capturing the velocity gate and pulling it to the clutter region, where the CFAR threshold rises and detection is lost.

docs.title: Cross-Eye Angle Deception
docs.text:
Cross-eye jamming exploits the monopulse angle-measurement mechanism. Two re-transmitter antennas separated by baseline \(\ell\) retransmit the intercepted signal with a phase difference \(\Delta\phi_{CE}\). The apparent angle error induced at the monopulse radar is:

\[\delta\theta_{CE} = \frac{\lambda}{2\pi k_{mon} d_{mon}} \cdot \frac{\Delta\phi_{CE}}{2}\tag{31.28}\]

where \(k_{mon}\) is the monopulse ratio slope and \(d_{mon}\) is the monopulse antenna aperture. When \(\Delta\phi_{CE} = \pi\) (180° phase difference), the apparent target position is driven to the null of the sum beam, causing maximum angle error. The two retransmitters must have near-equal amplitudes (within \(\pm\)0.5 dB) and the phase difference must be stable to \(\pm\)5° for effective deception.

docs.title: 31.5.3 Self-Protection, Escort, and Stand-Off Jammers
docs.text:
• Self-Protection Jammer (SPJ): Carried aboard the protected platform. Jammer EIRP limited by volume and power constraints. EIRP = \(P_j G_j\) typically 1–5 kW for combat aircraft SPJs. J/S improves as \(R^2\) (Equation (31.9)).

  • Escort Jammer: Dedicated EA aircraft flying in close formation with strike package. Higher EIRP (10–100 kW) from larger platform. AN/ALQ-99 on EA-18G Growler: five pods, each 200 W per band, 10 transmitters, 1–18 GHz coverage. J/S depends on escort geometry.

  • Stand-Off Jammer (SOJ): Orbits outside threat engagement zone, providing area suppression. Must achieve required J/S at long range; requires very high EIRP (1 MW effective). EC-130H Compass Call: 150 kW average transmit power across communication bands.

Power management in multi-threat environments requires prioritisation. The threat priority function is typically:

\[P_{threat,i} = w_1 \cdot \text{lethality}_i + w_2 \cdot \text{engagement\_prob}_i + w_3 \cdot (R_{BT,i}/R_i) + w_4 \cdot \text{track\_quality}_i\tag{31.29}\]

The jammer allocates its time budget inversely proportional to \(P_{threat}\) ranking, ensuring the most lethal immediate threat receives maximum jamming attention.

docs.title: 31.6.1 Flare Countermeasures
docs.text: Infrared-guided missiles are a primary threat to aircraft and large UAVs. Flares remain the most widely deployed IR countermeasure due to their simplicity, low cost, and effectiveness against older single-band seekers.

docs.title: MTV Flare Composition and Spectral Characteristics
docs.text:
The standard flare composition is magnesium/Teflon/Viton (MTV), which burns at 2000–2500 K. The spectral radiance follows Planck’s law:

\[L_\lambda(T) = \frac{2hc^2}{\lambda^5} \cdot \frac{\varepsilon(\lambda)}{\exp\!\left(\frac{hc}{\lambda k_B T}\right) - 1}\tag{31.30}\]

where \(h = 6.626\times10^{-34}\) J\(\cdot\)s, \(c = 3\times10^8\) m/s, \(k_B = 1.381\times10^{-23}\) J/K, and \(\varepsilon(\lambda)\) is the spectral emissivity of the burning material. For a 2300 K MTV flare, peak emission occurs at:

\[\lambda_{peak} = \frac{2898\,\mu\text{m}\cdot\text{K}}{T} = \frac{2898}{2300} \approx 1.26\,\mu\text{m}\tag{31.31}\]

However, the MTV composition contains MgF\(_2\) and CO\(_2\) spectral lines that produce strong emission bands at 2.7 \(\mu\)m (the primary MWIR seeker window), making flares effective decoys in this band. The jet engine plume temperature is typically 600–900 K (commercial) to 1200–1500 K (military afterburner), and the plume radiance in the 3–5 \(\mu\)m band is well-matched by the flare’s broad emission spectrum.

docs.title: Seeker Discrimination Against Flares
docs.text:
Modern dual-band and imaging IR (IIR) seekers discriminate flares from aircraft using several techniques:

  1. Spectral ratio discrimination: The ratio of radiance in two spectral bands (e.g., 2.7 \(\mu\)m vs 4.3 \(\mu\)m) differs between the aircraft exhaust (\(\mathrm{CO}_2\) absorption at 4.3 \(\mu\)m) and an MTV flare. The discrimination parameter is:

    \[D_{spec} = \frac{L_{band1}}{L_{band2}}\tag{31.32}\]

    Aircraft have \(D_{spec} \gg 1\) (engine hot); flares have \(D_{spec} \approx 0.5\)–2 depending on composition.

  2. Kinematic discrimination: A flare decelerates at \(\sim g\) after ejection and follows a ballistic trajectory; the aircraft continues powered flight. The angular acceleration of a flare relative to the missile’s seeker diverges from a manoeuvring target signature.

  3. Spatial discrimination: IIR seekers resolve the aircraft body from the point-source flare at ranges \(< 5\) km, enabling rejection of spatially separated decoys.

docs.title: 31.6.2 Directed Infrared Countermeasures (DIRCM)
docs.text:
DIRCM systems replace or supplement flares with a pointed, modulated laser beam that overwhelms or confuses the IR seeker’s tracking loop. The system consists of:

  1. Missile Approach Warning System (MAWS): UV or mid-wave IR sensor detecting missile plume; cues DIRCM within \(\sim\)1 s of launch.

  2. Fine Tracker: Narrow-FOV imaging sensor; acquires and tracks the incoming missile to \(<\)0.1 mrad pointing accuracy.

  3. Laser: Modulated laser (1–5 \(\mu\)m band) pointed at the seeker; disrupts tracking by saturating the detector or inducing false modulation in the seeker’s angle error loop.

The DIRCM laser must achieve sufficient irradiance at the seeker aperture to saturate it:

\[E_{seeker} = \frac{P_{laser} G_{laser}}{4\pi R^2} \cdot T_{atm}(R) \geq E_{sat}\tag{31.33}\]

where \(G_{laser}\) is the laser beam gain (related to divergence \(\theta_{beam}\) by \(G_{laser} = 4\pi/\theta_{beam}^2\)), \(T_{atm}\) is atmospheric transmission, and \(E_{sat}\) is the seeker saturation irradiance (typically \(10^{-5}\)–\(10^{-3}\) W/cm\(^2\)). Representative DIRCM systems include:

  • AN/AAQ-24(V) Nemesis (Northrop Grumman): First generation DIRCM; 1–3 \(\mu\)m Nd:YAG pumped OPO; fielded on C-130, C-17, special operations aircraft.

  • LAIRCM (Large Aircraft IRCM): Upgraded Nemesis with advanced MAWS integration; covers threats from 360° in azimuth via multiple turrets.

  • DIRCM/IDAS (Thales/ELTA): European standard; dual-band laser; modulation codes tailored to known seeker AGC and track loop parameters.

docs.title: 31.7.1 Principles of Chaff Operation
docs.text:
Chaff consists of a large number of thin, electrically conductive dipole elements dispersed in the air to create a region of high radar reflectivity that can mask or decoy radar-guided weapons. Each chaff element is a half-wave dipole at the threat radar frequency:

\[\ell_{element} = \frac{\lambda}{2} = \frac{c}{2f}\tag{31.34}\]

For a 10 GHz (X-band) radar: \(\ell = c/(2 \times 10^{10}) = 15\) mm. Chaff cartridges contain millions of elements cut to cover multiple threat frequency bands.

docs.title: 31.7.2 Chaff RCS
docs.text:
The radar cross-section of a resonant half-wave dipole is approximately \(0.86\lambda^2\). For a cloud of \(N\) randomly oriented dipoles (uniform random orientation, averaging over polarisations):

\[\sigma_{chaff} = N \cdot 0.15\,\lambda^2 \quad [\text{m}^2]\tag{31.35}\]

The factor 0.15 (rather than 0.86) accounts for the random orientation averaging. A chaff round containing \(N = 10^6\) elements at \(\lambda = 0.03\) m (X-band):

\[\sigma_{chaff} = 10^6 \times 0.15 \times (0.03)^2 = 135\,\text{m}^2\tag{31.36}\]

This greatly exceeds the RCS of a typical combat aircraft (1–10 m\(^2\)), producing a dominant return. The effectiveness ratio must satisfy:

\[\frac{\sigma_{chaff}}{\sigma_{aircraft}} \geq (J/S)_{required}\tag{31.37}\]

docs.title: 31.7.3 Chaff Deployment Tactics
docs.text:
1. Seduction: The aircraft fires chaff at the moment of missile launch detection, then manoeuvres sharply. The radar seeker, tracking the large chaff cloud, continues tracking the cloud while the aircraft escapes.

  2. Distraction: Pre-emptive chaff deployment before the aircraft enters a threat engagement zone, saturating the radar with multiple false targets and degrading track-while-scan capacity.

  3. Confusion: Multiple aircraft simultaneously firing chaff creates a complex multi-target scenario that overwhelms radar signal processing capacity.

Bloom time (the period during which chaff is an effective decoy) is typically 20–60 s depending on wind shear, element fall rate, and cloud dispersion. The chaff cloud angular subtense at the threat radar must exceed the radar’s angle tracking gate width for seduction to succeed.

docs.title: 31.8 Electronic Protection
docs.text: Electronic Protection (EP) encompasses all measures that maintain the effectiveness of friendly electromagnetic systems in the face of adversary EA. Modern radar and communication systems employ multiple complementary EP techniques.

docs.title: 31.8.1 Frequency Agility
docs.text:
A frequency-agile radar changes its carrier frequency from pulse to pulse (or burst to burst), hopping across a wide bandwidth. The jamming degradation against a spot jammer is:

\[\Delta_{JS,agility}\,[\text{dB}] = 10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{B_{hop}}{B_{spot}}\right)\tag{31.38}\]

where \(B_{hop}\) is the frequency hopping bandwidth and \(B_{spot}\) is the jammer bandwidth. An X-band radar hopping across 500 MHz against a 10 MHz spot jammer degrades jammer effectiveness by 17 dB. Frequency agility also provides intrinsic scintillation averaging (reduced \(\sigma\) fluctuations) and range sidelobe suppression in pulse compression.

docs.title: 31.8.2 Pulse Compression and LPI
docs.text:
Pulse compression allows a radar to transmit a long pulse (high energy) while achieving the range resolution of a short pulse. The compression is achieved by modulating the transmitted pulse (LFM chirp, phase coding) and matched-filtering the received signal:

\[R_{res} = \frac{c}{2B}\tag{31.39}\] \[G_{PC} = B \cdot \tau_{PW} \quad [\text{time-bandwidth product}]\tag{31.40}\]

where \(B\) is the chirp bandwidth and \(\tau_{PW}\) is the pulse width. A waveform with \(B = 50\) MHz and \(\tau_{PW} = 100\) \(\mu\)s achieves \(G_{PC} = 5000\) (37 dB). The peak power required is reduced by \(G_{PC}\) relative to an uncompressed pulse of the same energy, drastically lowering the peak power observable by ES receivers.

An FMCW (Frequency-Modulated Continuous Wave) LPI radar transmits continuously with low peak power:

\[P_{peak,FMCW} = P_{avg,FMCW}\tag{31.41}\] \[P_{peak,pulse} = P_{avg,pulse} / \text{duty cycle} \gg P_{avg,pulse}\tag{31.42}\]

The ES receiver using MDS (Equation (31.5)) must integrate over the FMCW sweep time \(T_{sweep}\) to detect it, requiring \(\sim G_{PC}\) longer integration than for a pulsed radar — providing a fundamental intercept advantage.

docs.title: 31.8.3 Monopulse Resistance to Angle Deception
docs.text:
Conical scan and lobing radars measure angle by comparing amplitude modulation of received pulses. A jammer can modulate its output at the scan frequency to inject false angle error — the inverse gain jamming technique. Monopulse eliminates this vulnerability by measuring the angle error from a single pulse using simultaneous sum (\(\Sigma\)) and difference (\(\Delta\)) beams:

\[\theta_{error} = k_{mon} \cdot \frac{\Delta}{\Sigma}\tag{31.43}\]

where \(k_{mon}\) is the monopulse ratio slope (rad\(^{-1}\)). Because both \(\Sigma\) and \(\Delta\) are measured simultaneously, inter-pulse amplitude modulation cannot inject angle error. Monopulse is highly resistant to all amplitude-based jamming, which is why cross-eye (phase-based deception, Section 31.5) is required against it.

docs.title: 31.8.4 Adaptive Beamforming and Null Steering
docs.text:
AESA (Active Electronically Scanned Array) radars can place precise nulls in their receive pattern in the direction of jammers. The weight vector \(\mathbf{w}\) that maximises SINR is given by the minimum variance distortionless response (MVDR) beamformer:

\[\mathbf{w}_{opt} = \frac{\mathbf{R}_{xx}^{-1} \mathbf{a}(\theta_0)} {\mathbf{a}^H(\theta_0) \mathbf{R}_{xx}^{-1} \mathbf{a}(\theta_0)}\tag{31.44}\]

where \(\mathbf{R}_{xx}\) is the measured received signal covariance matrix and \(\mathbf{a}(\theta_0)\) is the steering vector toward the target direction \(\theta_0\). The null depth achievable against a jammer at angle \(\theta_j\) is limited by the array calibration accuracy to approximately \(10\log_{10}(1/N_{elements}^2)\) relative to the main beam, typically 30–50 dB for large arrays.

Table 31.4 summarises EP technique effectiveness against major EA modes.

Table 31.4. EP Technique Effectiveness Against EA Modes EP Technique Barrage Spot DRFM Cross-eye Chaff Frequency agility Low High Medium Low Low Pulse compression High High Low Low Low FMCW/LPI High High Medium Low Low Monopulse Low Low Medium High Low Null steering (AESA) High High Medium Low Low PRF agility Low Low High Low Low MTI/DPCA Low Low Medium Low High

docs.title: 31.9.1 GPS Signal Vulnerability
docs.text:
The GPS L1 C/A signal arrives at a receiver antenna with power:

\[P_{GPS} \approx -130\,\text{dBm}\tag{31.45}\]

This extremely low received power makes GPS inherently vulnerable to jamming. Any narrowband or broadband jammer operating near 1575.42 MHz (L1) or 1227.6 MHz (L2) with even modest power can deny GPS service over a wide area.

docs.title: 31.9.2 Jamming Coverage Radius
docs.text:
The range at which a GPS jammer can deny service to a standard receiver is:

\[R_{j,GPS} = \frac{\lambda}{4\pi} \sqrt{\frac{P_j G_j}{(J/S)_{req} \cdot P_{GPS}}}\tag{31.46}\]

where \((J/S)_{req}\) is the minimum J/S to suppress the receiver’s tracking loops (typically 20–40 dB for a C/A code receiver). A 10 W omnidirectional jammer achieves:

\[R_{j,GPS} = \frac{0.19}{4\pi}\sqrt{\frac{10 \times 1}{1000 \times 10^{-16}}} \approx 50\,\text{km}\tag{31.47}\]

This explains the devastating effect of even small commercially available GPS jammers, and the operational significance of GPS anti-jamming measures.

docs.title: 31.9.3 GPS Spoofing
docs.text:
GPS spoofing transmits counterfeit GPS signals with higher power than authentic satellites, causing the receiver’s code tracking loops to lock onto the false signals. The spoofer must:

  1. Match the signal structure of authentic GPS (C/A code, L1 carrier, navigation message).

  2. Gradually increase signal power to capture the tracking loop without causing loss-of-lock.

  3. Introduce position/time errors consistent with the desired navigation deception.

The spoofing power advantage required over the authentic signal is typically only 3–6 dB, since the spoofer can transmit from a nearby position while authentic satellites are 20,200 km away.

docs.title: Controlled Radiation Pattern Antenna (CRPA)
docs.text:
A CRPA (typically 7-element phased array in a 25 cm aperture) nulls jammers in the receive pattern while maintaining gain toward GPS satellites. The null depth against a jammer is:

\[G_{null} = -10\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{1 + P_j G_j / (4\pi R_j^2 \cdot N_0 B)}{(J/S)_{receiver}}\right)\tag{31.48}\]

Operational CRPAs achieve 40–55 dB of jammer suppression per null. With \(N = 7\) elements, up to 6 simultaneous jammers can be nulled. The GPS military antenna (GAS-1 or similar) provides additional jamming resistance.

docs.title: M-Code and Selective Availability Anti-Spoofing Module (SAASM)
docs.text:
The GPS M-code military signal provides:

  • 24 dB higher effective signal power than C/A code.

  • Cryptographic authentication preventing signal spoofing.

  • Binary offset carrier (BOC) modulation providing sharper code correlation peaks.

  • Direct acquisition without dependency on C/A code.

docs.title: Anti-Spoofing Measures
docs.text:
\[\text{RAIM threshold} = \frac{P_{alert}\text{-equivalent pseudorange error}}{K_{RAIM}\sqrt{N_{sv}}}\tag{31.49}\]

Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring (RAIM) detects anomalous pseudorange measurements statistically inconsistent with the true satellite geometry. Complementary anti-spoofing measures include:

  • INS cross-check: GPS position solution verified against INS dead reckoning; large position jumps (spoofing artifacts) trigger alert.

  • Multi-constellation: Simultaneous GPS + GLONASS + Galileo + BeiDou; a spoofer must simultaneously spoof all constellations on different frequencies.

  • Angle-of-arrival: Spoofed signals arrive from a ground transmitter at low elevation; authentic satellites are above the horizon.

Table 31.5 compares anti-jamming techniques.

Table 31.5. GPS Anti-Jamming and Anti-Spoofing Technique Comparison Technique Anti-Jam (dB) Anti-Spoof Cost/Complexity Standard C/A receiver 0 None Low P(Y)-code receiver +20 Partial Medium M-code receiver +24 Yes (crypto) High CRPA (7-element) 40–55 None High CRPA + M-code 55–75 Yes Very high RAIM 0 Partial Low (software) Multi-constellation 0 Partial Low–Medium INS integration Graceful degradation Partial Medium

docs.title: 31.10.1 Against IR-Guided Missiles
docs.text: Infrared-homing missiles are defeated by a combination of kinematic and electromagnetic countermeasures. The fundamental requirement is to present the seeker with one or more false targets whose IR intensity exceeds that of the real target.

docs.title: Flare Employment Sequence
docs.text:
A fully integrated IR countermeasures sequence for an aircraft under MANPADS attack:

  1. MAWS detects missile launch (UV flash or MWIR plume signature); fires alert within 0.5 s.

  2. System assesses engagement geometry; selects countermeasure sequence.

  3. Flare cartridges dispensed at optimised rate (typically 4–6 per burst) and timing relative to manoeuvre initiation.

  4. Aircraft executes high-g break turn (loading the seeker with angular rate beyond its track bandwidth).

  5. DIRCM laser (if fitted) engages seeker continuously throughout.

The probability of aircraft survival given flare employment is modelled by:

\[P_{survival} = 1 - P_{kill|no\,CM} \cdot P_{kill|CM\,fail} \cdot (1-P_{CM\,success})\tag{31.50}\]

docs.title: Active Radar Homing (ARH) Missiles
docs.text:
Against missiles with ARH seekers (e.g., AIM-120 AMRAAM, R-77, Meteor):

  • Noise jamming: Raise noise floor in seeker’s IF bandwidth; reduce \(P_d/P_{fa}\).

  • DRFM deception: Inject false range/velocity targets; attempt RGPO/VGPO.

  • Chaff: Dispense chaff cloud; seeker must discriminate aircraft from cloud.

  • Terrain masking: Descend to terrain; place ground clutter in seeker passband; clutter return overwhelms Doppler discrimination.

  • Notch filter evasion: Manoeuvre to zero radial velocity relative to missile; drives target Doppler into notch; seeker loses track.

docs.title: Semi-Active Radar Homing (SARH)
docs.text:
SARH missiles require continuous illumination of the target by the launching radar. Countermeasures target the illuminating radar rather than the missile seeker:

  • Jam the CW illumination frequency with spot jamming.

  • Physically engage the illuminating radar with anti-radiation missile (ARM).

  • Terrain masking to break illumination line of sight.

docs.title: Towed Decoys
docs.text:
A towed decoy is a small RF repeater deployed on a long fibre-optic tether behind the aircraft. The decoy amplifies the threat radar signal and retransmits it with an RCS that exceeds the aircraft:

\[\sigma_{decoy} = \left(\frac{P_{retx} G_{retx}^2 \lambda^2}{(4\pi)^3 P_{radar} G_{radar}^2}\right)^{1/2}\tag{31.51}\]

The towed decoy draws an ARH or SARH missile away from the aircraft. The ALE-50 (unmodulated) and ALE-55 (fibre-optic, DRFM-capable) are the primary USAF systems. The decoy must present a continuously larger apparent RCS, achieved by increasing retransmission gain as the missile closes.

docs.title: Miniature Air-Launched Decoy (MALD)
docs.text:
The ADM-160B MALD (L-3 / Raytheon) is a powered, free-flying decoy:

  • Turbojet propulsion; 500+ km range; Mach 0.9 cruise.

  • RCS equivalent to a tactical fighter via calibrated retransmit.

  • Emulates fighter radar/communications emissions (MALD-J variant adds jamming).

  • Expendable; saturates integrated air defence systems (IADS) with false tracks.

docs.title: 31.11 Electronic Warfare Aircraft and Integrated Systems
31.11.1 EA-18G Growler
docs.text:
The EA-18G Growler is the US Navy’s dedicated carrier-based EW aircraft, derived from the F/A-18F. Its primary EW systems are:

  • AN/ALQ-99 Tactical Jamming System (TJS): External jamming pods covering 0.1–18 GHz in five bands; each pod contains two jamming transmitters; peak EIRP exceeds 1 MW per band. The ALQ-99 is a noise and modulated noise jammer; DRFM capability is limited.

  • AN/ALQ-218(V)2 Tactical Jamming Receiver: Wideband ESM system providing real-time threat characterisation, geo-location, and cueing for the ALQ-99.

  • AN/APG-79 AESA Radar: Used for normal A-A and A-G modes; provides passive track via AESA receive-only mode when ALQ-218 is active.

  • AGM-88E AARGM: Anti-Radiation Guided Missile; homes on threat radar emissions; attacks radiating SAM batteries.

The Growler’s next-generation replacement, the Next Generation Jammer (NGJ), incorporates DRFM-based deceptive jamming in all three bands (low, mid, high), beam agility via AESA transmit arrays, and cognitive EW processing for adaptive waveform selection.

docs.title: 31.11.2 F-35 AN/ASQ-239 Barracuda
docs.text:
The F-35’s integrated EW suite (AN/ASQ-239) demonstrates the fusion of EW with the aircraft’s sensor suite:

  • Full 360° azimuth ESM coverage from multiple antenna apertures distributed around the aircraft airframe (no dedicated external pod).

  • Passive ranging via TDOA using widely-spaced apertures and the aircraft’s INS timing reference.

  • Integrated with AN/AAQ-37 DAS (Distributed Aperture System): six IR cameras providing missile approach warning and passive tracking without dedicated MAWS.

  • SPJ function via internal transmit antennas; power limited compared to pod-mounted systems but fully integrated in track-while-jam operation.

docs.title: 31.11.3 RC-135V/W Rivet Joint
docs.text:
The Rivet Joint is the USAF’s primary SIGINT collection platform, providing:

  • Broadband ELINT collection: 0.1–40 GHz; characterises radar emission parameters for threat library updates.

  • COMINT collection: communication intercept; COMINT geolocation.

  • On-board analysis by specialised operators; real-time intelligence dissemination via datalink to theatre commanders.

  • High-accuracy TDOA/AOA geolocation of emitters to support targeting.

docs.title: 31.11.4 Drone Electronic Warfare Systems
docs.text:
Small UAVs are increasingly employed as EW platforms due to their low cost and expendability:

Table 31.6. Drone-Borne Electronic Warfare Systems System Platform Function Frequency Range MALD-J ADM-160C Expendable UAV Stand-in jamming + decoy 2–18 GHz SkyShield (Elbit) Pod on HALE/MALE SPJ; DIRCM 2–18 GHz + IR Coyote Block 3 Small UAV swarm Escort jammer; EA Custom CHAMP (AFRL) Cruise missile HPM payload; disable electronics Wideband Perdix swarm 3-in. expendable RF survey; C2 jamming 0.4–6 GHz

docs.title: 31.12.1 The Convergence of EW and Cyber
docs.text: The distinction between electronic warfare and cyber operations has largely dissolved in modern conflict. Any system with digital hardware accessible via electromagnetic coupling — an RF interface, conducted emission, or intentional injection — is simultaneously a cyber target. The CEMA concept formalises this convergence.

docs.title: 31.12.2 RF-Enabled Cyber Operations
docs.text:
Several attack vectors exist for cyber operations conducted via RF:

  • RF side-channel attack: Compromised processor emits RF emissions correlated with classified cryptographic operations; TEMPEST attacks exploit this.

  • Intentional RF injection: High-power narrowband signal couples into circuit board traces; modulates supply rail; injects false data into ADC. IEMI (Intentional Electromagnetic Interference) is the civilian analogue.

  • Protocol-layer exploit: Craft malformed datalink packet (e.g., MAVLink for UAV, TADIL-J for JTIDS) received by standard RF interface; exploit parser vulnerability in firmware.

  • Software Defined Radio (SDR) gateway: A compromised SDR node in a mesh network serves as a RF-to-IP bridge enabling cyber intrusion via the radio link.

docs.title: 31.12.3 Cognitive and AI-Driven EW
docs.text:
The exponential growth in adversary emitter diversity and waveform complexity is driving a shift toward machine-learning-based EW:

  • Deep learning emitter identification: Convolutional neural networks trained on I/Q sample libraries achieve emitter ID accuracy \(>\)97% on known emitters with SNR \(>5\) dB, and generalise to novel modulations through transfer learning.

  • Reinforcement learning jammer: The jammer is modelled as an agent in a Markov decision process; the reward function is the radar detection degradation. RL-trained jammers adapt their waveform against unknown radar ECCM in real time.

  • Cognitive spectrum access: EW system senses spectrum occupancy and dynamically selects jamming frequency, waveform, and power to maximise effectiveness while minimising interference to friendly systems.

The performance of an ML-based emitter classifier can be characterised by the confusion matrix and the minimum SNR for a target accuracy \(P_c\):

\[\text{SNR}_{min} = \frac{\sigma_n^2 \cdot Q^{-1}(1-P_c)^2}{2\|\boldsymbol{\Delta\mu}\|^2}\tag{31.52}\]

where \(\boldsymbol{\Delta\mu}\) is the feature vector difference between classes and \(\sigma_n^2\) is the feature noise variance.

docs.title: 31.12.4 Quantum Radar and Future EW
docs.text:
Quantum illumination radar exploits entangled photon pairs to achieve theoretically \(6e\) dB (where \(e\) is the base of natural logarithm) advantage in target detection SNR over classical radar at the same transmitted power in thermal noise environments. The quantum illumination SNR ratio is:

\[\frac{d^2_{QI}}{d^2_{classical}} \approx e^{-1}\tag{31.53}\]

The practical implication is that quantum radar, if realised, would be nearly impossible to jam via conventional noise injection, since it relies on quantum correlation rather than classical coherence. The microwave quantum illumination experiment at MIT (Shapiro/Lloyd, 2009) demonstrated the principle at optical frequencies; microwave implementation remains a major research challenge.

Photonic EW represents another frontier: photonic RF filters, photonic ADCs sampling at 100 GHz+, and fibre-optical beamforming enable EW systems operating into the EHF and THz bands where conventional electronic components reach their limits. THz sensing (0.3–3 THz) enables imaging through non-metallic concealment and new ELINT collection against emerging mmW systems.

docs.title: 31.13 EW System Design Trade-offs and Performance Analysis
31.13.1 EIRP vs Coverage vs Platform Constraints
docs.text:
The fundamental EW design equation balances EIRP requirements against platform constraints. For a stand-in jammer achieving required J/S at range \(R_{max}\):

\[\mathrm{EIRP}_{required} = P_j G_j = (J/S)_{req} \cdot P_t G_t \sigma \cdot \frac{R_j^2}{(4\pi) R_t^4}\tag{31.54}\]

The antenna aperture is limited by platform dimensions; gain is:

\[G_j = \eta \cdot \frac{4\pi A_{ant}}{\lambda^2}\tag{31.55}\]

For a 0.3 m\(\times\)0.3 m aperture at 10 GHz: \(G_j = 0.6 \times 4\pi \times 0.09 / (0.03)^2 = 754 = 28.8\) dBi.

Power amplifier efficiency \(\eta_{PA}\) converts DC power to RF:

\[P_{DC} = \frac{P_j}{\eta_{PA}}; \quad \eta_{PA} = 30\%\text{--}50\%\text{ (GaN PA)}\tag{31.56}\]

Thermal management is the critical constraint: a 1 kW average RF output jammer dissipates \(\sim\)1.5 kW of heat, requiring dedicated thermal management in a constrained airborne installation.

docs.title: 31.13.2 Integrated EW Architecture for Combat UAVs
docs.text:
Modern combat UAVs (e.g., XQ-58 Valkyrie, Loyal Wingman) must integrate EW with other mission functions. Table 31.7 illustrates a conceptual EW suite mass budget for a medium-class combat UAV.

Table 31.7. Conceptual EW Suite Mass Budget for Medium Combat UAV Subsystem Mass (kg) Power (W) Vol. (L) Function ESM/RWR antennas (8×) 1.2 5 0.4 Threat warning; freq measurement ESM processing unit 3.5 80 3.0 Pulse processing; emitter ID DRFM module 4.0 120 3.5 Deceptive EA waveform generation SPJ transmitter (GaN) 8.0 800 6.0 200 W RF output; 8–12 GHz DIRCM unit 6.0 300 5.0 IR laser; missile approach warning Chaff/flare dispenser 5.0 10 8.0 32-round dispenser; DIRCM interface EW management computer 2.0 60 1.5 Threat correlation; priority; control Total 29.7 1375 27.4

docs.title: 31.13.3 EW Test and Evaluation
docs.text:
EW system validation requires specialised test facilities:

  • Anechoic chamber: RF-absorber lined room; eliminates multipath; characterises antenna patterns and jammer EIRP. Must accommodate full-size aircraft (30 m\(\times\)15 m minimum for fighter-class).

  • Open-range threat simulator: Known-geometry range with programmable radar threat emulators; tests full EW system against representative threat waveforms.

  • Hardware-in-the-loop (HWIL): Full missile seeker in closed-loop simulation; IRCM/DIRCM system tested against simulated missile trajectory and seeker response.

  • Electronic Combat Range (ECR): Dedicated airspace (e.g., Utah Test and Training Range) with distributed threat radar network; live-fly EW effectiveness measurement.

docs.title: 31.14 Summary and Key Performance Metrics
docs.text:
Electronic warfare encompasses a broad spectrum of technologies and techniques, all governed by the fundamental physics of electromagnetic propagation. Key design parameters and their typical operational values are summarised below:

  • RWR sensitivity: \(-65\) to \(-90\) dBm (CVR to channelised); drives intercept range.

  • Self-protection J/S: \(>0\) dB noise; \(>+6\) dB deceptive; at maximum threat range.

  • DRFM dynamic range: \(>\)60 dB; 10–14 bit ADC; \(<\)100 ns latency.

  • DIRCM irradiance: \(>10^{-4}\) W/cm\(^2\) at 3 km for seeker saturation.

  • Chaff RCS: \(>10 \times \sigma_{aircraft}\) for 30 s bloom duration.

  • GPS CRPA null depth: 40–55 dB; protects against 1–100 W jammers at \(<\)5 km.

  • Towed decoy advantage: \(\sigma_{decoy}/\sigma_{aircraft} > 10\) (10 dB); draws seeker homing point 50–100 m aft of aircraft.

The trajectory of EW development follows three converging trends: increasing digitalisation (all-digital DRFM, SDR-based ESM), cognitive adaptation (AI-driven waveform selection and emitter identification), and platform miniaturisation (sub-10 kg EW suites for UCAV class vehicles). The adversary dynamics — driven by AESA radar proliferation, advanced IIR seekers with dual-band discrimination, and GPS-independent precision navigation — ensure that electronic warfare will remain one of the most technically demanding and rapidly evolving disciplines in aerospace defence engineering.

docs.title: 32.1 Introduction to Directed Energy Weapons
docs.text:
Directed energy weapons (DEWs) constitute a class of armaments that defeat targets by delivering energy in the form of electromagnetic radiation, particle beams, or plasma rather than by propelling a mass at high velocity. Unlike kinetic interceptors, a DEW engages its target at or near the speed of light, eliminating the need to compute a lead angle for all but the most extreme slant ranges. The phrase directed energy differentiates these weapons from nuclear or chemical weapons that release energy omnidirectionally; in a DEW the energy is coherently directed along a defined propagation path toward a specific aim point.

Three primary technology families define the DEW landscape:

  1. High Energy Laser (HEL) — coherent electromagnetic radiation in the optical or near-infrared spectrum, concentrated into a narrow beam that delivers thermal energy sufficient to heat, melt, ignite, or structurally weaken a target.

  2. High Power Microwave (HPM) — high-power radiofrequency pulses, typically in the 1–300 GHz range, that couple energy into electronic systems through antenna ports (front-door coupling) or structural apertures (back-door coupling), causing latch-up, burnout, or logic upset.

  3. Particle Beam Weapons (PBW) — streams of accelerated charged or neutralised particles whose kinetic and ionising energy interact directly with target material; primarily relevant in exo-atmospheric or near-space applications.

Table 35.1 provides a comparative overview of the three families.

Table 32.1. Comparative Overview of DEW Technology Families Parameter HEL HPM PBW Propagation speed \(c\) \(c\) \(\sim 0.8c\) Primary kill mechanism Thermal Electronic upset/burnout Ionisation/heating Effective atm. range 1–20 km 0.1–10 km \(<\)1 km (atmosphere) Weather sensitivity High Moderate Very high Magazine depth Deep (power-limited) Deep Limited (accelerator) Countermeasure Reflective coating, smoke Shielding, filtering Magnetic deflection Technology readiness TRL 8–9 (HEL) TRL 6–8 TRL 2–4

docs.title: 32.1.1 Speed-of-Light Delivery and Engagement Geometry
docs.text:
At tactical ranges of 1–20 km the propagation time for a laser or microwave beam is:

\[t_{\text{prop}} = \frac{R}{c} \approx \frac{10{,}000}{3 \times 10^8} \approx 33\;\mu\text{s}\tag{32.1}\]

This is negligible compared to any mechanical or electronic system latency, which typically lies in the millisecond regime. Consequently, no ballistic lead angle is required. For a target moving at \(V_T = 300\;\text{m/s}\) at range \(R = 5\;\text{km}\), the kinetic weapon would require a lead distance \(\Delta x = V_T \cdot t_{\text{flight}}\), where \(t_{\text{flight}}\) may be 10–20 s for a gun round. A DEW requires only accurate current pointing, dramatically simplifying the fire-control problem.

docs.title: 32.1.2 Advantages and Disadvantages of DEWs
docs.text:
Advantages:

  • Deep magazine: limited only by electrical power supply; a ship’s power plant or a vehicle generator can supply thousands of engagements;

  • Low per-shot cost: a \(5\,\text{USD}\) electricity cost per engagement for HEL, versus thousands to millions of dollars for kinetic interceptors;

  • Scalable effects: power and dwell time can be modulated — dazzle, damage, or destroy;

  • Precision: beam can be held on a specific sub-component (e.g., warhead fuze or optical seeker);

  • Near-zero collateral fragment hazard: no shrapnel.

Disadvantages:

  • Atmospheric propagation loss: molecular absorption, aerosol scattering, and thermal blooming attenuate the beam;

  • Thermal blooming: high-power beams heat the air, creating a refractive lens that defocuses the beam;

  • Beam jitter: platform vibration and atmospheric turbulence widen the effective spot;

  • Power supply mass and volume: multi-MW power conditioning plant required;

  • Dwell time requirement: target must be held in the beam for 1–10 s for thermal kill, requiring stable tracking.

docs.title: 32.2.1 Laser Physics
docs.text:
A laser (Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation) produces coherent, near-monochromatic electromagnetic radiation through the process of stimulated emission. When a photon of energy \(h\nu\) encounters an atom already in an excited state, it stimulates the emission of an identical photon — same frequency, phase, and direction — returning the atom to its ground state. Three conditions are necessary for laser operation:

  1. Population inversion: more atoms in the upper energy level \(N_2\) than the lower \(N_1\); required for net amplification rather than absorption.

  2. Gain medium: solid, liquid, gas, or semiconductor that supports population inversion; examples include Yb-doped silica glass fibre (1070 nm), Nd:YAG crystal (1064 nm), CO\(_2\) gas (10,600 nm), and chemical oxygen–iodine (1315 nm).

  3. Optical resonator (cavity): two mirrors (one partially transmissive) that recirculate photons through the gain medium, building coherent intensity; threshold condition requires round-trip gain to exceed round-trip loss.

The small-signal gain coefficient \(g_0\) of the medium is:

\[g_0 = \sigma_{21}\left(N_2 - \frac{g_2}{g_1}N_1\right)\tag{32.2}\]

where \(\sigma_{21}\) is the stimulated-emission cross-section, \(g_1\) and \(g_2\) are degeneracy factors, and \(N_1\), \(N_2\) are population densities. Lasing occurs when \(g_0 L > \alpha L + \ln(1/R_1 R_2)/2\), with cavity length \(L\), distributed loss \(\alpha\), and mirror reflectivities \(R_1\), \(R_2\).

docs.title: 32.2.2 Beam Divergence and Spot Size
docs.text:
A diffraction-limited Gaussian beam has a half-angle divergence:

\[\theta_{\text{diff}} = \frac{\lambda}{\pi w_0}\tag{32.3}\]

where \(\lambda\) is the wavelength and \(w_0\) is the beam waist radius. For a hard aperture of diameter \(D\), the far-field diffraction-limited full-angle divergence is approximated by the Rayleigh criterion:

\[\theta_{1/2} = 2.44\frac{\lambda}{D}\tag{32.4}\]

The 1/\(e^2\)-radius spot at range \(R\) for a perfect beam is:

\[r_{\text{spot}}(R) = \theta_{\text{diff}} \cdot R = \frac{\lambda R}{\pi w_0}\tag{32.5}\]

In practice, real beams are not diffraction-limited due to aberrations in the gain medium, optical elements, and the atmosphere. The beam quality factor \(M^2\) quantifies the departure:

\[\theta_{\text{real}} = M^2 \cdot \theta_{\text{diff}}\tag{32.6}\]

A perfect Gaussian beam has \(M^2 = 1.0\). High-quality fibre lasers achieve \(M^2 = 1.05\)–\(1.2\); slab amplifiers reach \(M^2 = 1.2\)–\(2.0\). Beam quality directly degrades irradiance on target, since irradiance scales as \(1/(M^2)^2\).

docs.title: 32.2.3 Irradiance on Target
docs.text:
The peak irradiance delivered to a target at range \(R\) by a laser of output power \(P\), accounting for beam quality \(M^2\), atmospheric transmission \(\eta_{\text{atm}}\), and optics transmission \(\eta_{\text{opt}}\), is:

\[I(R) = \frac{P \cdot \eta_{\text{atm}} \cdot \eta_{\text{opt}}}{\pi \left(\frac{M^2 \lambda R}{\pi w_0}\right)^2}\tag{32.7}\]

Substituting \(\theta = M^2 \lambda / (\pi w_0)\):

\[I(R) = \frac{P \cdot \eta_{\text{atm}} \cdot \eta_{\text{opt}}}{\pi (\theta R)^2}\tag{32.8}\]

For a 100 kW system with \(\theta = 2\;\mu\text{rad}\), \(\eta_{\text{atm}} = 0.8\), \(\eta_{\text{opt}} = 0.9\), at \(R = 5\,\text{km}\):

\[I = \frac{10^5 \times 0.8 \times 0.9}{\pi \times (2 \times 10^{-6} \times 5000)^2} = \frac{72000}{\pi \times 10^{-4}} \approx 2.3\;\text{MW/m}^2 = 230\;\text{W/cm}^2\tag{32.9}\]

Table 32.2 lists characteristic parameters for representative HEL systems.

Table 32.2. Representative High Energy Laser Parameters System Power \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}\) Aperture \(\boldsymbol{M^2}\) Platform Status HELIOS 60 kW 1070 nm 0.3 m 1.3 DDG destroyer IOC 2022 HEL TVD 50 kW 1070 nm 0.2 m 1.4 JLTV Demo 2023 Iron Beam 100 kW 1070 nm 0.35 m 1.2 Ground Oper. 2025 DragonFire 50 kW 1070 nm 0.25 m 1.3 Ship/Gnd Trials 2023 LAWS (AN/SEQ-3) 30 kW 1064 nm 0.15 m 1.5 LPD ship 2014 COIL ABL 1 MW 1315 nm 1.5 m 1.1 B-747 Retired 2012

docs.title: 32.2.4 Atmospheric Propagation
docs.text: The atmosphere attenuates and distorts a laser beam through four principal mechanisms:

docs.title: Molecular Absorption
docs.text:
Molecular absorption occurs when photons are absorbed by rotational-vibrational transitions of atmospheric gases. The primary absorbers are H\(_2\)O, CO\(_2\), and O\(_2\). The Beer–Lambert law gives the one-way atmospheric transmittance over path length \(R\):

\[T_{\text{atm}}(R) = \exp\!\left(-\int_0^R \alpha_{\text{abs}}(s)\,ds\right) \approx \exp(-\alpha_{\text{abs}} \cdot R)\tag{32.10}\]

where \(\alpha_{\text{abs}}\) is the wavelength-dependent absorption coefficient (m\(^{-1}\)). At 1070 nm (Yb fibre), \(\alpha_{\text{abs}} \approx 3 \times 10^{-5}\;\text{m}^{-1}\) in standard atmosphere, giving \(T_{\text{atm}} \approx 0.86\) at 5 km. Atmospheric windows with low absorption include \(1.0\)–\(1.1\;\mu\text{m}\), \(1.5\)–\(1.8\;\mu\text{m}\), \(3\)–\(5\;\mu\text{m}\), and \(8\)–\(12\;\mu\text{m}\).

docs.title: Mie and Rayleigh Scattering
docs.text:
Rayleigh scattering by molecules has a scattering coefficient \(\beta_R \propto \lambda^{-4}\), strongly penalising shorter wavelengths. Mie scattering by aerosols (fog, dust, haze) is approximately wavelength-independent in the \(1\;\mu\text{m}\) range. Total scattering extinction:

\[\alpha_{\text{scat}} = \beta_R + \beta_M\tag{32.11}\]

In clear atmosphere, aerosol extinction at 1 \(\mu\)m is approximately \(\alpha_{\text{scat}} \approx 10^{-4}\;\text{m}^{-1}\); in moderate haze it rises to \(5 \times 10^{-4}\;\text{m}^{-1}\), corresponding to a meteorological visibility of \(\sim\)8 km.

docs.title: Thermal Blooming
docs.text:
Thermal blooming occurs when the laser beam heats the air along its path, creating a temperature gradient and thus a refractive index gradient \(\Delta n \propto -\Delta T\). This acts as a negative (diverging) lens that spreads the beam, reducing peak irradiance. The dimensionless thermal distortion parameter \(N_D\) characterises the severity:

\[N_D = \frac{-2\alpha_{\text{abs}} P \frac{dn}{dT}}{\rho C_p V_{\perp} w_0 n_0}\tag{32.12}\]

where \(\rho\) is air density, \(C_p\) specific heat, \(V_\perp\) is the transverse wind speed, and \(dn/dT \approx -9.2 \times 10^{-7}\;\text{K}^{-1}\) for air at standard conditions. Blooming becomes significant when \(|N_D| > 1\). Wind \(V_\perp > 5\;\text{m/s}\) advects heated air out of the beam path, substantially reducing blooming — this is known as the slewing or wind clearing benefit.

docs.title: Atmospheric Turbulence and the Fried Parameter
docs.text:
Turbulence creates random refractive index fluctuations that scatter, tilt, and aberrate the beam. The Fried coherence length \(r_0\) describes the spatial scale over which the wavefront remains coherent:

\[r_0 = 0.185\left(\frac{\lambda^2}{C_n^2 R}\right)^{3/5}\tag{32.13}\]

where \(C_n^2\) is the refractive index structure constant (\(10^{-17}\)–\(10^{-13}\;\text{m}^{-2/3}\) depending on turbulence strength). For \(\lambda = 1070\;\text{nm}\), \(C_n^2 = 10^{-15}\;\text{m}^{-2/3}\), \(R = 5\;\text{km}\):

\[r_0 = 0.185\left(\frac{(1.07 \times 10^{-6})^2}{10^{-15} \times 5000}\right)^{3/5} \approx 0.185 \times (2.29 \times 10^{-4})^{0.6} \approx 5.2\;\text{cm}\tag{32.14}\]

When the aperture \(D > r_0\), turbulence-induced aberrations dominate the far-field spot size.

docs.title: 32.2.5 Adaptive Optics
docs.text:
Adaptive optics (AO) systems correct wavefront aberrations in real time to recover near-diffraction-limited performance. The three core subsystems are:

  1. Wavefront sensor (WFS): A Hartmann-Shack sensor divides the aperture into an array of microlenses, each focusing light onto a detector; local spot displacements measure the wavefront gradient \(\nabla W(x,y)\).

  2. Wavefront reconstructor: Least-squares inversion converts gradient measurements to phase map; typical update rate 1–10 kHz.

  3. Deformable mirror (DM): Piezoelectric or MEMS actuators deform a reflective surface to apply a conjugate phase correction \(\phi_{\text{DM}} = -W(x,y)\); typical actuator counts 100–5000.

Correction residual variance \(\sigma_{\text{AO}}^2\) in radians squared due to fitting error with \(N_{\text{act}}\) actuators across aperture \(D\):

\[\sigma_{\text{fit}}^2 = a_f \left(\frac{D}{N_{\text{act}}^{1/2} \cdot r_0}\right)^{5/3}\tag{32.15}\]

where \(a_f \approx 0.28\) for a square actuator grid. Strehl ratio after correction approximates:

\[S \approx \exp(-\sigma_{\text{total}}^2)\tag{32.16}\]

A Strehl ratio of \(S = 0.8\) corresponds to \(\sigma_{\text{total}} \approx 0.47\;\text{rad}\), typically achievable with a well-corrected AO system under moderate turbulence.

docs.title: 32.2.6 Target Interaction and Kill Mechanisms
docs.text:
The irradiance \(I\) at the target surface drives thermal heating. Surface temperature rise at the laser spot:

\[T_s(t) = \frac{2(1-\rho_r) I \sqrt{\alpha_{\text{th}} t}}{\sqrt{\pi} k_{\text{th}}}\tag{32.17}\]

where \(\rho_r\) is the surface reflectivity, \(\alpha_{\text{th}} = k_{\text{th}}/(\rho_m c_m)\) is thermal diffusivity, and \(k_{\text{th}}\) is thermal conductivity. Kill occurs when \(T_s\) exceeds either the melting temperature, the ignition temperature of a propellant, or the structural failure temperature of a composite. The kill fluence \(F_{\text{kill}}\) (J/cm\(^2\)) is the energy density required to achieve thermal kill:

\[F_{\text{kill}} = \frac{E_{\text{dep}}}{A_{\text{spot}}} = I \cdot t_{\text{dwell}}\tag{32.18}\]

Typical \(F_{\text{kill}}\) values:

  • Aluminium alloy structural panel (3 mm): \(\sim\)2–5 kJ/cm\(^2\)

  • Steel skin: \(\sim\)8–15 kJ/cm\(^2\)

  • Carbon fibre composite (drone body): \(\sim\)0.5–2 kJ/cm\(^2\)

  • Propellant ignition (rocket motor case): \(\sim\)0.1–0.5 kJ/cm\(^2\)

  • Optical seeker glass: \(\sim\)0.05–0.2 kJ/cm\(^2\)

docs.title: 32.2.7 Dwell Time Calculation
docs.text:
Required dwell time on target for thermal kill:

\[t_{\text{dwell}} = \frac{F_{\text{kill}} \cdot \pi r_{\text{spot}}^2(R)}{P \cdot \eta_{\text{total}}}\tag{32.19}\]

Substituting from Equation (32.8):

\[t_{\text{dwell}} = \frac{F_{\text{kill}}}{I(R)}\tag{32.20}\]

For a 100 kW laser at \(R = 3\;\text{km}\), \(\eta_{\text{total}} = 0.7\), \(\theta = 2\;\mu\text{rad}\): \(I = 2.5\;\text{kW/cm}^2\); for CFRP drone with \(F_{\text{kill}} = 1\;\text{kJ/cm}^2\): \(t_{\text{dwell}} = 0.4\;\text{s}\). This is tractable for a tracking system.

docs.title: Solid-State Lasers
docs.text:
Nd:YAG (1064 nm): Well-established; wall-plug efficiency \(\eta_{\text{wall}} \approx 10\)–\(15\%\); flash-lamp or diode-pumped; pulsed or CW; excellent for low-power applications.

Yb:YAG / Yb-fibre (1030–1080 nm): Currently dominant HEL technology. Diode-pumped; \(\eta_{\text{wall}} \approx 30\)–\(45\%\); inherently excellent beam quality in single-mode fibre; power scaled by coherent beam combination (CBC) or spectral beam combination (SBC) of many fibres.

Coherent Beam Combination: Multiple fibre amplifiers, each seeded from a master oscillator, are phase-locked using an adaptive phase controller. Output beams are combined at a beam splitter or diffractive element. For \(N\) fibres each of power \(P_f\) with phase error \(\sigma_\phi\):

\[P_{\text{combined}} = N^2 P_f \exp(-\sigma_\phi^2)\tag{32.21}\]

This quadratic scaling (for near-zero phase error) is the great advantage of CBC. Current demonstrations have combined up to 61 fibres with \(>\)90% combining efficiency.

docs.title: Chemical Lasers
docs.text:
COIL (Chemical Oxygen–Iodine Laser, 1315 nm): First megawatt-class HEL; used in the Airborne Laser (ABL) programme. Energy stored chemically; can achieve very high power without a large electrical plant. Primary disadvantage: corrosive chemicals (Cl\(_2\), H\(_2\)O\(_2\)), large logistics burden, effluent management.

HF/DF Laser (2700/3800 nm): Very high power density; operates in mid-IR where absorption is high; used in MIRACL (Mid-Infrared Advanced Chemical Laser), once the most powerful US laser at 2.2 MW; logistically demanding; no longer in active development.

docs.title: Free-Electron Laser (FEL)
docs.text:
The FEL passes a relativistic electron beam through a periodic magnetic field (undulator) to produce tunable coherent radiation. Wavelength is controllable by adjusting electron energy:

\[\lambda_{\text{FEL}} = \frac{\lambda_u}{2\gamma^2}\left(1 + \frac{K^2}{2}\right)\tag{32.22}\]

where \(\lambda_u\) is the undulator period, \(\gamma = E/(m_e c^2)\) is the Lorentz factor, and \(K = eB_0\lambda_u/(2\pi m_e c)\) is the undulator parameter. FELs are large, expensive, and not yet practical for tactical systems, but offer continuous wavelength tunability — the ability to select the atmospheric window with lowest attenuation on the fly.

docs.title: 32.3.1 USS Ponce AN/SEQ-3 LAWS
docs.text: The Laser Weapon System (LAWS) aboard USS Ponce was the first US Navy laser weapon deployed operationally in 2014. The solid-state, 30 kW system demonstrated the ability to engage small boats, UAVs, and mortar rounds in the Persian Gulf region. It used a commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) beam director and was integrated with the ship’s combat management system. Engagement of a small UAV at ranges up to 1 km was demonstrated, with burn-through times of 1–3 s.

docs.title: 32.3.2 HELIOS — High Energy Laser with Integrated Optical-dazzler and Surveillance
docs.text:
HELIOS, developed by Lockheed Martin, represents the first production HEL system for the US Navy’s Arleigh Burke–class destroyers (DDG-51 Flight III). Key specifications:

  • Laser power: 60 kW (upgradeable to 150 kW)

  • Wavelength: 1070 nm (Yb fibre)

  • Mission: C-UAS, C-USV (counter unmanned surface vessel), ISR (surveillance/dazzle mode)

  • Beam director: 0.3 m aperture; inertially stabilised gimbal

  • IOC: DDG-72 USS Dewey, 2022

  • Integration: Ship’s Aegis combat system; direct cueing from SPY-1D(V) radar

docs.title: 32.3.3 HEL TVD — High Energy Laser Tactical Vehicle Demonstrator
docs.text: Mounted on a Joint Light Tactical Vehicle (JLTV), the HEL TVD programme (50 kW, Raytheon/Kord Technologies) targets short-range air defence: UAVs, RPGs, and RAM (Rockets, Artillery, Mortars). The system demonstrated engagement of a 60 mm mortar round in 2023 trials, representing the hardest C-RAM intercept class for HEL due to the small RCS and short exposure time.

docs.title: 32.3.4 Iron Beam (Israel)
docs.text: Iron Beam, developed by Rafael and Elbit Systems, reached operational status in 2025 as the first HEL C-RAM system deployed in combat conditions. At 100 kW, it can engage rockets at 7–10 km range and drones at 4–7 km. During the 2023 Gaza conflict, Iron Dome intercepted  \(90\%\) of incoming rockets; Iron Beam is designed to handle the lower-cost saturation attacks that challenge kinetic interceptors. Cost per engagement is approximately $5 (electricity), versus $50,000–$100,000 per Iron Dome Tamir interceptor.

docs.title: 32.3.5 DragonFire (United Kingdom)
docs.text: DragonFire is a consortium programme involving Leonardo UK, MBDA, and QinetiQ, funded by the UK MOD. After successful trials at BUTEC (British Underwater Test and Evaluation Centre) range in 2023, the 50 kW system demonstrated engagement of aerial targets at ranges up to 3 km. The programme targets ship and ground vehicle integration, with service entry planned for 2027–2030.

docs.title: 32.4.1 HPM Principles
docs.text:
High Power Microwave weapons deliver nanosecond-to-microsecond pulses of radiofrequency energy at peak powers of 10 MW–10 GW into a target’s electronic subsystems. Damage is through:

  • Front-door coupling: Energy enters via the target’s own receive antenna; amplified by antenna gain; can destroy receiver front-ends with relatively modest field strengths.

  • Back-door coupling: Energy couples through structural apertures — seams, cable penetrations, vents — and propagates as a conducted or radiated disturbance onto circuit boards.

The susceptibility threshold for semiconductor junctions is expressed in terms of electric field \(E_{\text{thresh}}\) or power density \(S_{\text{thresh}}\):

\[P_{\text{damage}} = \frac{E_{\text{thresh}}^2}{Z_0} \cdot A_{\text{eff}}\tag{32.23}\]

where \(Z_0 = 377\;\Omega\) is the impedance of free space and \(A_{\text{eff}}\) is the effective receiving aperture of the coupling path.

docs.title: Magnetron
docs.text: The magnetron is a crossed-field device (perpendicular electric and magnetic fields) that produces high-power microwave pulses. Widely used in radar and industrial applications; wall-plug efficiency 50–70%; pulsed peak power 1 kW–5 MW; frequency 1–18 GHz. Magnetrons are coherent only within a single pulse — they lack phase memory pulse-to-pulse.

docs.title: Klystron
docs.text: The klystron is a linear-beam amplifier driven by an RF input signal; it produces very high-power, coherent output at fixed frequencies. Used in large radar transmitters and particle accelerators; peak power up to 100 MW; efficiency 40–60%.

docs.title: Vircator (Virtual Cathode Oscillator)
docs.text:
The vircator is a compact, single-pulse HPM source requiring no external magnetic field. A high-current electron beam is injected into a resonant cavity; when the space-charge limit is exceeded, a virtual cathode forms and oscillates, radiating at a frequency:

\[f_{\text{vircator}} \approx \frac{\omega_p}{2\pi} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{n_e e^2}{\epsilon_0 m_e}}\tag{32.24}\]

where \(n_e\) is electron density, \(e\) electron charge, and \(m_e\) electron mass. Peak powers of 1–10 GW are achievable in a package of \(<\)50 kg, making the vircator attractive for missile-deliverable HPM payloads. Efficiency is typically 1–5%.

docs.title: CHAMP (Counter-electronics High-powered Microwave Advanced Missile Project)
docs.text:
CHAMP, developed by Boeing for AFRL, is a cruise-missile-based HPM weapon. The weapon carries a repetitively-pulsed HPM source powered by a turbine generator from the JP-10 fuel supply. In a 2012 demonstration at the Utah Test and Training Range, CHAMP made ten passes over seven targets, successfully neutralising the electronics at each. The weapon then self-destructed. CHAMP demonstrated:

  • Multiple target engagement in a single sortie

  • Non-kinetic defeat of hardened facilities

  • Standoff engagement at cruise missile range (500–1000 km)

  • No collateral structural damage

docs.title: Active Denial System (ADS)
docs.text:
The ADS operates at 95 GHz, where the millimetre-wave radiation is absorbed in the outermost 0.4 mm of human skin (the epidermis), producing an intense heating sensation without penetrating to underlying tissue. Parameters:

  • Frequency: 95 GHz (3.16 mm wavelength)

  • Power: 100 kW (system); 10–50 kW at aperture

  • Beam divergence: \(\sim\)0.5° (Gaussian)

  • Effective range: 500–1000 m

  • Skin penetration: \(\delta = \sqrt{2/(\omega\mu\sigma)} \approx 0.4\;\text{mm}\) at 95 GHz

  • Pain onset: \(T_{\text{skin}} > 44^{\circ}\text{C}\) after \(\sim\)3 s exposure

The ADS is classified as a non-lethal weapon for crowd control. It was deployed to Afghanistan in 2010 but not operationally used; the perception of the weapon as a pain ray made it politically sensitive.

Table 32.3. HPM System Comparison System Freq. Peak Power Effect Platform Status CHAMP 1–3 GHz \(>\)1 GW (pulse) Electronics burnout Cruise missile Demo 2012 ADS 95 GHz 100 kW Non-lethal pain Vehicle Limited fielding THOR 3 GHz \(>\)100 MW C-UAS electronics Ground Demo 2020 EMP bomb 1–10 GHz \(>\)10 GW Area EMP Gravity bomb Classified Vircator warhead 1–5 GHz 1–10 GW Facility electronics Warhead R&D

docs.title: 32.4.4 THOR — Tactical High-power Operational Responder
docs.text: THOR, developed by AFRL, is a containerised ground-based HPM system designed specifically for counter-UAS applications. A single HPM pulse is sufficient to cause electronic upset or burnout in a small drone’s flight controller. THOR can engage multiple drones simultaneously within its beam footprint — a key advantage over single-track HEL systems. THOR underwent desert environment testing in 2020 and was loaned to the US Air Force for base perimeter defence evaluation.

docs.title: 32.4.5 Coupling Analysis
docs.text:
For a target at range \(R\) in the main beam of an HPM antenna with gain \(G_t\):

\[S_{\text{target}} = \frac{P_t G_t}{4\pi R^2}\tag{32.25}\]

Power coupled into a target aperture of effective area \(A_{\text{coup}}\):

\[P_{\text{coup}} = S_{\text{target}} \cdot A_{\text{coup}} = \frac{P_t G_t A_{\text{coup}}}{4\pi R^2}\tag{32.26}\]

For \(P_t = 1\;\text{GW}\), \(G_t = 30\;\text{dB} = 1000\), \(R = 1\;\text{km}\), \(A_{\text{coup}} = 0.01\;\text{m}^2\):

\[P_{\text{coup}} = \frac{10^9 \times 10^3 \times 0.01}{4\pi \times 10^6} = 796\;\text{W}\tag{32.27}\]

This is far above the semiconductor burnout threshold of milliwatts to watts, indicating that HPM readily defeats unshielded electronics at tactical ranges.

docs.title: 32.5.1 Principles
docs.text:
Particle beam weapons accelerate charged particles — electrons, protons, or heavier ions — through a particle accelerator to relativistic velocities. At the target, the beam deposits energy through:

  • Coulomb interactions: elastic and inelastic scattering; produces ionisation, excitation, and radiation damage in semiconductors and biological tissue;

  • Nuclear interactions: for protons and ions, nuclear spallation at high enough energies can disrupt nuclear material;

  • Bremsstrahlung radiation: electrons produce X-ray secondary radiation in dense targets.

The range of a proton in air (the Bragg curve) at kinetic energy \(E_k\) (MeV) follows approximately:

\[R_{\text{proton}} \approx 0.0022 \cdot E_k^{1.77}\;\text{m (in air at STP)}\tag{32.28}\]

A 100 MeV proton has a range of \(\sim\)8 m in air — far too short for weaponisable beam weapons in atmosphere.

docs.title: 32.5.2 Neutral Particle Beam (NPB)
docs.text: In space, where there is no atmosphere, a charged particle beam can propagate freely, though space-charge repulsion eventually spreads the beam. The NPB concept involves accelerating ions to high energy, then stripping an electron to produce a neutral atom beam that is unaffected by magnetic fields but propagates in a straight line. The SDI (Strategic Defense Initiative) programme in the 1980s developed NPB concepts for boost-phase intercept of ICBMs in mid-course. The Alpha Project demonstrated a 1 MeV hydrogen neutral beam. No operational space-based NPB system has been deployed.

docs.title: 32.5.3 Current Status
docs.text:
Particle beam weapons remain at TRL 2–4. The fundamental challenges are:

  1. Accelerator mass: linear accelerators producing 100 MeV beams weigh tens of tonnes;

  2. Atmospheric propagation: utterly impractical below 80 km altitude;

  3. Power: continuous high-energy beams require hundreds of megawatts;

  4. Beam pointing: relativistic beam deflection requires large superconducting magnets.

docs.title: 32.6.1 Slant Range for Ship-Based Engagement
docs.text:
For a ship-based HEL system at height \(H\) above the waterline engaging a target at elevation angle \(\varepsilon\):

\[R_{\text{slant}} = \frac{H}{\sin\varepsilon}\tag{32.29}\]

For a sea-skimming missile at 5 m altitude, hull height 15 m, and minimum detection range 10 km: \(\varepsilon = \arcsin(15/10{,}000) \approx 0.086°\) — very shallow, requiring a highly stabilised low-elevation beam director.

docs.title: 32.6.2 Effective Spot Size with Jitter
docs.text:
Beam wander due to platform vibration and atmospheric tip-tilt introduces an additional pointing error \(\sigma_j\) (rad). The effective irradiance-equivalent spot radius is:

\[r_{\text{eff}} = \sqrt{r_{\text{diff}}^2 + (\sigma_j R)^2}\tag{32.30}\]

where \(r_{\text{diff}} = M^2 \lambda R / (\pi w_0)\) is the diffraction-limited radius. Jitter reduces peak irradiance:

\[I_{\text{jitter}} = I_{\text{ideal}} \cdot \exp\!\left(-\frac{2\sigma_j^2 R^2}{r_{\text{diff}}^2}\right) \quad \text{(for } \sigma_j R \ll r_{\text{diff}}\text{)}\tag{32.31}\]

For \(\sigma_j = 1\;\mu\text{rad}\) (achievable with inertially stabilised beam director), \(R = 5\;\text{km}\), \(r_{\text{diff}} = 10\;\text{cm}\): \(\sigma_j R = 5\;\text{mm}\), which is small compared to \(r_{\text{diff}}\), so jitter is manageable. At longer ranges or with higher jitter (ship in sea-state 4), \(\sigma_j\) may rise to 5–10 \(\mu\)rad, significantly degrading irradiance.

docs.title: 32.6.3 Tracking Slew Rate Requirement
docs.text:
The fire-control system must track the target throughout the dwell time. The required angular slew rate:

\[\dot{\theta}_{\text{track}} = \frac{V_T}{R}\tag{32.32}\]

For a drone at \(V_T = 50\;\text{m/s}\), \(R = 2\;\text{km}\): \(\dot{\theta} = 25\;\text{mrad/s}\), easily achieved by modern gimbals (\(>\)3 rad/s). For a fast jet at \(V_T = 300\;\text{m/s}\), \(R = 1\;\text{km}\): \(\dot{\theta} = 300\;\text{mrad/s} = 17°/\text{s}\), requiring a fast-slewing gimbal and high control bandwidth.

docs.title: 32.6.4 Power Scaling Laws
docs.text:
From Equation (32.8), irradiance at range \(R\) scales as:

\[I \propto \frac{P}{R^2}\tag{32.33}\]

Halving the dwell time requires doubling \(I\), which requires doubling \(P\) (at fixed range). Halving the range at constant power quadruples \(I\), quartering the dwell time. These scaling laws drive the operational tactic of closing range before engaging with HEL.

docs.title: 32.7 Power Systems for Directed Energy Weapons
32.7.1 Wall-Plug Efficiency and Waste Heat
docs.text:
For a laser of wall-plug efficiency \(\eta_{\text{wall}}\), the thermal waste heat per unit of laser output power:

\[P_{\text{waste}} = P_{\text{laser}}\left(\frac{1}{\eta_{\text{wall}}} - 1\right)\tag{32.34}\]

For Yb fibre at \(\eta_{\text{wall}} = 0.40\) and \(P_{\text{laser}} = 100\;\text{kW}\):

\[P_{\text{waste}} = 10^5 \times (2.5 - 1) = 150\;\text{kW}\tag{32.35}\]

This 150 kW of waste heat must be managed by a thermal management system (TMS). At sea, seawater provides a convenient heat sink. For ground vehicles, the TMS is a major mass and volume driver.

docs.title: 32.7.2 Pulsed Power Systems
docs.text:
HPM weapons require very high instantaneous power (gigawatts) for very short durations (nanoseconds–microseconds). This is achieved through pulsed power systems:

  • Capacitor bank: stores energy \(U = \frac{1}{2}CV^2\); typical parameters: \(C = 10\;\text{mF}\), \(V = 100\;\text{kV}\), \(U = 50\;\text{kJ}\); switched by spark gaps or solid-state switches;

  • Marx generator: charges \(N\) capacitors in parallel, discharges in series; output voltage \(NV_0\); achieves \(>\)1 MV at \(>\)100 kJ in compact geometry;

  • Flux compression generator (FCG): single-use explosive-driven device; compresses magnetic flux to produce \(>\)100 MJ pulse; used in EMP bombs.

Pulse compression and forming: a pulse-forming network (PFN) shapes the discharge into a rectangular pulse of impedance-matched duration. For a transmission-line PFN of impedance \(Z_0\), pulse duration \(\tau = 2l/v_p\), where \(l\) is the electrical length and \(v_p\) is the propagation speed.

docs.title: 32.7.3 Continuous Power — Ship and Vehicle
docs.text:
For shipboard HEL, the vessel’s gas turbine or combined diesel-and-gas (CODAG) plant typically produces 30–100 MW. A 100 kW laser drawing 250 kW at the wall adds \(<\)1% to total ship load — entirely manageable. For ground vehicles, a JLTV-class platform produces \(\sim\)40 kW; a 50 kW HEL requires a dedicated generator trailer or next-generation vehicle with enhanced power generation. The US Army’s XM1299 Extended-Range Cannon Artillery (ERCA) programme considered a dedicated prime-mover for HEL power.

Table 32.4. DEW Power System Requirements Summary Platform DEW Power Wall-plug draw Waste heat Power source DDG destroyer 60 kW HEL 150 kW 90 kW Ship turbine DDG destroyer 100 kW HEL 250 kW 150 kW Ship turbine JLTV vehicle 50 kW HEL 125 kW 75 kW Generator trailer Cruise missile 1 GW HPM (pulse) N/A (pulsed) N/A Capacitor/Marx Ground base 100 kW HEL 250 kW 150 kW Grid/diesel gen B-747 (ABL) 1 MW COIL N/A (chemical) 3 MW (pumping) Chemical reaction

docs.title: 32.8.1 Reflective Coatings
docs.text: High-reflectivity coatings reduce the fraction of incident laser energy absorbed. Gold (\(\rho_r \approx 0.98\) at 1  extmum) and silver (\(\rho_r \approx 0.96\) at 1  extmum) are effective. However, at a sustained irradiance of 100 W/cm\(^2\), even 2% absorption equates to 2 W/cm\(^2\) deposited — sufficient for thermal damage over time. Furthermore, ablation of the coating itself eventually exposes the substrate.

docs.title: 32.8.2 Spinning and Tumbling
docs.text:
Inducing spin or tumble in the target distributes the laser energy around the circumference rather than concentrating it at one spot. For a cylinder of radius \(r\) and surface thermal conductivity \(k\), the reduction in peak temperature rise is approximately:

\[\frac{\Delta T_{\text{spin}}}{\Delta T_{\text{static}}} \approx \sqrt{\frac{\alpha_{\text{th}}}{r^2 \omega_{\text{spin}}}}\tag{32.36}\]

At high spin rate the target effectively sees a time-averaged irradiance, reducing the peak temperature rise. This is particularly relevant for spin-stabilised rockets.

docs.title: 32.8.3 Obscurants and Smoke
docs.text:
Aerosol clouds of graphite, aluminium flakes, or metallic foil chaff scatter and absorb laser energy. Attenuation in a dense smoke cloud can exceed 10 dB (90% energy loss) per 100 m. The extinction coefficient of a cloud of spherical particles of radius \(a\), number density \(n\), and extinction efficiency \(Q_{\text{ext}}\) is:

\[\mu_{\text{ext}} = n \cdot Q_{\text{ext}} \cdot \pi a^2\tag{32.37}\]

Modern obscurant grenades (e.g., L8 on UK Challenger 2 MBT) deploy within 0.5 s and create a cloud effective against 1–12 \(\mu\)m wavelengths. However, obscurants also blind the target’s own sensors.

docs.title: 32.8.4 Speed as a Counter-DEW Measure
docs.text:
For a fast-moving target at velocity \(V_T\) at range \(R\), the beam slew rate required is \(\dot\theta = V_T/R\). At extreme approach velocities, dwell time is limited by the finite length of the engagement window. For a Mach 3 (1020 m/s) target crossing the laser’s lethal range from \(R_{\text{outer}} = 5\;\text{km}\) to \(R_{\text{inner}} = 1\;\text{km}\):

\[t_{\text{window}} = \frac{R_{\text{outer}} - R_{\text{inner}}}{V_T} = \frac{4000}{1020} \approx 3.9\;\text{s}\tag{32.38}\]

If the target requires 5 s of continuous dwell at the beam irradiance achievable at those ranges, the laser cannot complete the engagement — speed is an effective countermeasure.

docs.title: 32.8.5 Ablative Shielding
docs.text:
Ablative materials absorb laser energy through pyrolysis (chemical decomposition) rather than conduction. The ablation rate limits temperature rise:

\[\dot{m}_{\text{abl}} = \frac{I \cdot A_{\text{spot}}}{L_{\text{abl}}}\tag{32.39}\]

where \(L_{\text{abl}}\) (J/kg) is the ablation enthalpy (latent heat plus decomposition energy). Carbon–phenolic ablators have \(L_{\text{abl}} \approx 10^7\;\text{J/kg}\), providing effective protection at moderate fluences, at the cost of added mass.

docs.title: 32.9 Future Directions in Directed Energy Weapons
32.9.1 Multi-Kilowatt to Megawatt Scaling
docs.text:
The path to megawatt-class solid-state HEL involves:

  1. Coherent Beam Combination (CBC): Phase-locking hundreds of fibre amplifiers; each fibre limited to \(\sim\)3–5 kW before nonlinear effects (stimulated Brillouin scattering) degrade beam quality;

  2. Spectral Beam Combination (SBC): Combining beams at different wavelengths with a diffraction grating; no phase-locking required; multi-wavelength output;

  3. Next-generation gain media: Tm-fibre (2 \(\mu\)m), Ho-YAG (2.1 \(\mu\)m) for atmospheric window matching.

docs.title: 32.9.2 Tactical High Energy Laser (THEL) and IRON BEAM Succession
docs.text: Post-2025, the Israel MOD plans integration of Iron Beam into a multi-tier air defence architecture alongside Iron Dome, David’s Sling, and Arrow. The key technology push is to extend HEL range to 10–15 km while maintaining kill probability \(>\)95% against salvo attacks of 10+ simultaneous targets.

docs.title: 32.9.3 DEW for Anti-Satellite (ASAT) Applications
docs.text: Ground-based DEW has been used for satellite dazzling (temporary blinding of imaging sensors) since the 1970s. Permanent damage to satellite solar panels or sensors requires fluences of \(>\)0.1 kJ/cm\(^2\) through the full atmospheric column (\(\sim\)80 km effective zenith path). Adaptive optics on large-aperture telescopes (1–4 m) can deliver this level under good seeing conditions.

docs.title: 32.9.4 Integration with AI Fire Control
docs.text:
Modern DEW fire-control systems incorporate AI-based algorithms for:

  • Real-time atmospheric propagation estimation (using guide-star or point-ahead angle data);

  • Predictive aimpoint selection (targeting the most vulnerable sub-system);

  • Multi-target prioritisation in swarm engagements;

  • Engagement authority management (human-machine interface for Rules of Engagement compliance).

docs.title: 32.10 Summary
docs.text:
Directed energy weapons represent a transformative technology in the aerospace and defence sector. High Energy Laser systems have crossed the threshold from laboratory demonstrations to operational deployment, with HEL weapons now defending naval vessels and fixed sites in multiple countries. High Power Microwave weapons have demonstrated the ability to non-kinetically neutralise electronics over wide areas. Both technologies address a critical cost asymmetry: a $5 laser shot versus a $100,000 missile interceptor fundamentally changes the economics of air defence against mass drone and rocket attacks.

Critical remaining challenges are: improving atmospheric propagation in adverse weather; reducing SWaP (Size, Weight, and Power) of the power conditioning and thermal management systems; and achieving multi-target, multi-layer DEW architectures that can handle saturation attacks by large drone swarms. The next decade will likely see 300 kW–1 MW HEL systems deployed on major surface combatants, providing a qualitative step change in air defence capability.

docs.title: 33.1 Introduction: The Counter-UAS Challenge
docs.text:
The proliferation of unmanned aerial systems (UAS) across commercial, recreational, and military domains has created an asymmetric threat of unprecedented scale. A decade ago, air defence doctrine focused almost exclusively on crewed aircraft and ballistic missiles. Today, operational commanders must simultaneously defend against a threat spectrum ranging from sub-250 g toy quadrotors carrying improvised explosives to military-grade group 4/5 unmanned combat aerial vehicles (UCAVs) with precision strike capability, and — most challenging of all — coordinated swarms of hundreds to thousands of autonomous vehicles executing distributed attack profiles.

Counter-UAS (C-UAS) is the collective term for all measures, systems, and operational concepts designed to detect, identify, track, and defeat hostile unmanned systems. The discipline is characterised by extreme cost asymmetry, multi-domain complexity (kinetic, electronic, cyber, legal), and the need to operate in densely populated civil environments where collateral damage constraints are severe.

docs.title: 33.1.1 Threat Taxonomy
docs.text:
The UAS threat spans five DoD Group classifications:

Table 33.1. DoD UAS Group Classification and Counter-UAS Implications Group Max GW (kg) Alt (ft AGL) Speed (kt) RCS (m\(^2\)) C-UAS Challenge 1 \(<\) 9 \(<\) 1200 \(<\) 100 0.001–0.01 Micro-Doppler; clutter; no ADS-B 2 9.5–25 \(<\) 3500 \(<\) 250 0.01–0.1 Low RCS; speed; small target 3 25–600 \(<\) FL180 \(<\) 250 0.1–1.0 Manoeuvre; standoff payload 4 \(<\) 600 \(>\) FL180 Any 0.5–5.0 Similar to crewed aircraft 5 \(>\) 600 \(>\) FL180 Any 5–50 UCAV; stealth possible

Groups 1–3 represent the most challenging C-UAS problem: their small size yields radar cross-sections of \(0.001\)–\(1.0\) m\(^2\), compared to \(1\)–\(10\) m\(^2\) for fighter aircraft. Combined with flight at low altitude in terrain and urban clutter, and with no cooperative identification, they are exceptionally difficult to detect and engage.

docs.title: 33.1.2 Attack Vectors
docs.text:
Hostile UAS exploit multiple attack vectors:

  1. Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance (ISR): Persistent overhead observation of positions, routes, and activities; enables accurate mortar/artillery fire correction.

  2. Precision payload delivery: Dropping grenades, IEDs, or chemical/biological agents from altitude; highly effective when defender’s perimeter sensor coverage is incomplete.
